02-23.title: George Frideric Handel went blind writing music
02-23.story:
Handel continued composing and performing after losing his sight, dictating revisions from memory. Audiences reported he still improvised organ solos flawlessly.

The blindness came on gradually from around 1751, during work on the oratorio Jephtha, and he noted the difficulty in the manuscript itself. Several operations by the surgeon John Taylor — a travelling oculist of dubious competence who also operated on Bach, with equally poor results — made things worse rather than better.

He kept working. Revisions were dictated to assistants, and he continued to appear publicly at the organ, where his improvisation had always been a substantial part of the draw. Accounts from the period describe the playing as undiminished, which is plausible: keyboard improvisation is largely a matter of internalised pattern and hearing, and sight contributes less to it than one might assume.

By this point he had been in London for forty years and had shifted his entire business model from Italian opera to English oratorio, which turned out to be both artistically productive and commercially necessary.

He died in 1759 and was buried in Westminster Abbey with a reported three thousand mourners — an extraordinary turnout for a composer, and an indication of how thoroughly a German-born musician had become a British institution.
facts: He was buried in Westminster Abbey with 3,000 mourners
His late oratorios were largely written without being able to see the page

02-24.title: The Sugarhill Gang were not a real group
02-24.story:
Label owner Sylvia Robinson assembled three unknowns after hearing rap at a party. One was auditioned while working at a pizzeria.

Robinson had a long career behind her — a hit as half of Mickey & Sylvia, then a label owner — and she recognised a commercial opportunity that the people actually making the music had not yet monetised. Rap existed in parks, community centres, and clubs across the Bronx and Harlem, and none of it was on record.

Rather than sign an established crew, she assembled a group. Big Bank Hank was working at a pizzeria in New Jersey when he was auditioned, and the three members had no standing in the scene whatsoever.

The part that still rankles is the rhymes. Hank's verse draws on lyrics by Grandmaster Caz of the Cold Crush Brothers, who by most accounts lent him a notebook and received no credit and no royalties. One of the most commercially significant records in the genre's history contains uncredited work by a man who never saw a penny from it.

That set a pattern the industry repeated for years: outsiders capturing the commercial value of a form while the people who built it watched. The record opened the door, and a lot of the people who had been standing at it were not the ones who walked through.
facts: Big Bank Hank reportedly borrowed rhymes from Grandmaster Caz
Caz received no credit or royalties for lines used on the record

02-25.title: George Harrison's sitar lesson changed rock
02-25.story:
Harrison studied under Ravi Shankar, who insisted he learn properly rather than use the instrument as decoration. Indian modes then filtered into Western pop.

Shankar was a serious classical musician with no particular interest in Western pop and, by his own account, no clear idea who the Beatles were when they were introduced. His condition for teaching was that Harrison approach the instrument as a discipline — sitting properly, learning scales and rhythmic cycles — rather than treating it as an exotic sound to layer onto a rock record.

Harrison had already used sitar decoratively on 'Norwegian Wood', which he later described as fairly rudimentary. The study that followed produced something different: 'Within You Without You' is built on Indian classical structure, features no other Beatle, and uses tabla and dilruba players rather than the band.

The wider consequence was a vocabulary shift. Drones, modal scales that do not resolve the way Western harmony does, and long non-developmental forms entered rock and stayed, feeding directly into psychedelia and later into minimalism's popular reception.

It also opened a long and complicated conversation about appropriation that has not closed. Shankar himself was ambivalent, welcoming the attention to Indian music and frequently exasperated by audiences who treated a centuries-old tradition as a lifestyle accessory.
facts: Shankar initially had no idea who the Beatles were
'Within You Without You' features no other Beatle

02-26.title: Fats Domino sold more records than anyone but Elvis
02-26.story:
The New Orleans pianist's rolling triplets defined early rock piano. He recorded almost everything at Cosimo Matassa's tiny J&M studio.

The triplet figure — the right hand rolling three notes to the beat against a steady backbeat — became the default vocabulary for rock and roll piano, and it descends from New Orleans barrelhouse and boogie traditions that predate the term rock and roll by decades. Domino did not invent it. He made it the standard.

J&M Recording was in the back of an appliance shop on Rampart Street, and it was small enough that the room itself shaped the sound: a natural slapback, limited separation, and a house band of extraordinary New Orleans musicians who played on an enormous share of the era's records. Little Richard, Lloyd Price, and Ray Charles all cut there.

Domino's commercial position in the fifties is frequently understated. He sold more records than any rock and roll artist of the decade other than Elvis Presley, and he did it while touring a segregated country under conditions that put him in genuine danger.

He refused to leave New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 and was initially reported missing before being rescued from his flooded Lower Ninth Ward home. He died there in 2017.
facts: The studio was in the back of an appliance shop
Its cramped room created the signature slapback sound

02-27.title: Brooklyn's Prospect Park bandshell started a free summer tradition
02-27.story:
Celebrate Brooklyn began as a modest neighborhood series and grew into one of America's longest-running free outdoor festivals, minutes from Ditmas Park.

The founding context matters. New York in the late seventies was near-bankrupt, park maintenance had collapsed, and Prospect Park had a reputation for danger that kept a lot of people out of it. Programming free concerts at the bandshell was partly cultural and partly a deliberate effort to give the surrounding neighbourhoods a reason to walk back into the park after dark.

It worked, slowly, and the series has now run for more than four decades — among the longest-running free outdoor performance festivals in the country. The booking has stayed unusually broad: Afrobeat, salsa, indie rock, jazz, classical, film screenings with live scores, and a steady presence of Brooklyn artists alongside international names.

The bandshell sits at the Prospect Park West and Ninth Street corner, walkable from Ditmas Park, Flatbush, Windsor Terrace, and Park Slope, which is most of why it functions as a genuinely shared event rather than one neighbourhood's.

Entry remains free for the majority of the programme, with a small number of benefit shows ticketed to fund the rest. That model is the whole argument: the thing works because nobody has to decide whether it is worth the money.
facts: It launched partly to bring people back into the park after a rough decade
Acts range from Afrobeat legends to local Brooklyn bands

02-28.title: The Moog synthesizer needed a hit to be taken seriously
02-28.story:
Wendy Carlos's 'Switched-On Bach' proved the Moog could make music, not just noise. It became one of the best-selling classical records ever.

The instrument had been available for a few years and was largely regarded as a laboratory curiosity or a source of sound effects. Robert Moog's modular system was difficult to use, unstable in tuning, and had no obvious repertoire, and the electronic music being made with comparable equipment was largely academic and forbidding.

Carlos's choice of Bach was strategic. Bach's writing is contrapuntal, precisely notated, and instrumentally neutral — it has been transcribed for every ensemble imaginable for two centuries — so realising it electronically was a demonstration rather than a provocation.

The labour involved was enormous. The Moog was monophonic, playing one note at a time, so every voice in a fugue had to be recorded separately and layered, with tuning drifting between passes and requiring constant correction. Carlos worked with Rachel Elkind on the production across many months.

It sold in the hundreds of thousands and became one of the best-selling classical records ever released, which put the synthesizer in front of musicians who had dismissed it.

Carlos went on to score A Clockwork Orange and Tron, and is a trans woman who came out publicly in 1979, at considerable personal cost.
facts: Each note had to be played and layered one at a time
The instrument was monophonic, so chords required many passes

02-29.title: Leap day gave Gioachino Rossini a rare birthday
02-29.story:
Born on 29 February, Rossini joked he only aged once every four years. He retired from opera at 37 and spent decades writing small pieces and cooking.

The retirement is the genuinely strange part. Rossini was the most successful opera composer in Europe, had written roughly forty operas by his late thirties, and then stopped almost entirely after William Tell in 1829, living another thirty-nine years without producing another one. Explanations have included illness, exhaustion, wealth, and simple disinclination, and none of them fully account for it.

He wrote fast when he was writing. The Barber of Seville was completed in something like three weeks, and he was notorious for reusing overtures between operas when the deadline demanded it — the Barber's overture had already served two previous works.

What he did instead was cook and write small pieces. He was a serious gastronome, several dishes carry his name, and the late piano and vocal miniatures he produced for private performance were collected under the title Sins of Old Age. Several are named after food.

He died in 1868 and left the bulk of a substantial fortune to endow a music conservatory in his home town of Pesaro, which still operates.

By his own count he had lived about nineteen birthdays.
facts: He wrote 'The Barber of Seville' in about three weeks
He named several compositions after food

03-01.title: Chopin and the piano that never left the room
03-01.story:
Chopin wrote almost exclusively for solo piano, rarely performing in large halls because his playing was too quiet. He preferred salons of a few dozen listeners.

The scale was a genuine limitation rather than an affectation. Contemporaries who heard him in a small room described the playing as extraordinary; those who heard him in a concert hall complained they could barely make it out. He gave roughly thirty public concerts in his entire life, which for a musician of his stature in the nineteenth century is almost nothing, and made most of his income teaching wealthy students.

That setting shaped the music. Writing for a room of forty people rather than a hall of two thousand permits an enormous dynamic range at the quiet end, and Chopin's scores are full of markings that only make sense if the listener is close enough to hear a whisper.

His rubato — the elastic stretching of tempo within a phrase — was described by his pupils with a specific image: the left hand keeps strict time while the right hand moves freely around it, like a tree standing still while its leaves sway. Most modern performances loosen both hands, which is a different effect entirely.

He was born in Poland, left at twenty, and never returned. Almost everything he wrote was composed in exile.
facts: He gave roughly 30 public concerts in his entire life
His pupils described his rubato as 'the tree keeps time, the leaves sway'

03-02.title: Lou Reed recorded an album designed to be unlistenable
03-02.story:
'Metal Machine Music' was 64 minutes of guitar feedback. Reed said it was sincere; the label suspected he was escaping a contract.

The record contains no rhythm, no melody, and no vocals — four sides of guitar feedback produced by leaning instruments against amplifiers at different tunings and recording the resulting oscillations, then layering and varispeeding the tapes. It was released on RCA as a commercial album, in the racks, at full price.

Returns were extraordinary. Retailers sent it back in volume, RCA withdrew it within weeks, and it has a decent claim to being the most returned major-label release of the decade. Reed's public statements were contradictory in a way that was probably deliberate: at times he insisted it was serious music with classical antecedents, at times he seemed to enjoy the damage.

The contractual theory has never been proven and remains plausible. He owed the label albums and had reasons to want out.

What is not in doubt is the afterlife. The record became a foundational reference for noise music and industrial, and in 2002 the German ensemble Zeitkratzer transcribed sections of it for acoustic instruments and performed it as scored contemporary music, with Reed appearing on stage.

A joke, a breach of contract, and a genuine piece of work — possibly all three at once.
facts: It was returned by buyers in enormous numbers
Decades later, an ensemble performed it as scored contemporary music

03-03.title: 'The Star-Spangled Banner' was set to a drinking song
03-03.story:
Francis Scott Key's poem was matched to 'To Anacreon in Heaven', a British social club tune notorious for its difficult octave-and-a-half range.

The Anacreontic Society was a gentlemen's musical club in London, and the song was its constitutional anthem — a genial celebration of wine and music named after the Greek poet Anacreon. Setting a patriotic American poem to a British club tune during a war against Britain is a piece of irony that the period seems not to have found troubling.

The range is the practical problem. The melody spans an octave and a half, which is comfortable for a trained singer and brutal for anyone else, and it puts its highest note on the phrase 'land of the free' — the exact moment when a stadium performance is most exposed. Almost every famous failure at a sporting event happens at that interval.

Key wrote the poem in 1814 after watching the bombardment of Fort McHenry, and it circulated widely for over a century in an unofficial capacity. It was used by the military from the 1890s but only became the official national anthem by act of Congress in 1931.

Other anthems were in contention, including 'America the Beautiful', which is considerably easier to sing and lost anyway.
facts: That range is why singers so often struggle with it
It became the official anthem only in 1931

03-04.title: Antonio Vivaldi taught music at an orphanage
03-04.story:
Vivaldi spent decades directing music at a Venetian institution for abandoned girls. Much of his catalogue was written for those young musicians.

The Ospedale della Pietà was a foundling hospital, and its music programme was exceptional by any standard. The girls trained there performed behind screens in the chapel, and the ensemble became famous enough across Europe that travellers routed through Venice specifically to hear them. Visitors' accounts describe astonishment at the level of playing.

Vivaldi was employed there, on and off, for most of his career, and the practical consequence is that a large share of his enormous output — hundreds of concertos — was written for particular students whose strengths he knew. Some of the more extreme solo writing exists because a specific girl could play it.

He was also an ordained priest, nicknamed the Red Priest for his hair, and was excused from saying Mass, apparently on health grounds.

He died in poverty in Vienna in 1741, his music having gone out of fashion, and was buried in a simple grave. His work was almost entirely forgotten for roughly two hundred years.

The revival came in the twentieth century, when manuscripts were rediscovered and catalogued. The Four Seasons is now among the most recorded pieces in existence, which would have astonished everyone involved.
facts: Visitors traveled to Venice specifically to hear them play
His works were largely forgotten until a 20th-century revival

03-05.title: The Notorious B.I.G. was killed at 24
03-05.story:
Wallace died in Los Angeles weeks before releasing 'Life After Death'. Brooklyn responded with an impromptu street procession through Bed-Stuy.

He was shot in a drive-by after a party in Los Angeles on 9 March 1997, six months after Tupac Shakur had been killed in Nashville. Neither murder has been solved, and the failure to solve them is itself part of the story — both cases have been the subject of decades of investigation, litigation, and allegations of police mishandling.

The album arrived sixteen days later. Its title had been chosen before his death, following a debut called Ready to Die, which gave the sequence a grim symmetry nobody wanted.

The funeral procession through Brooklyn is the part people who were there still describe first. The route ran through Bed-Stuy past the blocks he had grown up on, and thousands of people came out onto Fulton Street. It turned into something between a wake and a street celebration, and it was broken up by police, which added a final note of friction.

Brooklyn later co-named the corner of St. James Place and Fulton as Christopher Wallace Way.

He was twenty-four, and had released one album in his lifetime.
facts: His funeral procession drew thousands to Fulton Street
Brooklyn later co-named a block Christopher Wallace Way

03-06.title: Sampling law changed because of one bass note
03-06.story:
A court ruled that even a two-second sample required clearance, forcing producers to either pay or replay parts. Entire production styles became legally impossible.

The case was Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films, decided by the Sixth Circuit, and it concerned a two-second guitar chord from a Funkadelic record used in an N.W.A track. The court's ruling was blunt: get a licence or do not sample. It explicitly declined to apply the usual de minimis threshold to sound recordings, meaning that in that circuit even an unrecognisable fragment required clearance.

The economic consequence was immediate. Clearing a sample requires permission from both the recording owner and the publisher, each of whom can refuse or set any price, and a track built from thirty sources becomes commercially impossible regardless of budget.

That is why records like the Beastie Boys' Paul's Boutique and Public Enemy's densest work belong to a specific window. Chuck D and others have said plainly that those albums could not be made and released today.

Producers adapted by replaying parts with session musicians, using royalty-free sample libraries, or building from original material.

A later Ninth Circuit decision disagreed with Bridgeport, creating a split between circuits that remains unresolved. In practice, labels clear everything, because the downside of being wrong is enormous.
facts: Records like 'Paul's Boutique' could not be cleared today
Producers pivoted to live replays and original loops

03-07.title: Maurice Ravel wrote 'Boléro' as an experiment in repetition
03-07.story:
Ravel called it 'orchestral tissue without music', a single melody repeated with growing instrumentation and no development. He was surprised it became famous.

The structure is almost aggressively simple. One melody, stated eighteen times, over an unchanging snare drum pattern that runs the entire fifteen-odd minutes, with a single key change near the end. There is no development, no counter-subject, no departure. The only thing that changes is orchestration and volume.

That makes it a piece about timbre rather than about music in the conventional sense — which is precisely what Ravel meant by his dismissive description of it. He was demonstrating that colour alone could sustain a listener's attention for a quarter of an hour, and he appears to have regarded the demonstration as a technical exercise rather than a masterpiece.

The orchestration is genuinely virtuosic. Instruments are combined in unusual pairings to produce composite tones, including a passage where a horn, celesta, and piccolos are voiced to imitate the harmonics of an organ.

The snare player has one of the least enviable jobs in the repertoire: the same two-bar rhythm, unbroken, for the entire piece, with the tempo and dynamic control that everything else depends on.

It became the most performed and most lucrative work he ever wrote, to his visible irritation.
facts: The snare drum plays the same rhythm for roughly 15 minutes
He reportedly said the piece contained 'no music in it whatsoever'

03-08.title: Jay-Z grew up in Marcy Houses
03-08.story:
Shawn Carter's Bed-Stuy childhood is stitched through his catalogue. Like Biggie, he famously records without writing lyrics down.

Marcy Houses is a New York City Housing Authority development in Bedford-Stuyvesant, and it recurs by name across three decades of his work — not as an origin story told once, but as a fixed reference point he keeps returning to from different vantages as his circumstances change.

The non-writing method he has attributed to watching Biggie. He composes in his head, holding verses in memory until the take, which produces a rhythm shaped by breath and phrasing rather than by how lines look on a page. He has demonstrated it on camera, which is the only reason people believe it.

The more consequential decision was structural. Labels passed on signing him, so he co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records with Damon Dash and Kareem Burke and released his own debut, retaining ownership. That put him on the other side of the table at the start of his career rather than fifteen years into it, which is the entire explanation for what followed.

He later ran Def Jam, built Roc Nation, and became a minority owner of the Brooklyn Nets — the arena for which sits about two miles from Marcy.

The distance is short and the trajectory is not one many people make.
facts: He founded Roc-A-Fella after labels passed on signing him
Marcy Houses appears by name across three decades of his songs

03-09.title: Ella Fitzgerald invented her scat by copying horns
03-09.story:
Fitzgerald built solos by imitating trumpet and saxophone lines rather than singing words, turning her voice into a brass instrument.

Scat existed before her, but she systematised it. Rather than treating wordless singing as decoration between verses, she approached a solo the way a horn player would — building lines from the same bebop vocabulary, using the same rhythmic displacement, and phrasing across the bar rather than within it.

She could reproduce recorded solos note for note, which is a skill closer to transcription than to improvisation and which gave her an enormous stock of material to draw on. Her live version of 'How High the Moon' quotes a long string of other melodies inside a single solo, at speed, as an audible joke for anyone tracking it.

The technical prerequisite is intonation. Singing chromatic bebop lines without an instrument to check against requires pitch accuracy that very few singers have, and it is why so few have attempted the approach seriously since.

The Songbook series she recorded for Verve across the late fifties and early sixties — Gershwin, Porter, Ellington, Berlin, and more — did a different kind of work. It gathered the American popular repertoire into a canonical form at exactly the point when rock and roll was displacing it, and largely determined which songs survived as standards.
facts: She could reproduce bebop solos note for note
Her 'Songbook' series helped canonize American standards

03-10.title: The first commercial radio broadcast changed listening forever
03-10.story:
Early stations discovered that recorded music filled airtime cheaply. Within a decade, radio play, not sheet music, determined what became a hit.

Before radio, the music industry was a printing industry. A hit meant sheet music sales, and the business was organised around getting songs into pianos in domestic parlours — which is why Tin Pan Alley existed and why song pluggers were employed to perform new material in shops.

Radio destroyed that model in about a decade. Sheet music sales collapsed as people stopped needing to play music themselves in order to hear it, and the definition of a hit shifted from copies sold to plays broadcast.

Record labels initially fought it hard. The reasoning seemed sound: if people could hear a song for free, why would they buy it? Some pressings were labelled as not licensed for radio broadcast. The industry took years to accept that airplay drove sales rather than replacing them, an argument it would repeat almost verbatim about home taping, then about digital downloads, then about streaming.

What radio also did was standardise. A national broadcast meant a single performance became the definitive version of a song, where previously a song existed as notation that everyone realised differently.

Recorded music became the work itself, rather than a document of it.
facts: Sheet music sales collapsed as radio grew
Record labels initially fought radio, fearing it would kill sales

03-11.title: Bobby McFerrin used no instruments at all
03-11.story:
'Don't Worry, Be Happy' is entirely voice and body percussion, multitracked. Listeners assumed they were hearing a full band.

Every sound on the record is McFerrin: the melody, the harmony parts, the bassline, and the percussion, which is his hand striking his own chest and body. There are no instruments and no samples. Most listeners at the time assumed they were hearing a small band with a whistling lead.

It was the first a cappella song to reach number one on the US chart, and it won record and song of the year at the Grammys, which for a track made entirely of one man's body is an unusual outcome.

The song's enormous ubiquity did him no favours artistically. He was a serious jazz vocalist with a technique — simultaneous melody and bass, rapid register jumps, improvisation across a full four-octave range — that almost nobody else possessed, and the hit flattened his public identity into a single cheerful chorus. He stopped performing it live for years.

His father, Robert McFerrin Sr., was the first Black man to sing with the Metropolitan Opera and dubbed Sidney Poitier's singing in Porgy and Bess.

McFerrin went on to conduct orchestras, which is roughly the opposite career move from the one the hit implied.
facts: Every sound including the bass is McFerrin's own voice
It was the first a cappella song to top the US chart

03-12.title: Ditmas Park's Victorian porches became rehearsal rooms
03-12.story:
The freestanding wooden houses around Cortelyou Road gave Brooklyn musicians something rare: space to make noise. Porch sessions became an informal neighborhood circuit.

The housing stock is the whole reason. Around 1900, developers laid out Prospect Park South and the surrounding blocks as a planned suburb of detached wood-frame houses on generous lots — Dean Alvord's Prospect Park South is the best-known example — marketed to Manhattan professionals who could commute by train. The result is one of the largest concentrations of Victorian houses anywhere in America, sitting inside New York City.

What that means practically for a musician is a detached building with a basement, an attic, and neighbours who are not sharing a wall. In a city where the standard rehearsal option is an hourly room in an industrial building, a house you can make noise in is close to unobtainable.

The district's protection is why any of it survived. The Ditmas Park and Prospect Park South historic districts were designated in the late seventies and early eighties, at a point when the economics strongly favoured demolition and replacement.

House concerts still run on the same blocks — living rooms, porches, and back gardens, publicised by word of mouth, with a hat passed. It is an informal circuit and it has been continuous for decades.
facts: The district holds one of the largest concentrations of Victorian homes in America
Local house concerts still run on the same blocks

03-13.title: Neil Diamond wrote hits in a Brill Building cubicle
03-13.story:
Before stardom, the Brooklyn-born Diamond wrote songs for hire in a tiny Manhattan office with a piano and a chair, competing with dozens of writers per floor.

The Brill Building system was industrial songwriting. Publishers rented small rooms — barely more than a cubicle with an upright piano — to teams of writers who produced material on demand for whichever artist needed a single. Carole King and Gerry Goffin, Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, and Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman all worked this way, often on the same floor, in open competition.

The conditions were unglamorous and productive. A writer could hear a rival's melody through the wall, and the pressure to produce something better by the end of the day was constant.

Diamond, who grew up in Brooklyn and attended Erasmus Hall in Flatbush, spent years in that system with limited success before writing 'I'm a Believer' as work-for-hire. The Monkees took it to number one, which gave him leverage he had not previously had.

He then did what almost nobody in the system managed: moved from writing for others to performing his own material, and sustained a career at that level for decades.

The system itself did not survive the shift to self-contained bands writing their own songs, which the Beatles made the industry standard within a few years.
facts: He grew up in Brooklyn and attended Erasmus Hall
'I'm a Believer' was written as work-for-hire and became a Monkees hit

03-14.title: Quincy Jones arranged for Sinatra at 29
03-14.story:
Jones's charts gave Sinatra's Basie-era records their swing. He later moved from jazz arranging to producing the best-selling album in history.

He started as a trumpeter, touring with Lionel Hampton as a teenager, and moved into arranging early because he was better at it. By his twenties he was writing for major artists and studying composition in Paris with Nadia Boulanger, who had taught a substantial share of the twentieth century's serious composers.

The Sinatra–Basie collaborations are the clearest demonstration of what an arranger does. Sinatra could sing with any band; what Jones supplied was the specific relationship between voice and orchestra — where the horns punch, where they get out of the way, how a chart breathes around a phrase that is never sung the same way twice.

The range of what followed is difficult to summarise. Film scores, television themes, a record label, decades of production work, and then Off the Wall, Thriller, and Bad with Michael Jackson.

Thriller remains the best-selling album ever released, and the production is a large part of why: it moves between disco, rock, pop, and ballad without the record fragmenting, which is an arranger's skill applied at album scale.

He died in 2024, having worked across seven decades of American popular music.
facts: He began as a trumpeter touring with Lionel Hampton
He produced 'Thriller' two decades later

03-15.title: Sister Rosetta Tharpe played electric guitar before Chuck Berry
03-15.story:
Tharpe's distorted gospel guitar and showmanship directly shaped rock and roll. Berry, Presley and Little Richard all cited her.

She was playing solid-body and hollow-body electric guitar with heavy distortion in the 1930s and 1940s, in churches and on the gospel circuit, with a technique built on bent notes, aggressive attack, and single-string soloing. Everything people describe as the invention of rock guitar in the mid-fifties is already present in her recordings a decade earlier.

'Strange Things Happening Every Day', recorded in 1944, is on many people's shortlist for the first rock and roll record, and it charted on the race records chart at a time when gospel almost never crossed over.

Her position was uncomfortable throughout. Churches objected to a woman playing secular-sounding electric guitar and performing in nightclubs; the secular world did not fully claim her either. She was recording gospel and performing in clubs simultaneously, which satisfied nobody's categories.

Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Johnny Cash all cited her directly. Berry in particular has been quoted saying his career was essentially one long Rosetta Tharpe impression.

She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018, forty-five years after her death and long after everyone she influenced.
facts: She played a solid-body electric in churches, scandalizing congregations
She was inducted into the Rock Hall only in 2018

03-16.title: The Ramones played 2:30 songs to fit more into a set
03-16.story:
Their debut cost about $6,400 and ran under 30 minutes. Speed and brevity were economic decisions as much as aesthetic ones.

The budget explains a great deal. Roughly six thousand dollars in 1976 bought about a week of studio time, which meant the album had to be recorded essentially live with minimal overdubs. There was no money for experimentation, so the band played the songs the way they played them in clubs and moved on.

The brevity was similarly practical. Fourteen songs in under thirty minutes meant a set could get through a lot of material fast, keep energy continuous, and never give an audience a reason to drift. Every song is counted in identically — one-two-three-four — which functioned as a structural device as much as a count-off.

What made it influential was the demonstration rather than the innovation. The record proved that a band with limited technique, no budget, and no studio access could make something that sounded finished, which is the message that reached kids in Britain and produced the entire first wave of UK punk within about eighteen months.

The band never had a hit single and never sold in significant numbers during its existence. Its influence is wildly out of proportion to its commercial performance, which is true of remarkably few records.
facts: They counted off every song identically
The whole album was recorded in about a week

03-17.title: Nas recorded 'Illmatic' with four different producers
03-17.story:
Rather than one house sound, Nas invited DJ Premier, Pete Rock, Q-Tip and Large Professor. The album runs under 40 minutes with no filler.

The convention at the time was a single producer or a single crew supplying a coherent sound across an album. Assembling four of the best working producers on one record risked incoherence, and the fact that it does not sound fragmented is largely down to the material — the writing is specific enough to hold the record together regardless of who made the beat.

He was twenty when it came out, writing about the Queensbridge Houses with a level of detail and compression that has kept the album on critics' lists for thirty years. The imagery is dense and the perspective is fixed: it is reportage from one place rather than a career narrative.

The brevity was deliberate. Ten tracks, under forty minutes, with material cut for repeating an idea already covered — at a point when the CD had pushed rap albums toward seventy minutes because the format allowed it. Almost every long album of the era has filler, and this one has none because it refused the space.

It sold modestly at first. Its reputation was built by other rappers, which is generally the more durable route.
facts: He was 20 when it was released
Its brevity was deliberate; he cut anything that repeated an idea

03-18.title: John Coltrane practiced until his lips bled
03-18.story:
Bandmates described Coltrane practicing 12 hours a day, sometimes falling asleep with the horn in his mouth. 'Giant Steps' came from that obsession.

The accounts are consistent across many people who worked with him: he practised constantly, in dressing rooms, between sets, on tour buses, and at home, to a degree his contemporaries found extreme even by the standards of a demanding profession. Several described him falling asleep still holding the saxophone.

What came out of it was a harmonic system. The chord movement on 'Giant Steps' — now universally called Coltrane changes — cycles through keys a major third apart at high speed, which produces a sequence that is extremely difficult to improvise over because the ear cannot rely on conventional expectations. It remains a standard test piece for jazz students.

The famous evidence of that difficulty is on the recording itself. Tommy Flanagan, an exceptional pianist, was reading the changes at the session and his solo is audibly a struggle, which he discussed with good humour for decades afterward. Coltrane had been living inside the material for months; nobody else had.

He moved on quickly. Within a few years he had largely abandoned that density in favour of modal and then free playing, treating the system as something to pass through rather than arrive at.

He died of liver cancer in 1967, at forty.
facts: Its chord changes are still a rite of passage for jazz students
Pianist Tommy Flanagan sight-read the session and struggled famously

03-19.title: Wagner built a theater to control how his music was heard
03-19.story:
Frustrated by noisy houses, Wagner designed Bayreuth with a hidden orchestra pit and a darkened hall, inventing conventions concert audiences still follow.

Opera houses of the period were social venues. The auditorium stayed lit, people talked, moved between boxes, and treated the performance as a backdrop. Wagner regarded this as intolerable and built his own theatre at Bayreuth to eliminate it.

Two of his solutions became universal. Darkening the auditorium so the audience cannot see each other was considered radical and slightly hostile; it forces attention onto the stage and effectively ends conversation. And the sunken, covered orchestra pit hides the players entirely, which removes the visual distraction and blends the instrumental sound into a single mass before it reaches the audience — Bayreuth's pit produces a warmth that cannot be reproduced in a conventional house.

The seating was also unusual: a single raked fan of seats with no boxes, which flattened the social hierarchy that Italian opera house design encoded architecturally.

Every convention of concert etiquette people now treat as natural — lights down, silence, applause only at the end — descends substantially from one composer's irritation.

Wagner's antisemitism was explicit, published, and vicious, and the Bayreuth festival's later relationship with the Nazi regime was close. Both things sit in the same building.
facts: Darkening the auditorium was considered radical
The sunken pit blends the orchestra into a single sound

03-20.title: The first rap record label ran out of a New Jersey house
03-20.story:
Sugar Hill Records began as a family operation with a house band and minimal equipment, pressing records faster than major labels could react.

Sylvia Robinson had a career behind her. She had a hit in the fifties as half of Mickey & Sylvia, another as a solo artist in the seventies, and had run a label before. When she heard rapping at a party and recognised that nobody was putting it on record, she had both the ear and the infrastructure to act immediately.

The operation was small and fast: a house band that could replay any groove, a studio, and the ability to get a record pressed and into stores while major labels were still deciding whether rap was a novelty. That speed is the entire reason the label defined the genre's first years.

The roster included Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, whose 'The Message' in 1982 established that rap could carry serious social reportage rather than party material.

The majors stayed out for years, treating the form as a fad that would pass. By the time they moved in, an independent Black-owned label in New Jersey had already established the commercial template.

Sugar Hill's own relationships with its artists were, by many accounts, poor. Payment disputes and credit disputes ran through the catalogue.
facts: Sylvia Robinson had been a hit singer herself in the fifties
Majors dismissed rap as a novelty for years

03-21.title: Bach was jailed for trying to quit his job
03-21.story:
Bach spent nearly a month in detention after asking too insistently to leave a court position. He kept composing during his confinement.

The episode took place in Weimar in 1717. Bach had been offered a better post at Köthen and requested his release; his employer, Duke Wilhelm Ernst, refused and then had him detained for roughly four weeks for what the court record describes as too stubbornly forcing the issue of his dismissal. He was released and dismissed in disgrace.

It is a useful corrective to the image of the composer as a free artist. Musicians of the period were employees, frequently with limited right to leave, and Bach spent his career negotiating with churches, town councils, and aristocrats who regarded him as staff.

He reportedly continued composing during the detention, which fits everything else known about his working habits.

He fathered twenty children across two marriages, ten of whom survived to adulthood, and several became significant composers in their own right — Carl Philipp Emanuel was more famous than his father for much of the eighteenth century.

Most of his music was unpublished when he died in 1750 and he was remembered primarily as an organist. The revival began seriously with Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of the St Matthew Passion, nearly eighty years later.
facts: He fathered 20 children, several becoming composers
Much of his music was unpublished at his death

03-22.title: Brooklyn's Fania sound made salsa a global export
03-22.story:
Fania Records' live shows, many featuring Brooklyn and Bronx players, turned New York salsa into an international movement.

Salsa is a New York music. Its ingredients are Cuban — son, mambo, guaracha — but the form as it developed in the sixties and seventies came out of Puerto Rican, Dominican, and Cuban communities in the Bronx and Brooklyn, played by musicians who had grown up with jazz and R&B alongside the Caribbean repertoire.

Fania, founded by Johnny Pacheco and Jerry Masucci, functioned as both a label and a touring collective. The Fania All-Stars gathered its roster — Celia Cruz, Willie Colón, Héctor Lavoe, Ray Barretto, Rubén Blades and others — into a single band, and the live recordings are the genre's defining documents.

The 1973 Yankee Stadium concert ended early when the crowd rushed the field, which stopped the show and produced footage that became part of the mythology.

What the label did commercially was export it. Salsa moved from New York neighbourhoods to Latin America and then globally, in a reversal of the usual direction of travel — a diaspora music going back and becoming dominant in the countries the diaspora had left.

Brooklyn's Puerto Rican and Dominican communities were central to the scene and remain so.
facts: Their Yankee Stadium concert ended when fans rushed the field
Brooklyn's Puerto Rican and Dominican communities were core to the scene

03-23.title: Kate Bush choreographed her own videos to tell the story
03-23.story:
Trained in mime and dance, Bush treated the promo video as performance art at a time when most artists simply lip-synced.

She had studied dance with Lindsay Kemp, who had also taught David Bowie, and mime alongside it. That training is the reason the early videos look nothing like their contemporaries: instead of a band performing, you get a single figure using physical vocabulary drawn from dance and expressionist theatre to enact the song.

'Wuthering Heights' reached number one in the UK when she was nineteen, making her the first woman to top the British chart with a self-written song. She wrote it after catching the last ten minutes of a television adaptation of the novel and going straight to the piano.

The vocal is the other unusual element — a very high, deliberately strange register that record executives reportedly wanted changed, and which she refused to change.

She took control of production early and by the mid-eighties was self-producing, building albums at her own studio over long periods with a level of autonomy almost no woman in British pop had at the time.

She has toured live only twice in five decades, which for an artist of her stature is close to unheard of and appears to be entirely a matter of preference.
facts: She was 19 when 'Wuthering Heights' topped the UK chart
She wrote it after catching the last 10 minutes of a TV adaptation

03-24.title: The Wrecking Crew played on records credited to bands
03-24.story:
A pool of Los Angeles session musicians performed on hits attributed to famous groups. Many listeners never knew.

The arrangement was standard practice and largely unspoken. A band would be signed on the strength of its singer and image, and when it came time to record, producers brought in session players who could deliver a usable take in two passes rather than twenty. The band's name went on the sleeve.

The pool included Carol Kaye, Hal Blaine, Tommy Tedesco, Glen Campbell, and Leon Russell among many others, and their playing appears on an enormous share of the era's American hits — Beach Boys records, Phil Spector productions, the Monkees, television themes, film scores.

Carol Kaye's bass playing in particular is on hundreds of records people would attribute to someone else, and she was one of very few women working at that level in any studio.

Some bands genuinely did not know until the record came out, and a few learned their own parts afterward in order to perform them live.

The practice is less hidden now but has not stopped. What changed is the disclosure norm — credits are more complete, and the assumption that the people pictured played the notes has quietly been abandoned.
facts: Carol Kaye played bass on hundreds of well-known records
Some bands only learned their own parts after release

03-25.title: Aretha Franklin was born, and learned in her father's church
03-25.story:
Franklin grew up singing gospel in Detroit under her preacher father, absorbing a call-and-response phrasing she never abandoned in secular music.

C. L. Franklin was a nationally known preacher whose recorded sermons sold well, and the household was a stop for touring gospel musicians. Mahalia Jackson, Clara Ward, and Sam Cooke were present in her childhood, which is an education no conservatory can supply.

What gospel gave her structurally was call and response — a lead line answered by a group, with the answer shaping what the lead does next. That architecture is present in almost all her secular work, and it is why her records feel like an event happening in a room rather than a performance delivered at one.

Her first label got it wrong. Columbia signed her and spent years trying to make her a supper-club pop singer, recording standards with orchestral arrangements that gave her nothing to push against. The records are competent and inert.

The move to Atlantic and to Muscle Shoals in 1967 fixed it in a single session, largely by putting her behind a piano with a rhythm section and letting her lead.

She played piano on a great deal of her own work, which is frequently left out of descriptions of her, and it is a substantial part of why the arrangements sit where they do.
facts: She played piano on many of her own recordings
Her Atlantic breakthrough came after Columbia tried to make her a pop crooner

03-26.title: Pink Floyd recorded a heartbeat to open an album
03-26.story:
'The Dark Side of the Moon' opens with a treated bass drum simulating a pulse, then loops of interviews with studio staff answering existential questions.

The interviews are the more interesting device. Roger Waters wrote a set of questions on flashcards — about violence, madness, and death — and put them to anyone passing through Abbey Road: roadies, staff, the doorman Gerry O'Driscoll, whose closing line about there being no dark side of the moon ends the record. Paul McCartney was interviewed and his answers went unused, reportedly because he was too self-aware to be useful.

That method gives the album its unusual texture: non-musicians speaking plainly, unrehearsed, threaded between highly produced music.

The engineering was Alan Parsons, working with a new sixteen-track machine and using the studio's resources aggressively — tape loops assembled by hand for the clock and cash-register sequences, VCS3 synthesiser, and Clare Torry's improvised wordless vocal on 'The Great Gig in the Sky', which she was paid a session fee for and successfully sued over decades later.

The album spent an extraordinary run on the Billboard chart, well past nine hundred weeks in total across its various stints, which is a chart record by a wide margin.
facts: Paul McCartney was interviewed but his answers were unused
The album charted for over 900 weeks

03-27.title: Mariah Carey co-wrote nearly everything she sang
03-27.story:
Unusual for a young pop signing, Carey held writing credits from her debut, giving her long-term control of her catalogue.

The standard arrangement for a young pop artist is to sing material written by others, which means the performer earns from records and touring while the writers earn from the songs — an income stream that keeps paying long after a career peaks. Carey held co-writing credits from the beginning, which is the reason her position decades later is what it is.

The demo reached Tommy Mottola, then head of Columbia, at a party, essentially by chance. He signed her, married her, and the professional and personal entanglement went badly.

Her vocal signature is the whistle register — the range above the normal soprano top, produced differently from ordinary singing and accessible to very few people. She used it as a compositional element rather than a stunt, writing lines that go there deliberately.

The other durable thing she did was help normalise rap features on pop records. The remix culture around her mid-nineties singles, pairing her with hip-hop artists, was not standard practice at the time and became so.

'All I Want for Christmas Is You', which she co-wrote, returns to the chart every December and has become one of the most valuable copyrights in popular music.
facts: She uses the whistle register, a rare vocal extreme
Her demo reached a label head at a party by chance

03-28.title: Brooklyn's Bushwick lofts became a DIY venue circuit
03-28.story:
Cheap industrial space turned into all-ages venues run without licenses, incubating a generation of indie bands before rents rose.

The raw material was disused manufacturing space. Bushwick and East Williamsburg had large industrial buildings with cheap rent, high ceilings, and no residential neighbours to complain, which is precisely the specification for a venue. Artists took loft leases, lived in them, and started putting on shows.

None of it was licensed. There were no liquor licences, no place of assembly permits, and frequently no functioning fire exits, which is the part that eventually caught up with the circuit. Venues were shut down periodically, and the risk was real — the Ghost Ship fire in Oakland in 2016 killed thirty-six people in exactly this kind of space and prompted a wave of closures nationally.

What the circuit produced was substantial. All-ages, cheap, and unconcerned with commercial viability, it incubated a generation of bands, several of whom went on to headline rooms an order of magnitude larger — including the arena a few miles west.

The ending is the familiar one. The presence of the scene made the neighbourhood desirable, rents rose accordingly, and the spaces converted to apartments and offices. The circuit moved further east and south, as it always does.
facts: Many were shut down over fire-code violations
The circuit launched acts that later headlined Barclays Center

03-29.title: The theremin is played without being touched
03-29.story:
Leon Theremin's instrument responds to hand position in an electromagnetic field. It requires perfect pitch because there is nothing to feel.

The mechanism is genuinely strange. Two antennas generate electromagnetic fields; the player's hands alter the capacitance of those fields, one controlling pitch and the other volume, and the instrument responds to proximity rather than contact. There is nothing to press, no fret, no key, and no tactile feedback of any kind.

That makes it one of the hardest instruments to play well. Pitch is continuous rather than stepped, so every note must be found by ear in mid-air, and a small movement of the wrist is a large interval. Clara Rockmore, a trained violinist who became its greatest exponent, developed a fingering technique to make precise leaps possible.

Theremin demonstrated it across Europe and the Soviet Union — Lenin reportedly tried playing it and was enthusiastic — and it was briefly marketed as a home instrument by RCA, which failed, because almost nobody could play it.

Theremin himself was returned to the Soviet Union in the late thirties, in circumstances that remain disputed, and spent years working in a state laboratory designing surveillance devices.

The instrument found its lasting role in film. Its unstable, vocal, sliding tone became the standard sound of science fiction and psychological unease.
facts: Lenin personally tried playing it
It later gave science-fiction film its signature eerie tone

03-30.title: Tracy Chapman's breakthrough happened by accident
03-30.story:
When Stevie Wonder's gear failed at a televised benefit, Chapman was sent back out alone with a guitar. Her album sales exploded within days.

The event was the Nelson Mandela seventieth birthday tribute at Wembley Stadium, broadcast to an audience estimated in the hundreds of millions. Chapman had already played a short early slot. When a technical problem with Stevie Wonder's equipment left a gap in the schedule, she was sent back on with an acoustic guitar and no band, in front of a stadium and a global broadcast.

She played 'Fast Car'. Album sales moved immediately and enormously, and the record went on to sell in the millions.

The song itself is a piece of compressed writing that repays attention. It is a first-person narrative about escaping poverty that quietly reveals, verse by verse, that the escape did not happen — the same circumstances reproduce themselves a generation on. The chorus sounds hopeful and the structure of the song is telling you it is not.

She had been busking in Boston and playing coffeehouses a few years earlier.

The song returned to the top of the charts in 2023 in a country version by Luke Combs, which sent the original back into wide circulation and made Chapman the first Black woman to write a solo number one on the country songs chart.
facts: She played 'Fast Car' to an audience of hundreds of millions
She had been busking in Boston a few years earlier

03-31.title: Marvin Gaye had to fight his label to release 'What's Going On'
03-31.story:
Berry Gordy called the record uncommercial and refused to put it out. Gaye went on strike until Motown relented, and it became their landmark album.

Gordy's objection was consistent with the entire Motown strategy. The label had built its success on tightly written, politically neutral pop that could cross to white radio, and a slow, jazz-inflected album about Vietnam, police violence, and environmental collapse was a direct threat to that formula. He reportedly called it the worst thing he had ever heard.

Gaye's leverage was that he was Motown's biggest male star and was prepared to stop recording entirely. He refused to make anything else until the single was released, and Motown eventually put it out — by some accounts without Gordy's approval — whereupon it sold immediately and heavily.

The album's sound is unlike the label's house style. It flows continuously between tracks, uses layered lead vocals where Gaye sings against himself, and opens with party chatter recorded at an actual gathering, which places the listener inside a room rather than in front of a record.

The subject matter came partly from his brother Frankie's letters home from Vietnam.

Gordy later acknowledged plainly that he had been wrong. It is generally regarded as the best record the label released.
facts: Gordy later admitted he was wrong
The overlapping party chatter was recorded at a real gathering

04-01.title: The 'Funky Drummer' break that built a thousand hits
04-01.story:
Clyde Stubblefield's drum break on James Brown's 'Funky Drummer' was improvised filler. It became one of the most sampled recordings in history.

The break arrives about five and a half minutes in, after Brown tells the band to give the drummer some. What follows is roughly eight bars of Stubblefield alone, playing a pattern built on ghost notes — the quiet, almost-inaudible strokes between the main hits that give the groove its shuffle. He has said he was not doing anything special and did not think about it again.

What made it so useful to producers is the ghost notes. A pattern with that much internal detail can be chopped, slowed, sped up, or rearranged and still sound like a human being playing, which is exactly what a drum machine could not do in 1986.

Public Enemy, Run-DMC, LL Cool J, Sinéad O'Connor, George Michael, and hundreds of others built records on it. It is among the two or three most sampled recordings ever made.

Stubblefield received no sampling royalties. He was a session player on a work-for-hire basis and had no claim under the law as it stood. He said repeatedly that he did not object to people using the music — what bothered him was not being named.

He died in 2017.
facts: Public Enemy, Run-DMC, LL Cool J and George Michael all used it
Stubblefield was never paid sampling royalties and said he didn't mind the music, only the credit

hits: LL Cool J - Mama Said Knock You Out

04-02.title: Which 'Respect' wins: Otis or Aretha?
04-02.story:
Otis Redding wrote it in 1965 as a working man's plea. Aretha Franklin rebuilt it in 1967 as a demand, adding the spelling hook and her sisters' backing vocals.

The two versions are worth hearing back to back because almost nothing changes on paper. Same title, largely the same words, similar tempo. Redding's is a man coming home from work asking to be treated properly in his own house — the tone is tired and slightly pleading, and the arrangement pushes forward like someone making a case.

Franklin's inverts the power relationship completely. The narrator is not asking. She is stating terms, and the spelled-out hook — invented in the studio with her sisters Carolyn and Erma — functions as an instruction rather than a chorus.

The arrangement does its share. King Curtis's saxophone solo quotes 'When Something Is Wrong with My Baby', the rhythm section drives rather than swings, and the whole thing was built quickly at Atlantic with Jerry Wexler and the Muscle Shoals players.

Redding took it well and appears to have found it funny, joking at Monterey that the girl had taken his song away from him.

Most covers disappear behind the original. This is one of the few cases where the second version became the definitive one, and the first became the interesting footnote.
facts: Redding joked she had stolen the song for good
Aretha's version was cut in a single afternoon session

04-03.title: Nile Rodgers' guitar is on more hits than you think
04-03.story:
The Chic guitarist's clipped 'chucking' style powered his own band, then Bowie's 'Let's Dance', Madonna's 'Like a Virgin' and Daft Punk's 'Get Lucky'.

The technique is deceptively simple to describe and hard to do. He plays tightly muted sixteenth-note chords with almost no sustain, so the guitar functions as a percussion instrument that also supplies harmony. The notes are short enough that they occupy almost no space in a mix, which is why a Rodgers part can sit in a dense arrangement without fighting anything.

He calls the approach chucking, and he plays almost all of it on the same 1960 Stratocaster he refers to as the Hitmaker.

With Bernard Edwards he wrote and produced not just Chic but Sister Sledge's catalogue and Diana Ross's 'Upside Down', and the Chic rhythm section is one of the most sampled and interpolated in existence — 'Good Times' alone underpins 'Rapper's Delight' and a long list of records after it.

His second career as a producer for hire is arguably larger than his first. Bowie's Let's Dance, Madonna's Like a Virgin, Duran Duran, INXS, and much later Daft Punk's 'Get Lucky' all carry the same guitar.

He has survived cancer twice and has been unusually candid in public about both his health and his sobriety.
facts: He uses a 1960 Stratocaster he calls 'The Hitmaker'
He and Bernard Edwards wrote Sister Sledge's catalogue too

04-04.title: Marvin Gaye's 'Inner City Blues' hid a second bassline
04-04.story:
Bassist Bob Babbitt and James Jamerson both appear across the album, and Gaye layered a second bass an octave apart to thicken the low end.

Doubling a bass part an octave up is a trick that solves a specific problem: sub-bass frequencies vanish on small speakers, so a second bass carrying the same line higher keeps the melodic movement audible on a car radio while the low octave supplies the weight. It is why the What's Going On low end feels enormous and still reads clearly.

The Funk Brothers were Motown's uncredited house band, and Jamerson was their most consequential member. He played most of his parts with a single index finger — nicknamed the Hook — which forced a particular kind of economy and produced lines that are melodically independent rather than simply following the root.

The story about him recording lying flat on his back is one of the better-known Motown anecdotes and comes from a session where he had been drinking; whether it happened once or often depends on who is telling it.

The Funk Brothers went uncredited on Motown sleeves for years despite playing on more number ones than the Beatles, the Beach Boys, and Elvis combined. Recognition arrived largely after most of them had died.
facts: Jamerson famously recorded lying flat on his back
He played most parts with a single index finger, nicknamed 'The Hook'

04-05.title: The Amen break is six seconds long and built three genres
04-05.story:
Chopped and sped up, the Winstons' break became the engine of jungle, drum and bass and UK hardcore, often at double its original tempo.

What British producers did with it in the early nineties went well beyond looping. The break was sliced into its individual drum hits and reassembled into entirely new patterns, then time-stretched to tempos around 160 to 180 beats per minute — roughly double the original — while keeping the pitch usable. That editing process is the actual compositional technique of jungle, and it required the sampler to be treated as an instrument rather than a playback device.

The result is a genre in which almost every record is built from the same six seconds and almost none of them sound alike.

Its reach extends far past dance music. It appears on N.W.A's Straight Outta Compton, the Prodigy's 'Firestarter', an Oasis single, television idents, and an enormous volume of advertising.

Nobody in the Winstons was ever paid for any of it. Richard Spencer, the band's leader and the copyright holder, was aware and had no practical route to enforcement.

A crowdfunding campaign in the UK raised a modest sum for him in 2015 — a voluntary gesture from producers rather than anything the industry required.
facts: Producers slice it into individual hits and rebuild new patterns
A crowdfunding campaign later raised money for the surviving band member

hits: Oasis - D'You Know What I Mean?

04-06.title: Which 'Hallelujah' wins: Cohen or Buckley?
04-06.story:
Leonard Cohen wrote around 80 verses and released a restrained gospel-tinged version. Jeff Buckley's 1994 reading, learned from John Cale's cover, made it a standard.

Cohen's writing process was famously agonising. He worked on the song for years and produced something in the region of eighty verses, and he described a low point spent on a hotel room floor in his underwear, banging his head, unable to finish it. The version he released in 1984 is restrained, organ-backed, and closer to a hymn than a ballad. His label initially refused to release the album it came from in the United States.

The chain of transmission matters. John Cale recorded a stripped-down piano version for a Cohen tribute album, selecting a different set of verses from the many Cohen sent him. Jeff Buckley learned the song from Cale's version rather than Cohen's, which is why the words most people know are Cale's edit.

Buckley's recording is essentially one electric guitar and a voice, largely captured live, and it treats the song as intimate and sexual rather than liturgical.

The song's subsequent ubiquity — talent shows, funerals, films — has worn it down considerably, which is a strange fate for something that took a decade to write and sat ignored for another.
facts: Cohen spent years writing it, reportedly banging his head on a hotel floor
Buckley's take is a single guitar and voice, recorded largely live

04-07.title: Billie Holiday recorded a protest song no label would touch
04-07.story:
Columbia refused 'Strange Fruit', so Holiday cut it for tiny Commodore Records. Clubs made her close with it, lights out, no encore.

The lyric began as a poem by Abel Meeropol, a Jewish schoolteacher from the Bronx writing under the name Lewis Allan, after he saw a photograph of a lynching. It is an unflinching piece of writing that describes what it describes without metaphor beyond the title itself.

Columbia would not touch it, fearing the reaction in the South and from radio. The label granted Holiday a one-off release to record it for Commodore, a small jazz label run out of a record shop.

The performance protocol at Café Society, the integrated Greenwich Village club where she introduced it, was strict and deliberate: it closed the set, service stopped, the room went dark except for a single spotlight, and there was no encore. The audience was given nothing to follow it with.

Holliday said singing it made her physically ill, and she performed it for the rest of her life anyway.

It sold well and was widely censored. It is frequently cited as the first significant protest song of the era, and it made her a target of federal harassment that continued until her death in 1959, at forty-four.
facts: The lyric began as a poem by a Bronx schoolteacher
She said singing it made her physically ill every time

04-08.title: Brooklyn's Bed-Stuy gave hip-hop its densest block
04-08.story:
Within a few square blocks, Big Daddy Kane, Jay-Z, Biggie, Lil' Kim and Masta Ace all emerged, a concentration unmatched anywhere.

The concentration is genuinely unusual. Scenes normally cluster around an institution — a club, a label, a studio — and this one clustered around a neighbourhood, with park jams and street corners functioning as the proving ground long before any label was paying attention.

Big Daddy Kane set the technical standard. His delivery in the late eighties was faster and more intricate than almost anything around it, with multisyllabic rhyme and breath control that other rappers openly studied, and he was a direct influence on Jay-Z, who has said as much repeatedly.

What that produced was a local competitive environment where the bar was set by people you could actually run into. Biggie, Jay-Z, Lil' Kim, and Masta Ace all came up inside a few square blocks of it.

The economics underneath were not benign. Bed-Stuy in the late eighties was dealing with disinvestment, the crack epidemic, and aggressive policing, and the same conditions that produced the music produced a great deal of harm.

The neighbourhood is now substantially gentrified, and the blocks in question are unaffordable to the families that produced all of this.
facts: Kane's rapid-fire delivery set the technical bar for the era
Local park jams were the proving ground before any label interest

04-09.title: Rick Rubin produced by taking things away
04-09.story:
Rubin's method was subtraction: strip the arrangement until only the essential remains. He applied it to Run-DMC, Slayer, Johnny Cash and Adele.

The early hip-hop work is the clearest demonstration. Where contemporaries were layering samples and synths, Rubin stripped tracks down to a hard drum machine pattern, a guitar, and a voice — Run-DMC's records sound enormous because there is almost nothing in them, so each element occupies the full width of the mix.

He cannot play an instrument to any useful standard and does not engineer. What he does is closer to editing: identifying which parts of a record are load-bearing and removing everything else, and getting a performance rather than a construction.

The American Recordings sessions with Johnny Cash are the most extreme version. A man in his sixties whose career had stalled, recorded with an acoustic guitar and essentially nothing else, singing covers of songs from outside his tradition. The results reset his reputation entirely in the last decade of his life.

The range is the striking part: Def Jam, founded in an NYU dorm room with Russell Simmons, then Slayer, the Beastie Boys, Red Hot Chili Peppers, System of a Down, Dixie Chicks, and Adele.

The common thread is not a sound. It is the willingness to say that most of what has been recorded should be deleted.
facts: He often cannot play any instrument on the records he makes
His Def Jam label started in an NYU dorm room

04-10.title: 'Under Pressure' was a jam nobody planned
04-10.story:
Bowie and Queen were in the same Swiss studio and started improvising. The famous bassline came from John Deacon noodling during a break.

The two acts were working at Mountain Studios in Montreux at the same time, and what began as Bowie dropping in to add backing vocals to something else turned into an all-day improvisation. Neither party arrived with a song.

The origin of the bassline is genuinely disputed. Most accounts credit John Deacon playing it during a break; Brian May has suggested Bowie changed it; Deacon has given differing versions over the years. The likeliest explanation is that nobody was paying attention at the moment it happened because nobody knew it mattered yet.

The vocal was built by a method Bowie proposed: each singer went into the booth without hearing what the other had done, sang over the track, and the results were combined. That is why the two voices overlap and interrupt rather than trading verses politely.

Both parties later expressed reservations about the mix, having run out of patience by the end of the session.

Vanilla Ice used the bassline on 'Ice Ice Baby' in 1990, initially claimed it was different because of an added note, and eventually settled with credit and payment.
facts: Accounts differ on who actually invented the riff
Vanilla Ice later used it and initially denied the resemblance

04-11.title: Which 'I Will Always Love You' wins: Dolly or Whitney?
04-11.story:
Dolly Parton wrote it as a quiet goodbye to her mentor. Whitney Houston's 1992 version added the a cappella opening that producer David Foster fought for.

Parton's original is a country ballad in the truest sense — restrained, conversational, and addressed to a specific person, Porter Wagoner, whose show had made her and whose partnership she was leaving. It works because it does not escalate. The emotional force comes from what is being held back.

Houston's version does the opposite and is equally correct on its own terms. The a cappella opening was David Foster's idea and was contested internally as too risky for radio; it survived, and it is the reason the record is instantly identifiable from its first two seconds. Kevin Costner has said he pushed for it.

The key change before the final chorus is one of the most conspicuous in pop and works because Houston had the instrument to justify it.

Parton had refused to hand publishing to Elvis Presley's manager twenty years earlier, which meant the enormous royalties from The Bodyguard came to her. She has described hearing the Houston version on the car radio for the first time and having to pull over.

Two readings of the same words, both definitive, which almost never happens.
facts: Parton has said she cried hearing Whitney's version on the radio
The a cappella intro was nearly cut for being too risky

04-12.title: The 'Think' break gave hip-hop its whistle
04-12.story:
Lyn Collins' 'Think (About It)', produced by James Brown, supplied the 'woo! yeah!' stabs heard on hundreds of records.

The useful material is two vocal exclamations and a drum break, and their value is entirely rhythmic. The stabs are short, percussive, and pitched high enough to cut through a dense mix, which makes them ideal punctuation — a producer can drop one at the end of a bar and it functions like a cymbal that happens to be a human voice.

Rob Base and DJ E-Z Rock's 'It Takes Two' is built almost entirely on it, and once that record hit in 1988 the sample became shorthand for a party record. It has been used so widely since that most listeners recognise it without ever having heard the original.

Lyn Collins sang for the James Brown revue and was billed as the Female Preacher. Her own career never reached the scale her voice warranted, which was a common outcome for singers inside Brown's organisation — he controlled the productions, the arrangements, and the release schedules.

Brown's catalogue as a whole is the single largest source of sampled material in hip-hop, and the payment situation for the musicians who played on it was, throughout, poor.

Collins died in 2005.
facts: Rob Base and DJ E-Z Rock built an entire hit on it
The vocal stabs are now shorthand for party records

04-13.title: Carole King wrote hits in Brooklyn before singing them
04-13.story:
Born in Manhattan and raised in Brooklyn, King wrote dozens of standards with Gerry Goffin before 'Tapestry' made her a performer.

She attended James Madison High School in Brooklyn and was writing professionally as a teenager. 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow', written with Gerry Goffin when she was around seventeen, became the first number one by a Black girl group when the Shirelles recorded it — and it is a remarkably adult piece of writing about the morning after, which is not what the market expected from a teenager in 1960.

The Goffin–King partnership produced an extraordinary run: 'The Loco-Motion', 'Up on the Roof', '(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman', 'Pleasant Valley Sunday'. She wrote the music, he wrote the lyrics, and they worked inside the Brill Building system alongside a floor of direct competitors.

The move to performing came after the marriage ended and after the industry had shifted toward artists writing their own material. Tapestry, in 1971, was one of the best-selling albums of the decade and reframed her entirely — the same songs, sung by the person who wrote them, at a piano.

Her version of 'A Natural Woman' arrived four years after Aretha Franklin's, which is an unusual direction of travel.
facts: She attended James Madison High School in Brooklyn
'Will You Love Me Tomorrow' was written when she was 17

04-14.title: Bernie Worrell made the synthesizer funky
04-14.story:
Parliament-Funkadelic's keyboardist treated the Moog as a bass instrument, inventing the squelching low end that shaped G-funk two decades later.

The innovation was conceptual before it was technical. Synthesizers in the mid-seventies were treated as lead or texture instruments; Worrell used the Minimoog as a bass, playing lines with portamento and filter sweeps that a bass guitar physically cannot produce. The result is the sliding, rubbery low end on records like 'Flash Light', which is one of the most influential sounds in American popular music.

He was classically trained. He began piano at three, wrote a concerto as a child, and attended the New England Conservatory, which is not the background one assumes for the P-Funk keyboard chair — and it is precisely why the harmony on those records is more sophisticated than the party framing suggests.

Dr. Dre's nineties productions lean directly on this vocabulary. G-funk is essentially the P-Funk synth bass and lead-line language slowed down and given more space, and Worrell's playing is sampled and interpolated throughout it.

He later worked with Talking Heads, appearing prominently in Stop Making Sense, which put him in front of an entirely different audience.

He died in 2016. The financial arrangements around the P-Funk catalogue were contested for decades and he saw comparatively little from it.
facts: He was classically trained and wrote a concerto as a child
Dr. Dre's nineties productions lean directly on his vocabulary

04-15.title: Which 'Tainted Love' wins: Gloria Jones or Soft Cell?
04-15.story:
Gloria Jones cut a fast Northern Soul stomper that flopped. Soft Cell slowed it to a synth crawl in 1981 and had a worldwide hit.

Jones's original is fast, brass-driven, and relentlessly forward-moving — a soul record built for dancing that failed commercially on release and then found a second life in the UK. Northern Soul clubs in the north of England were built on exactly this kind of obscure American single, and the record became a floor favourite there for over a decade before anyone thought to cover it.

Soft Cell's version keeps the melody almost intact and inverts everything else. The tempo drops, the arrangement becomes a sparse synthesizer pattern with an enormous amount of space, and the vocal shifts from defiant to exhausted. The same words describing a relationship gone toxic read completely differently at half the energy.

It became one of the biggest-selling singles of 1981 and held a long run on the American chart.

Jones later played keyboards in Marc Bolan's band and was his partner; she was driving the car in the 1977 crash that killed him.

The pair is a useful demonstration that arrangement is not decoration. Nothing meaningful changed in the writing and the song became a different song.
facts: The song was a UK club favourite for years before the cover
Soft Cell's version keeps the melody but inverts the energy entirely

04-16.title: Dub plates were one-off records made for a single night
04-16.story:
Sound systems cut exclusive acetates so rivals could not play their tunes. The discs wore out after a few dozen plays.

An acetate is an aluminium disc coated in soft lacquer, cut directly by a lathe rather than pressed from a stamper. It can be produced as a single copy within hours, and it degrades audibly with every play — a few dozen passes and the high end is gone.

For a sound system operator that was the entire appeal. Exclusivity, not fidelity, was the point. Having a tune nobody else could play was a competitive advantage in a culture where two systems set up on the same street and the crowd decided who won, and it was worth paying a studio to cut a version with a vocalist naming your system directly.

That practice — commissioning a personalised version of an existing rhythm — is what produced the enormous Jamaican tradition of multiple vocalists over the same instrumental.
