The convention travelled with the diaspora. UK jungle, garage, and grime all adopted dubplate culture wholesale, with producers cutting exclusives for specific DJs and MCs recording custom versions.

Digital distribution has removed the physical constraint without removing the social one. Exclusives still circulate, they just no longer wear out.
facts: Exclusivity, not fidelity, was the point
The practice migrated to UK garage and grime decades later

04-17.title: 'Superstition' began as a gift to a guitarist
04-17.story:
Stevie Wonder wrote the clavinet riff for Jeff Beck. When Motown heard it, they insisted Wonder keep it, straining the friendship.

The arrangement had been informal: Beck would play on Wonder's Talking Book sessions, and Wonder would write him a song in return. He came up with the clavinet riff more or less on the spot, reportedly while Beck was in the room playing a drum pattern.

The clavinet is the key to the record. It is an electric keyboard whose strings are struck and immediately damped, producing a short, plucked, percussive attack that behaves more like a rhythm guitar than a piano — which is precisely why a guitarist's song works without a guitar on it.

Wonder played essentially everything: drums, clavinet, Moog bass, and the horn arrangement written over it.

When Motown heard the finished track they refused to let it go, correctly identifying it as a hit. Beck was, by all accounts, unhappy. He did record his own version with Beck, Bogert & Appice, but it came out after Wonder's had already reached number one, which rather defeated the purpose.

The two remained on speaking terms. Beck described the situation, years later, with a resignation that suggests he had never entirely got over it.
facts: Wonder played drums, clavinet and moog bass himself
Beck did record a version, but it came out after Wonder's

04-18.title: The producer who never let artists hear playback
04-18.story:
Phil Spector often refused to let performers hear the full mix, keeping the arrangement in his head so no one could argue with it.

The control was total by design. Sessions at Gold Star ran for hours with dozens of musicians playing doubled and tripled parts, and the only person who knew what the finished record would sound like was Spector. Singers frequently cut vocals without hearing the assembled arrangement, which removed any basis on which they could object to it.

That method produced records of genuine power and a working environment that was, by many first-hand accounts, controlling and frightening well before it became criminal.

Darlene Love is the clearest case. Her voice is on records credited to the Crystals and to Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, and Spector released her performances under whichever group name suited him commercially. She spent years in litigation over royalties and credit and was at one point cleaning houses while hearing her own uncredited voice on the radio at Christmas.

Spector was convicted of the second-degree murder of Lana Clarkson in 2009 and died in prison in 2021.

The records remain in the canon. The people who made them were treated as raw material by a man whose method depended on them not knowing what they were making.
facts: Sessions ran for hours with dozens of players
Darlene Love's voice appeared on records credited to other groups

04-19.title: 'Apache' is called the national anthem of hip-hop
04-19.story:
The Incredible Bongo Band's cover gave DJs a long percussion break perfect for cutting between two turntables.

The song began as a British instrumental hit for the Shadows in 1960. The Incredible Bongo Band — a loose Los Angeles studio project — recorded a cover in 1973 that nobody paid much attention to at the time, and it contains a long percussion passage built around congas and bongos with almost no melodic content.

That passage is what mattered. A break needs to be rhythmically strong and harmonically neutral so a DJ can loop it indefinitely without the ear tiring of a chord sequence, and this one runs longer than most, which makes cutting between two copies considerably easier.

Kool Herc played it at Bronx block parties in the mid-seventies, and it became a foundational record for the whole form — sampled by the Sugarhill Gang, Nas, LL Cool J, and hundreds of others, and used as the backing for countless routines.

The phrase national anthem of hip-hop attaches to it because for a period in the seventies it functioned as one: the record everyone played, that everyone recognised, that reliably filled a floor.

Almost nobody involved in making it had any idea what it would become.
facts: Kool Herc played it at Bronx block parties
The break is essentially a drum solo with congas

hits: LL Cool J - You Can't Dance

04-20.title: Luther Vandross sang jingles before he sang ballads
04-20.story:
Vandross earned a living singing commercials and backing vocals for Bowie and Chic before launching a solo career.

The session and jingle world was, for a long time, where the best singers in New York actually made their money. It paid reliably, it was anonymous, and it demanded a specific skill — the ability to deliver a perfect take quickly, blend with anyone, and sing whatever was in front of you without ego.

Vandross was exceptional at it. He sang on commercials for soft drinks and fast food chains, did session work across the industry, and arranged the backing vocals on David Bowie's Young Americans — a substantial creative contribution on a landmark record, credited but not headlined. He also sang with Chic and appeared on a long list of other people's albums.

The solo career took years to start because the industry had him filed as a background voice, which is a common trap: being excellent at supporting work makes you too useful to release.

When he did break through, the voice that had been trained by all that session discipline turned out to be one of the great instruments in R&B — extraordinarily controlled, with a sense of phrasing that comes from years of serving somebody else's song.

He died in 2005, at fifty-four.
facts: He arranged the backing vocals on Bowie's 'Young Americans'
He sang on ads for soft drinks and fast food chains

04-21.title: Prince died, leaving a vault of unreleased music
04-21.story:
Prince recorded relentlessly, storing thousands of unreleased tracks in a bank-style vault at Paisley Park. Estimates suggest decades of material.

The vault is literal — a climate-controlled room with a bank-style door at Paisley Park, containing tapes going back to the seventies. Estimates of its contents vary wildly, but people who have been inside describe enough finished and near-finished material to release albums for decades.

The working method explains the volume. He recorded alone through the night, playing every part and frequently engineering himself, and he did it continuously for forty years. Finished songs were shelved not because they were weak but because he had already moved on.

He also gave enormous amounts away. 'Nothing Compares 2 U', 'Manic Monday', and 'I Feel for You' were written by him and became hits for other people, in some cases before most listeners knew who had written them.

He died in April 2016 of an accidental fentanyl overdose, having been treated for chronic hip pain for years, and left no will — which produced a long and expensive estate dispute before any of the vault material could be released.

The posthumous releases have been careful. Whether he would have sanctioned any of them is unknowable and was, throughout his life, the thing he cared most about controlling.
facts: He often recorded alone overnight, engineering himself
Some vault songs date to the seventies

04-22.title: Which 'Girls Just Want to Have Fun' wins: Hazard or Lauper?
04-22.story:
Robert Hazard wrote it from a man's perspective as a demo. Cyndi Lauper rewrote the meaning entirely, turning it into a feminist anthem.

Hazard's demo is sung by a man who is pleased that girls want to have fun, which is a different proposition entirely — the women in it are objects of the narrator's satisfaction rather than subjects of their own.

Lauper's initial reaction was refusal. She disliked the song and did not want to record it, and only agreed after reworking the lyric so that the perspective shifted to the women themselves. The changes are not extensive on the page and they relocate the song completely: it becomes a statement about autonomy made by the people it concerns.

The arrangement supports the reading. It is bright, fast, and slightly chaotic, and Lauper's vocal is deliberately unpolished in a way that reads as a person rather than a product.

The video did comparable work, casting her mother and featuring a visibly diverse cast at a point when MTV was not notable for either.

It is one of the clearest examples of a performer's interpretation constituting authorship. The notes are largely Hazard's. What the song means is Lauper's, and the meaning is the reason anyone still plays it.
facts: Lauper initially disliked the song and refused to record it
She rewrote lyrics to flip the point of view

04-23.title: Ray Charles fused gospel and blues and offended both
04-23.story:
'I Got a Woman' set secular lyrics to a gospel structure. Churches called it sacrilege; it also invented soul music.

The specific transgression was structural rather than vague. Charles took the harmonic and rhythmic architecture of a gospel song — reportedly reworking 'It Must Be Jesus' — and put lyrics about a woman over it, complete with the call-and-response phrasing, the melisma, and the ecstatic delivery that belonged, in the understanding of the time, to worship.

Churches were furious, and the objection was not unreasonable on its own terms: the vocabulary of religious ecstasy was being used to describe something else entirely, and the resemblance was the point.

Radio did not know what to do with it either. It was too raw for pop, too worldly for gospel, and not quite blues.

What it created was soul music, which is essentially that fusion made permanent. Everything from Aretha Franklin to Otis Redding to Al Green runs through the door Charles opened, and most of those artists came out of church themselves.

He went on to do the same thing to country music a decade later with Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music, which offended a different set of people and sold enormously.

His instinct throughout was that genre boundaries were commercial fictions.
facts: He rewrote an existing gospel song's changes
Radio programmers were unsure which format it belonged to

04-24.title: Kool Herc invented the breakbeat at a Bronx party
04-24.story:
Herc noticed dancers waited for the drum break, so he used two copies of a record to loop it indefinitely. Hip-hop starts there.

The observation came first. Playing records at parties, he noticed that the floor filled during the short percussion passage in the middle of a funk record and emptied when the vocals returned. The breaks were where the dancing actually happened, and they lasted about ten seconds.

The solution was mechanical. Two copies of the same record on two turntables, cueing the second back to the start of the break while the first played, then switching — extending ten seconds into as long as he wanted. He called it the merry-go-round.

Everything else follows from that. Dancers who specialised in the break became b-boys. The MC's role grew out of talking over the extended instrumental. Sampling is the technological version of the same idea.

The party in question, on 11 August 1973 at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, was a back-to-school fundraiser organised by his sister Cindy Campbell to buy clothes. It is as good a founding date as any genre has.

Herc was born in Kingston and brought Jamaican sound system practice with him, which is the direct line connecting Caribbean street culture to the Bronx.

He has never made significant money from any of it.
facts: He called it the 'merry-go-round' technique
The party was a back-to-school fundraiser for his sister

04-25.title: Ella and Louis recorded almost entirely live
04-25.story:
Their duet albums were cut with both singers in the room, no overdubs, letting the timing breathe imperfectly on purpose.

The two voices could hardly be more different. Fitzgerald's is precise, agile, and immaculately in tune; Armstrong's is a gravelled rasp with limited range and a sense of time that pulls against the beat constantly. On paper the pairing should not work.

What makes it work is the room. Both singers were recorded together, live, without overdubs, which means every response is a real response — the small hesitations, the overlaps, and the moments where one clearly amuses the other are events rather than edits.

Producer Norman Granz kept takes with audible laughter in them, which was not standard practice and is most of why the records feel like eavesdropping rather than listening.

The rhythm section was Oscar Peterson's trio with Buddy Rich on drums, playing with unusual restraint. Armstrong's trumpet appears throughout, and his playing is the other half of his contribution — by 1956 the voice had worn considerably and the horn had not.

Modern recording would fix everything that makes these records what they are. Both parts would be cut separately, tuned, and aligned, and the result would be cleaner and completely inert.
facts: Producer Norman Granz kept takes with audible laughter
The rhythm section was Oscar Peterson's trio

04-26.title: Grandmaster Flash built his mixer by hand
04-26.story:
Trained in electronics, Flash rigged a crossfader and cue system so he could hear the next record before the crowd did.

The problem he was solving was precise. Kool Herc's technique required switching between two copies of a record at exactly the right moment, and there was no way to check where the second record was without the audience hearing it. Herc did it by eye and by feel, and it was frequently approximate.

Flash had studied electronics at a vocational school, and he wired a preview system — a single-pole double-throw switch feeding a headphone amp — that let him cue the second turntable silently. Parts were salvaged from junked stereos and car audio.

That single capability is the foundation of everything DJs do now. Being able to hear the next record before the crowd is what makes accurate beat-matching possible, and once it was possible, mixing became a craft with a technical standard rather than an approximation.

He built the rest of the vocabulary on top of it: backspinning, punch phrasing, and the clock theory of marking a record so he could find a specific point instantly.

The crossfader as a standard feature on DJ mixers exists because manufacturers eventually copied what he and his contemporaries had already built for themselves.
facts: He soldered parts salvaged from junked stereos
That preview capability made beat-matching possible

04-27.title: 'Change the Beat' gave the world its most-scratched sound
04-27.story:
The 'ahhh, fresh' vocoder phrase at the end of Fab 5 Freddy's record became the single most-scratched sample in DJ history.

The phrase lasts under two seconds. It was recorded through a vocoder at the very end of the B-side, apparently as an afterthought when there was tape left, and by most accounts was spoken by Beeside — the French rapper on the record — rather than Fab 5 Freddy himself.

What made it the standard is acoustic. The sound has a sharp transient at the front and a sustained vowel behind it, which is exactly what a scratch needs: something that speaks clearly when the record is moved a short distance and stays legible when the direction reverses. Turntablists tested a great deal of material over the years and kept coming back to this.

It is almost certainly the most-scratched sample in existence. It appears in Herbie Hancock's 'Rockit', in an enormous proportion of battle routines, and on records across five decades.

DJ battles are judged on technique, and having a common reference sound means competitors can be compared directly — which turned a throwaway two seconds into something closer to a standard tuning note.

Fab 5 Freddy, a Brooklyn artist, was also the bridge between the downtown art world and the uptown hip-hop scene.
facts: It was recorded almost as an afterthought at the session's end
Nearly every turntablist routine still uses it

04-28.title: Ann Peebles wrote a hit about wanting bad weather
04-28.story:
'I Can't Stand the Rain' came from an offhand complaint about going out in a storm. Her co-writers turned the line into the hook on the spot.

The origin is as ordinary as it sounds. Peebles was heading out for the evening, it was raining, and she said she could not stand the rain. Her partner Don Bryant and the broadcaster Bernard 'Bernie' Miller recognised a hook in the sentence immediately, and the three of them wrote the song that night.

The production is the reason it endures. The opening sound — a repeating high electric timbale figure imitating individual raindrops — was played on a Univox electric timbale, and it establishes the entire mood before a word is sung. Willie Mitchell produced it at Hi Records in Memphis, using the same house band and the same warm, understated approach that made Al Green's records.

John Lennon is widely quoted as calling it the best song he had ever heard, which he said on the radio and which did the record no harm at all.

It was covered repeatedly, sampled by Missy Elliott on 'The Rain', and has had a longer afterlife than its modest chart placing suggested.

Peebles was a genuinely powerful singer whose career was quieter than her talent warranted. She died in 2024.
facts: John Lennon called it the best song he'd ever heard
The opening electric timbale imitates falling rain

04-29.title: Duke Ellington wrote for specific players, not instruments
04-29.story:
Ellington composed around individual musicians' quirks, writing parts only they could play. Replacing a member meant rewriting the music.

This is the thing that separates him from every other composer of comparable stature. A conventional score specifies trumpet; Ellington's specified Cootie Williams, or Bubber Miley, or Johnny Hodges — and the part exploited that particular player's tone, growl technique, or way of bending a note. He described his orchestra as his instrument, and he meant it literally.

The consequence is that the band was not replaceable. When a member left, the music written for them either left with him or had to be rewritten, and Ellington's players consequently stayed for decades, which is unheard of in a business where sidemen rotate constantly.

It also means the recordings are the compositions in a way that written scores are not. Later performances by other orchestras are, unavoidably, arrangements of something that was never fully notated.

He composed constantly and largely on the move — on trains between engagements, in hotel rooms, on the back of whatever paper was available — across a career spanning fifty years and thousands of pieces.

Billy Strayhorn was his writing partner for nearly three decades, and the division of authorship between them remains genuinely difficult to untangle.
facts: He called his orchestra his real instrument
He wrote on trains between gigs for decades

04-30.title: The Ditmas Park porch concert circuit
04-30.story:
Neighbors around Cortelyou Road turned Victorian porches into micro-venues, hosting acoustic sets for audiences of thirty. The tradition continues each summer.

The format works because of the architecture. The blocks around Cortelyou were laid out around 1900 as freestanding wood-frame houses with deep front porches set close to the sidewalk — a design intended to encourage exactly this kind of semi-public sociability, a century before anyone thought to book a band on one.

A porch is a genuinely good small venue. It is raised, so sightlines work; it is covered, so weather is survivable; and the audience stands on a lawn and a sidewalk, which means passers-by become part of the crowd without having to decide to attend.

The scale is the appeal. Thirty people, no PA or a very small one, no ticket, and a hat passed. Nothing about it scales up, which is the point — it produces the kind of listening that a room of a thousand cannot.

Some porches host annual multi-act bills that have been running for years and are publicised almost entirely by word of mouth and neighbourhood mailing lists.

The lineage runs back through house-party culture across Flatbush and, further, to rent parties and stoop gatherings. Cortelyou's version is the same instinct with better woodwork.
facts: Some porches host annual multi-act bills
The format traces back to house-party culture across Flatbush

05-01.title: 'Sunshine of Your Love' came from a bass riff heard at a gig
05-01.story:
Jack Bruce wrote the riff after seeing Jimi Hendrix play live and going home to his bass at dawn.

Cream had gone to see Hendrix at a London club, and Bruce came away rattled. By his account he went home in the early hours, picked up a double bass, and worked out the descending figure that opens the song more or less immediately — a direct response to having watched someone reset the standard for what a guitarist could do.

The riff is unusual in that it is a bass line the guitar doubles rather than a guitar riff with bass underneath, which is why it sits so low and heavy.

Ginger Baker's drum part is the other distinctive element. Rather than marking the backbeat, he plays a tom pattern across the beat that he described as drawing on Native American rhythms, and the effect is that the song does not push forward so much as circle.

The band nearly discarded it. Eric Clapton in particular reportedly thought it too simple, and it took Ahmet Ertegun at Atlantic to insist it was a single.

It became Cream's biggest American hit and one of the most recognisable riffs in rock, which is a reasonable return on a sleepless night.
facts: Ginger Baker's tom pattern was inspired by Native American rhythms
The band nearly rejected it as too simple

05-02.title: Which 'Blinded by the Light' wins: Springsteen or Manfred Mann?
05-02.story:
Springsteen's original is a wordy folk-rock rush. Manfred Mann's Earth Band slowed it, changed a lyric and scored the only Springsteen-written US number one.

The original, from Greetings from Asbury Park, is early Springsteen at his most verbally dense — a torrent of internal rhyme delivered at speed, closer to Dylan than to anything he would do later. It sold almost nothing.

Manfred Mann's Earth Band rebuilt it three years later as a prog-inflected arrangement with a long instrumental introduction, a slower tempo, and considerably more space around the words. It went to number one in America.

The famous misheard lyric belongs to that version. Springsteen wrote 'cut loose like a deuce'; Mann sang 'revved up like a deuce', and the combination of the phrasing and the arrangement has produced decades of listeners hearing something anatomical instead.

Springsteen has joked about the situation more than once: the only American number one he has written as a songwriter is a record by somebody else, and it contains a lyric he did not write.

The pairing is a decent argument that tempo is a compositional decision. The words are largely the same and the second version is legible in a way the first is not, simply because the listener is given room to follow it.
facts: Springsteen has joked he never had a chart-topper with his own version
The famous misheard lyric comes from Mann's rewrite

05-03.title: James Jamerson never wrote his basslines down
05-03.story:
Motown's uncredited bassist improvised most parts on first take. Because nothing was notated, many lines were lost when he died.

He came out of Detroit jazz and approached the bass as a melodic instrument rather than a rhythmic one. His lines move constantly, use chromatic passing tones and syncopation that no arranger would have written, and frequently work against the vocal rather than supporting it — which is precisely why Motown records feel busier and more alive than their contemporaries.

He played with a single index finger, nicknamed the Hook, on a Fender Precision he refused to have cleaned, with strings he never changed.

Almost none of it was notated. He improvised parts on the first or second take and moved to the next session, so the record is the only document. Bass players have spent fifty years transcribing his playing by ear.

He appears on more number one singles than the Beatles, the Beach Boys, and Elvis Presley combined, and he was not credited on album sleeves for most of his career. The Funk Brothers as a group were essentially anonymous by label policy.

When Motown moved to Los Angeles in 1972, most of the band was left behind. Jamerson's later years were difficult and he died in 1983, at forty-seven.
facts: He appears on more number ones than the Beatles and Elvis combined
He was not credited on album sleeves for most of his career

05-04.title: 'Sing Sing' delivered the drums for a hip-hop decade
05-04.story:
Gaz's 'Sing Sing' and its cousins supplied breaks that New York DJs guarded like secrets, soaking labels off records to hide titles.

The secrecy was competitive and total. A DJ's value at a block party rested on having breaks nobody else could identify, so records were carried in blank sleeves and their labels were soaked off in water or scratched into illegibility. Rivals would push toward the turntables during a set specifically to read a label, and getting close enough was a genuine victory.

That culture is the direct origin of crate digging as a discipline. Finding a usable break meant listening through entire albums of unpromising material for a few seconds of drums, in thrift stores, church sales, and the bargain bins of shops that had no idea what they were holding.

Break compilations began appearing in the eighties — bootleg records collecting the useful passages in one place — which democratised access and infuriated the DJs who had done the searching.

What the practice produced was an enormous act of collective musical archaeology. Records that had failed commercially and been forgotten were rediscovered, recontextualised, and given a second life entirely detached from their original purpose.

Most of the musicians who played on them never knew.
facts: DJs soaked or scratched off labels to protect their sources
Digging culture grew directly from that secrecy

05-05.title: Bo Diddley built his own rectangular guitars
05-05.story:
Diddley designed square-bodied guitars because standard shapes were awkward when he jumped around on stage. His clave-derived rhythm became a genre unto itself.

The square shape was ergonomic rather than decorative. He moved constantly on stage, and a conventional guitar body swung awkwardly and dug into him; a rectangle balanced better and stayed put. He built early versions himself in a workshop before Gretsch began making them for him.

The rhythm is the larger legacy. The Bo Diddley beat — three strokes, rest, two strokes — is closely related to the Afro-Cuban clave, and it arrives in his records via the long transmission of African rhythm through the Caribbean into American music. It is a pattern rather than a chord sequence, which means a song can be built on it with essentially no harmonic movement at all.

Hundreds of records use it: Buddy Holly's 'Not Fade Away', the Rolling Stones, the Who, U2, George Michael, and an enormous quantity of garage rock.

He was also an early user of tremolo and distortion, and his guitar sound was considerably more aggressive than most of what surrounded it in 1955.

Like most Black artists of his generation on Chess, he was paid badly and spent decades saying so publicly and without much diplomacy.
facts: The 'Bo Diddley beat' underpins hundreds of rock songs
He built early guitars himself in a workshop

05-06.title: Sam Cooke wrote 'A Change Is Gonna Come' after hearing Dylan
05-06.story:
Cooke was struck that a white songwriter had written 'Blowin' in the Wind' before he had written anything like it, and responded within months.

His reaction, as reported by people around him, was closer to embarrassment than admiration. He thought the song was good and that it should not have taken a young white folk singer to write it — that this was material he had a stronger claim to and had been avoiding.

The avoidance was commercial and rational. Cooke had built a crossover career singing to white audiences, and explicitly political material threatened it. He had also, shortly before writing the song, been arrested with his band for trying to register at a whites-only motel in Louisiana.

The arrangement is unusual for R&B of the period: a full string and horn score with timpani, closer to film music than to a soul single, which gives the song a weight the radio format did not normally permit.

He was reportedly uneasy performing it live, describing it as too personal, and it was played publicly only a handful of times before his death.

Cooke was shot and killed in December 1964 in circumstances that remain disputed. The song was released as a single days after his funeral.
facts: He was nervous performing it live, calling it too personal
The string arrangement was unusually cinematic for R&B

05-07.title: 'La Di Da Di' is a rap record with no instruments
05-07.story:
Doug E. Fresh beatboxed the entire backing track while Slick Rick rapped over it. Nothing else appears on the recording.

There is no drum machine, no sample, and no instrument on the record. Doug E. Fresh produces the entire rhythm track with his mouth — kick, snare, hi-hat, and a bassline — while Slick Rick delivers a narrative verse over the top, and both performances are essentially live.

Beatboxing was a practical solution before it was an art form. Crews without equipment needed a beat, and a human being was the cheapest available drum machine. Doug E. Fresh was the performer who demonstrated it could be the record rather than a substitute for one.

Slick Rick's contribution is the other half. His delivery is conversational, comic, and built around storytelling with character voices, and it established a narrative style that a large part of the genre followed.

The record has been sampled, interpolated, and rebuilt hundreds of times. Snoop Dogg's 'Lodi Dodi' reproduces the lyrics almost wholesale, Biggie's 'Hypnotize' quotes it, and it turns up in pop records decades later.

For something made by two people and a microphone, its footprint is disproportionate to almost anything else from the period.
facts: It has been sampled on hundreds of songs
Snoop Dogg rebuilt an entire track from its lyrics

extra.src: Doug E. Fresh & Slick Rick - La Di Da Di (1985)

05-08.title: Robert Moog never intended to build a music instrument
05-08.story:
Moog was a theremin hobbyist and engineer who built modules to order. Musicians told him what they needed and the synthesizer emerged.

He started by selling theremin kits as a teenager, out of genuine hobbyist enthusiasm rather than any commercial plan. The synthesizer developed from conversations with musicians — particularly the composer Herbert Deutsch — about what they wanted a circuit to do, and Moog built modules in response to requests.

The design decisions that made it usable came from that dialogue. Voltage control, which allows one module to govern another and is the fundamental principle of the whole instrument, was an engineering solution to a musical request. The keyboard was added because players kept asking for one; there was nothing inherent in the technology that required it.

He described himself as a toolmaker rather than a musician, and consistently deflected credit toward the people who used what he built.

The commercial history was less happy. He was a poor businessman by his own admission, lost control of his own company, and for a period was legally unable to use his own name on products.

Wendy Carlos's Switched-On Bach in 1968 is what made the instrument credible to musicians who had dismissed it as a novelty.
facts: The keyboard was added because players asked for one
He said he thought of himself as a toolmaker, not a musician

05-09.title: Which 'Nothing Compares 2 U' wins: Prince or Sinéad?
05-09.story:
Prince wrote it for his side project The Family. Sinéad O'Connor's 1990 version, with its single-shot video, became definitive.

The Family's original is a full band arrangement with saxophone, buried on an album by a Prince side project that lasted one record. Almost nobody heard it, and Prince rarely performed the song himself until after O'Connor's version succeeded.

Her reading strips it to a sparse arrangement and a vocal that moves from restrained to broken over four minutes. Producer Nellee Hooper's arrangement leaves an enormous amount of space, which puts all the weight on the performance.

The video is close to a single continuous shot of her face, and the tears near the end were reportedly not planned — she has said she was thinking about her mother, who had died in 1985. That accident is a large part of why the record landed the way it did.

O'Connor's relationship with fame afterward was adversarial and principled. Her 1992 protest against the Catholic Church on live television cost her enormously at the time and looks quite different now.

She died in 2023. Her account of Prince's own behaviour toward her was, by her telling, frightening — the two never had a comfortable relationship over a song that made them both.
facts: Her tears in the video were reportedly unplanned
Prince rarely performed it before her version succeeded

05-10.title: Bo Hansson and the rise of the bedroom studio
05-10.story:
Long before home recording was normal, musicians began assembling private studios, shifting power away from label-owned rooms.

The economics had been fixed for decades. Recording required a studio, a studio cost money by the hour, and the label paid — which meant the label controlled access, scheduling, and ultimately what got made. An artist without a deal had essentially no route to a finished record.

Multitrack tape machines becoming affordable in the seventies broke that. Once a musician could own four or eight tracks, they could work at their own pace, experiment without a meter running, and arrive at a label with something finished rather than a request.

The Swedish keyboardist Bo Hansson is an early and fairly obscure example — his Lord of the Rings album was assembled largely in a private setup — and the pattern repeats through Brian Eno, through eighties four-track cassette recording, through the sampler and the sequencer, and into the laptop.

What changed each time was not sound quality but who was permitted to make a record.

The current end point is that professional-standard production is available on hardware most people already own. The consequence is an enormous increase in supply and a corresponding collapse in the value of distribution, which is the industry's actual problem now.
facts: Multitrack tape became affordable in the seventies
This lineage runs directly to laptop production today

05-11.title: Bob Marley survived being shot and played two days later
05-11.story:
Gunmen wounded Marley at his Kingston home before a peace concert. He performed anyway, showing the crowd his injured arm.

The context was a Jamaican election campaign of extraordinary violence, with the two major parties operating through armed gangs in Kingston neighbourhoods. Marley had agreed to play Smile Jamaica, a free concert intended to ease tensions, and the event had been widely read as aligning him with the governing party regardless of his intentions.

Gunmen entered his home at 56 Hope Road two days before the show. Marley was hit in the arm and chest, his wife Rita was shot in the head, and his manager Don Taylor was seriously wounded. All survived.

He played the concert. He appeared on stage with his arm visibly injured, performed for a substantial set rather than the short appearance expected, and at one point opened his shirt and raised his arms to show the crowd the wounds.

His remark afterward — that the people trying to make this world worse were not taking a day off, so he could not either — is the most-quoted thing he ever said outside a lyric.

He left Jamaica for London shortly after and stayed away for roughly eighteen months, recording Exodus in exile.
facts: He said 'the people who are trying to make this world worse aren't taking a day off'
He left Jamaica for London shortly after

05-12.title: The Winstons' break has its own documentary
05-12.story:
Decades after 'Amen, Brother', filmmakers traced how six seconds spawned entire scenes without the band's knowledge or payment.

Nate Harrison's 2004 video essay Can I Get an Amen? is the best-known account, and it makes an argument beyond the anecdote: that copyright as constructed does not recognise the thing that was actually valuable. Gregory Coleman's performance — the specific way he played those bars — is not itself protected in a way that generated any income for him, while the underlying composition and the recording sit with rights holders who had no part in it.

The scale of the uncompensated use is difficult to overstate. Jungle and drum and bass are built on it essentially wholesale, Aphex Twin and Squarepusher constructed careers partly on manipulating it, and it appears across rave, hip-hop, pop, and advertising.

Richard Spencer, the Winstons' leader, held the copyright and never pursued enforcement, which would have been ruinously expensive and legally uncertain across decades and jurisdictions.

A UK crowdfunding campaign in 2015 raised a modest amount and handed it to him — an entirely voluntary gesture from producers who felt the debt, with no legal basis whatsoever.

Coleman died homeless in 2006, having received nothing.
facts: Copyright never protected the drummer's performance itself
Public fundraising eventually delivered some belated compensation

05-13.title: Stevie Wonder's harmonica part was a first take
05-13.story:
'Fingertips' captured a 12-year-old improvising live, including a bassist audibly asking 'What key? What key?' as the band scrambled.

The recording is from a Motortown Revue performance, and it is genuinely chaotic. Wonder, billed as Little Stevie Wonder, finished the number, left the stage, and then came back on and started playing again — which nobody had planned for. The band that had been setting up for the next act had to rejoin mid-song.

The bass player Larry Moses had already packed up, so the previous act's bassist Joe Swift stepped in, and his shouted question — what key, what key — is audible on the released record. Motown left it in.

That decision is a large part of why the record works. It is a document of something going wrong and being rescued in real time, with a crowd audibly responding to it, and the excitement is not manufactured.

It became Motown's first live recording to reach number one, and it made Wonder, at twelve, the youngest artist to top the American chart.

The label spent the following years unsure what to do with him as his voice changed. The autonomy that produced his great run was still a decade away.
facts: That confused shout is on the released record
It became Motown's first live number one

05-14.title: Sister Nancy's 'Bam Bam' is reggae's most reused hook
05-14.story:
Recorded quickly over an existing riddim, it became one of the most sampled Jamaican records ever, though she saw little income for decades.

The track was cut at Channel One over the Stalag riddim, a rhythm track from 1973 that has been reused hundreds of times — the Jamaican convention of multiple artists recording over a shared instrumental, which has no real equivalent in American practice.

She was among very few women working as a deejay in a scene that was almost entirely male, and the record established a template that later dancehall vocalists followed closely.

What happened afterward is the familiar part. The song was sampled and licensed extensively for decades — Kanye West, Jay-Z, Lauryn Hill, films, advertising — and she received essentially nothing. She has described discovering her own voice in a film while sitting in a cinema, with no prior knowledge that it had been used.

She was working as an accountant in New Jersey through much of this period.

She eventually pursued the matter and regained rights to her recording, and has since been able to tour and earn from the song. That resolution took roughly thirty years and happened because she pushed for it, not because any system corrected itself.
facts: She discovered her song in a film only by chance
She later won back rights to her recording

05-15.title: Brooklyn's Coney Island Baby and the doo-wop corners
05-15.story:
Street-corner harmony groups rehearsed in Brooklyn subway entrances and hallways for the natural reverb, an early form of free studio time.

The acoustics were the entire point. A tiled subway stairwell or a tenement hallway is a hard-surfaced reverberant box, and singing four-part harmony into one produces a natural reverb that a group could not otherwise access. Studio time cost money nobody had; a stairwell was free and open all night.

That sound is audible on the records. Doo-wop production frequently tried to reproduce the hallway rather than the concert hall, and groups auditioned by singing under overpasses and in entryways because that was where they sounded like themselves.

The form itself was a working-class Black and Italian American street tradition across Brooklyn, Harlem, and the Bronx — a cappella harmony built on a nonsense-syllable bass line, requiring no instruments and therefore no money.

Most groups never recorded. Those that did were frequently signed to small labels on terms that returned almost nothing, and the pattern of teenagers signing away rights they did not understand was close to universal.

The influence carried forward directly into soul, into Motown's vocal group arrangements, and into the harmony singing underneath a great deal of what followed.
facts: Tiled stairwells acted as echo chambers
Groups auditioned by singing under overpasses

05-16.title: Which 'Mr. Tambourine Man' wins: Dylan or The Byrds?
05-16.story:
Dylan's original is a long acoustic reverie. The Byrds cut it to two and a half minutes with a 12-string Rickenbacker and invented folk-rock.

Dylan's version runs over five minutes across several verses, acoustic, unhurried, and structurally closer to a poem set to a tune than to a pop single.

The Byrds kept one verse, added a chorus at each end, put it in a different key, and built it on Roger McGuinn's twelve-string Rickenbacker with close vocal harmony. Two and a half minutes, radio-shaped, and effectively the founding record of folk-rock — a genre that then absorbed a substantial part of the American charts within a year.

The recording is not really the band. Columbia's producer used session players — the Los Angeles pool later known as the Wrecking Crew — for the instrumental track, with only McGuinn among the Byrds actually playing. The vocals are the group.

That was normal practice and it does not diminish the arrangement, which is the actual innovation: the jangling twelve-string against harmony singing became one of the most copied textures in rock, running through the Beatles' mid-period work, R.E.M., and a great deal after.

Dylan reportedly heard it and observed that you could dance to it, which was not something anyone had said about his songs before.
facts: Only one Byrd actually played on the recording
Session players filled in the rest

05-17.title: Bill Withers was making toilet seats for airplanes
05-17.story:
Withers kept his factory job while recording 'Ain't No Sunshine', assuming music would not last. The famous repeated 'I know' was a placeholder.

He was thirty-two, had spent nine years in the Navy, and was working at a factory making aircraft lavatory fittings. He recorded his first album while still employed there, and photographs from the period show him at the studio holding his lunchbox, because he was going to work afterward.

The caution was rational. He had watched the industry chew through people and had no reason to believe he would be an exception, and he kept the job until the record was demonstrably working.

The repeated 'I know' — twenty-six times in a row — was a placeholder. He intended to write a proper verse there and was told by the people in the room, including Booker T. Jones, to leave it. It is now the most memorable thing in the song, and it works because the repetition does something a lyric could not: it enacts the obsessiveness the words are describing.

He left the industry in the mid-eighties after protracted conflict with his label about creative control, and simply stopped. He gave interviews occasionally and declined, for decades, to come back.

He died in 2020.
facts: He meant to write real lyrics there but was told to keep it
He brought his lunchbox to the studio

05-18.title: Delia Derbyshire realized the Doctor Who theme with tape
05-18.story:
Working without synthesizers, Derbyshire built the theme by recording single tones, cutting the tape and splicing pitches by hand.

The BBC Radiophonic Workshop had no synthesizers because none existed commercially. What it had was oscillators, tape machines, filters, and an enormous amount of patience, and every sound had to be constructed physically.

Derbyshire's method for the theme was close to insane by modern standards. Individual notes were generated as single tones, recorded to tape, cut to length with a razor, and spliced together in sequence — with the length of each piece of tape determining the duration of the note and the tape speed determining its pitch. Lengths were measured with a ruler.

The bassline, the swooping effects, and the melody were all assembled this way and then synchronised across multiple machines running simultaneously, because there was no multitrack.

Ron Grainer wrote the melody and, on hearing what she had made of it, reportedly asked whether he had written it. He wanted to give her a co-credit and BBC policy prevented it — Workshop staff were not credited as composers. She received no on-screen credit for years.

It is one of the first pieces of electronic music heard weekly by a mass audience, and it was made by cutting up tape with a blade.
facts: Each note was measured with a ruler
She received no on-screen composer credit for years

05-19.title: 'Impeach the President' gave hip-hop its snare
05-19.story:
The Honey Drippers' record, cut by a high-school band, contains a drum intro that became a foundation of nineties New York production.

The players were teenagers. Roy C. Hammond recorded the track with a group of high school students from Long Island, and the opening bars — drums alone, before anything else enters — are what producers came for two decades later.

The snare is the specific asset. It has a particular crack and decay that sits perfectly in a mid-tempo loop, and it became the default snare sound of boom-bap New York production. Once you know it, you hear it constantly across the early nineties.

The song itself is explicitly political, released during Watergate, which is a fairly unusual origin for something that became primarily valued as raw material.

It appears on records by Nas, Digable Planets, Audio Two, Janet Jackson, and a very long list beyond, and it is one of the handful of breaks — alongside the Amen, Funky Drummer, and Apache — that effectively defined a genre's rhythmic vocabulary.

Hammond has been more successful than most in pursuing sample income, which puts him in a small minority among the people whose recordings hip-hop was built from.
facts: Its snare defines much of the boom-bap era
The players were teenagers when they recorded it

extra.src: The Honey Drippers - Impeach the President (1973)
hits: Janet Jackson - That's the Way Love Goes

05-20.title: Bach's music was rescued by a butcher's wrapping paper
05-20.story:
Legend holds Mendelssohn found Bach manuscripts used as packing material, sparking the revival that restored Bach to the canon.

The wrapping paper story is almost certainly embellished — versions of it attach to several composers and the documentary basis is thin. What is solid is that Bach's music had substantially fallen out of performance after his death in 1750, that he was remembered primarily as an organist and a technician rather than a composer, and that a great deal of the manuscript material sat unpublished and unperformed.

Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of the St Matthew Passion in Berlin is the event that changed it. He was twenty, he cut and reorchestrated the work considerably to suit the forces and tastes of the time, and the performance was a public sensation. It is generally treated as the beginning of the Bach revival.

The broader point is uncomfortable. A composer now regarded as foundational to Western music spent roughly eighty years in near-obscurity, and his return depended on a wealthy, well-connected young musician deciding to take the trouble.

What else did not get a Mendelssohn is unanswerable, which is precisely the problem with canons. They record what survived, not what was best.
facts: He staged the St Matthew Passion after 100 years of neglect
Bach was known mainly as an organist in his lifetime

05-21.title: The Bomb Squad layered dozens of samples per track
05-21.story:
Public Enemy's producers stacked sirens, horn stabs and drums into deliberately abrasive collages, a technique legally impossible today.

The approach was maximalist and deliberately unpleasant. Hank Shocklee and the Bomb Squad built tracks from twenty or more distinct sources — James Brown fragments, sirens, squealing saxophone, speech, noise — layered until the result was dense to the point of physical discomfort. The stated intention was that the music should sound like the environment it described.

It worked because nothing was cleared. In 1988 sample clearance was not systematically enforced, so a producer could use thirty sources without a lawyer being involved, and the entire aesthetic depended on that freedom.

The legal environment closed within a few years. Once clearance became mandatory and the 2005 Bridgeport ruling removed any de minimis threshold, the arithmetic became impossible: thirty sources means sixty rights holders, any of whom can refuse.

Chuck D and Shocklee have both said plainly that It Takes a Nation of Millions could not be made now at any budget.

That means a specific production style is not merely out of fashion but legally foreclosed — a window of about five years in which a form of music was possible and after which it was not.
facts: Some tracks contain over 20 distinct sources
Clearance costs would now exceed any budget

05-22.title: 'Trans-Europe Express' became the spine of electro
05-22.story:
Afrika Bambaataa built 'Planet Rock' on Kraftwerk's melody and a TR-808, connecting Düsseldorf to the Bronx.

The combination was audacious. Bambaataa took the melody from Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express', the rhythm from their 'Numbers', put both over a Roland TR-808, and produced a record that sounded like nothing before it. The connection it made — between German electronic art music and Bronx block party culture — was not obvious to anyone except the DJs who had been playing Kraftwerk records to dancers for years.

That is the part often missed. Kraftwerk were already popular in the Bronx. 'Trans-Europe Express' worked on a dancefloor, and DJs treated it as functional party music rather than as European conceptualism.

The rights position was not settled in advance, and Kraftwerk's publishers pursued the matter afterward, resulting in a settlement.

What 'Planet Rock' created was electro, essentially whole: 808 drums, synthesizer melody, vocoder, and a rhythmic feel distinct from both funk and disco. Miami bass, Detroit techno, and a substantial portion of subsequent dance music descend from it directly.

It is also the record that put the 808 at the centre of American popular music, where it has remained for forty years.
facts: Kraftwerk's label pursued the matter afterward
The record effectively created electro as a genre

05-23.title: Rosetta Tharpe played a train station gig
05-23.story:
Promoters staged a concert on a disused British railway platform with the audience across the tracks. Tharpe arrived by carriage and played in the rain.

The event was part of the American Folk Blues and Gospel Caravan tour, and the venue was a disused station at Wilbraham Road in Manchester. Granada Television filmed it. The staging was theatrical to the point of absurdity: the performers played on one platform while the audience sat on the opposite one, across the tracks, and Tharpe was delivered to the stage in a horse-drawn carriage.

It then rained, and she played through it without stopping, in a fur coat, on a Gibson SG, performing 'Didn't It Rain' — which is either an extraordinary coincidence or an extraordinary piece of professional presence of mind.

The footage survives and is now among the most widely seen documents of her playing. It shows the technique clearly: aggressive attack, bent notes, and a command of the audience that has nothing to do with the guitar.

British audiences of the period were far more receptive to Black American gospel and blues artists than American ones, and a number of musicians found late-career work and genuine respect touring Britain when the domestic circuit had dried up.

She was fifty at the time and had been playing electric guitar for nearly thirty years.
facts: The footage became one of her best-known performances
She improvised through a downpour without stopping

05-24.title: Bob Dylan went electric and got booed
05-24.story:
At Newport, Dylan plugged in and split the folk audience. The hostility followed him across a world tour.

The Newport Folk Festival set was short — three electric songs with members of the Paul Butterfield Blues Band — and the accounts of what happened are genuinely contradictory. Some present insist the booing was about the sound quality and the brevity of the set rather than the electricity; others describe real hostility. Both are probably partly true.

What is not in doubt is the reaction over the following year. The 1966 world tour, with the Hawks behind him, met organised heckling in Britain night after night, with audiences slow-clapping and shouting through the electric half.

The most famous moment was at the Free Trade Hall in Manchester, where a voice from the audience shouted 'Judas'. Dylan responded that he did not believe him, called him a liar, and told the band to play it loud. What followed was a version of 'Like a Rolling Stone' played with genuine aggression.

The underlying argument was about authenticity and ownership — a folk audience that regarded acoustic music as morally serious and amplification as commercial betrayal, and a songwriter who had no interest in being anyone's property.
facts: A famous heckler shouted 'Judas' in Manchester
He responded by telling the band to play louder

05-25.title: Miles Davis plugged in and lost half his audience
05-25.story:
'Bitches Brew' used electric instruments and studio editing, alienating purists while inventing fusion.

The electric instruments were only half of it. The more radical decision was structural: producer Teo Macero recorded long, loosely directed sessions and then assembled the album afterward with tape splices, looping passages, repeating sections, and constructing pieces that were never performed continuously by anyone.

That is a rock and pop production method applied to jazz, and to a substantial part of the jazz audience it was a betrayal of the form's founding principle — that a recording documents musicians playing.

Davis was explicit about his motivation. He had watched Sly Stone and Jimi Hendrix reach audiences that jazz was losing, and he had no interest in curating a museum.

The personnel is remarkable in hindsight: Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock, John McLaughlin, Joe Zawinul, Jack DeJohnette. Nearly all of them went on to lead the fusion movement the album started.

It sold better than any jazz record he had made and cost him a substantial part of his existing audience.

He did this repeatedly across his career — bebop, cool, modal, fusion — and each time the people who had followed him to the last position objected to the next.
facts: Producer Teo Macero spliced the tapes like a film editor
Long passages were assembled, not performed continuously

05-26.title: Which 'Killing Me Softly' wins: Flack or the Fugees?
05-26.story:
Roberta Flack's version is intimate and slow. The Fugees rebuilt it in 1996 over a hip-hop break with Lauryn Hill's lead.

Flack's is the definitive reading for a generation: slow, close, with an arrangement that recedes almost entirely behind the voice. She heard Lori Lieberman's original on a plane, worked on her interpretation for months, and the result is a masterclass in restraint — she never pushes, and the song is more devastating for it.

The Fugees kept the melody essentially unchanged and rebuilt everything around it, putting Lauryn Hill's lead over a hip-hop drum loop with the group's vocals responding around her. It is a cover in the most literal sense and it functions as a completely different record.

What makes it work is that they did not try to out-sing Flack. The arrangement supplies the energy and Hill's delivery stays conversational, which leaves the song's intimacy intact inside a much bigger production.

Flack praised the version publicly and without qualification, which is not the standard response of an artist watching a younger group take a signature song.

It introduced the song to an audience that had not been born when the original charted, and both versions now circulate simultaneously — which is the best outcome a cover can produce.
facts: Flack publicly praised the remake
The Fugees kept the melody almost unchanged

05-27.title: Brooklyn's Fulton Street record shops fed the DJs
05-27.story:
Independent shops along Fulton and Flatbush stocked breaks, imports and white labels that defined what Brooklyn DJs could play.

The shops were infrastructure, not retail. In a period before any digital distribution, what a DJ could play was determined entirely by what was physically available within travelling distance, and the independent shops along Fulton and Flatbush were where Brooklyn's supply came from — breaks, Jamaican imports, promotional white labels, and records the chains would never stock.

Shop owners functioned as informal A&R. They knew what was selling, who was buying, and which unknown record was being asked for repeatedly, and that information moved faster than any label's research. A recommendation from behind the counter could put a record into a dozen DJ crates in a week.

The shops were also social. Crews formed in the aisles, DJs met producers, and the flow of information about what was coming ran through those rooms.

Almost all of them are gone. The combination of digital distribution, rising commercial rents along both corridors, and the collapse of physical singles removed the economic basis within about a decade.

What was lost with them is harder to replace than the records: a physical place where the people who cared about this music encountered each other by default.
facts: Shop owners often acted as informal A&R
Many crews formed in the aisles

05-28.title: Gladys Knight had the first 'Grapevine' hit, then lost it
05-28.story:
Gladys Knight and the Pips charted with 'I Heard It Through the Grapevine' before Marvin Gaye's slower version eclipsed it entirely.

Gaye actually recorded it first, in early 1967. Motown's quality control committee — a real internal body that voted on which records the label released — rejected it, and the song was given to Gladys Knight and the Pips, whose faster, gospel-driven version went to number two.

Gaye's take sat on the shelf for over a year and was eventually released as an album track. Radio programmers found it themselves and began playing it, and the demand became large enough that Motown had no choice but to issue it as a single.

It became the label's biggest-selling record to that point.

The two versions are a good demonstration of what tempo does to meaning. Knight's is defiant and propulsive — a person confronting a betrayal with energy. Gaye's is slow, sparse, and paranoid, and the arrangement leaves so much space that the vocal sounds genuinely isolated.

The song was written by Norman Whitfield and Barrett Strong, and Whitfield had pushed hard for the Gaye version against the committee's judgement. He was right, and the committee's process — which normally worked well — produced one of the label's clearest misjudgements.
facts: Motown shelved Gaye's take for over a year
Gaye's version became the label's biggest-selling single to that point

05-29.title: Stravinsky's premiere caused a riot
05-29.story:
'The Rite of Spring' provoked shouting and fistfights at its Paris debut. The dancers could not hear the orchestra over the noise.

The disturbance began early and escalated. Accounts describe shouting, whistling, objects thrown, and physical fights in the aisles, with the police called at some point during the performance. The noise became loud enough that the dancers could not hear the orchestra, and Nijinsky, the choreographer, stood in the wings shouting counts at them.

How much of it was the music and how much the choreography is still argued. Stravinsky's score is genuinely violent — irregular metre, brutal dissonance, a bassoon opening in a register at the top of its range — but Nijinsky's choreography was equally confrontational: turned-in feet, stamping, and a deliberate rejection of everything classical ballet had established.

There is also a reasonable case that a portion of the audience arrived expecting a scandal and supplied one.

The work was performed again shortly afterward without incident, and it is now standard repertoire, played by student orchestras and used in a Disney film.

What the episode preserves is a genuine cultural rupture point — a moment when an audience understood clearly that something had changed and objected in real time.
facts: The choreographer shouted counts from the wings
It is now standard repertoire worldwide

05-30.title: The SP-1200 forced producers to be brief
05-30.story:
The sampler held only about ten seconds of audio, so producers chopped tightly and sped samples up, creating a gritty sound now sought deliberately.

The memory limit was around ten seconds total, split across banks. That is not enough for a loop of any length, so producers developed a workaround: record the sample at a faster tape speed so it takes up less memory, then pitch it back down on playback. That process degrades the audio, and the degradation is the sound.

The machine's twelve-bit converters added the rest. Twelve-bit resolution is coarse by any modern standard and introduces a specific grit and compression to the low end, which producers came to want rather than tolerate.

The constraint shaped the entire aesthetic of early-nineties New York production. Short, tightly chopped samples, hard swing, and a slightly dirty texture are all consequences of a machine that could not do more.

DJ Premier, Pete Rock, Large Professor, and RZA all built their signatures on it.

Modern plugins now emulate those limitations deliberately — twelve-bit reduction, memory-constrained workflow, the specific filter curve — which is a strange endpoint. Producers with unlimited resources pay to reintroduce restrictions that everyone in 1987 was working around.
facts: Its 12-bit conversion added the crunch producers loved
Modern plugins emulate its limitations on purpose

05-31.title: 'Ashley's Roachclip' hid a break at the very end
05-31.story:
The Soul Searchers buried a drum break near the track's close, which producers found decades later and used everywhere.

It sits near the end of the track, after several minutes of music that gives no indication it is coming. Finding it required listening to the whole thing, which is precisely the work that crate digging consisted of — hours of unpromising records played through in full for the possibility of a few usable seconds.

The break itself has a distinctive tambourine layered over the drums, which is what makes it instantly identifiable once you know it.

It drives Eric B. & Rakim's 'Paid in Full', PM Dawn's 'Set Adrift on Memory Bliss', and Milli Vanilli's 'Girl You Know It's True' — which means one buried passage from a modestly selling 1974 record underpins both a foundational hip-hop album track and one of the biggest and most notorious pop hits of the eighties.

The Soul Searchers were led by Chuck Brown, who went on to essentially invent go-go, the Washington DC funk style built on continuous percussion and call-and-response.

The economics of all this were, as usual, one-directional. The value created by the break vastly exceeded anything that flowed back to the people who played it.
facts: Digging often meant listening to full albums for seconds of usable audio
The break drives one of the biggest pop hits of the eighties

hits: Eric B. & Rakim - Paid in Full
Milli Vanilli - Girl You Know It's True
PM Dawn - Set Adrift on Memory Bliss

06-01.title: Marilyn Monroe's birthday and the art of the breathy mic
06-01.story:
Close-mic crooning only became possible with sensitive condenser microphones, letting singers whisper instead of project.

Before electrical recording, a singer's job was partly athletic. Acoustic recording required enough volume to physically move a diaphragm, and live performance in a large room required filling it without amplification — which is why the popular singers of the early twentieth century sound like opera singers whether or not they were trained as such.

The condenser microphone changed the arithmetic entirely. Suddenly a whisper could be captured with detail, and singers could work at conversational volume with all the nuance that permits: breath, consonants, the slight break in a held note. Bing Crosby was the first major figure to build a style on it, and everything called crooning descends from that technical shift.

Monroe's singing voice is the extreme case. It has almost no projection and enormous intimacy, and it only functions as a recorded and amplified instrument. A hundred years earlier there would have been no way for it to exist professionally.

The broader point is that vocal style is downstream of microphone technology more often than of taste. Belting, crooning, close-mic rap delivery, and modern pop's heavily compressed intimacy are each responses to what the equipment of the period rewarded.
facts: Before electric mics, singers needed opera-level volume
The intimate vocal style is a technology story as much as a taste one

06-02.title: Charlie Watts kept time by leaving the hi-hat out
06-02.story:
The Rolling Stones drummer lifted his hi-hat hand on backbeats, a jazz habit that gave the band its slight, distinctive drag.

The technique is small and its consequences are not. Most rock drummers play continuous eighth notes on the hi-hat while the snare hits the backbeat, so both hands strike together on beats two and four. Watts lifted his right hand off the hi-hat at exactly those moments, so the snare lands alone.

The result is a fractional gap in the texture on every backbeat, which the ear reads as the beat pulling slightly rather than driving. It is most of why Stones grooves feel loose and slightly behind, and it is why drummers who play the parts note-perfectly still fail to sound like the records.

He took the habit from jazz, which is what he actually cared about. He described himself as a jazz drummer for his entire life, played in jazz ensembles throughout, and was reportedly bemused to have spent sixty years in a rock band.

His playing is also notably economical. He rarely fills, almost never solos, and leaves an enormous amount of space, which is what allows two guitars playing simultaneously to sit where they do.

He died in 2021, having played with essentially the same feel since 1963.
facts: He considered himself a jazz drummer his whole life
That tiny gap is why Stones grooves feel loose

06-03.title: Which 'Twist and Shout' wins: Isley Brothers or Beatles?
06-03.story:
The Isley Brothers cut the definitive early version. Lennon recorded the Beatles' take last on a session day with a shredded throat.

The Isleys' 1962 recording is the one that established the song — call and response, building intensity, and a vocal arrangement that everything afterward copied. It was not the first version; the Top Notes cut it a year earlier in an arrangement Bert Berns, who co-wrote it, reportedly hated.

The Beatles recorded theirs at the end of a single day in which they had cut most of their debut album. Lennon had a cold, had been singing for something in the region of twelve hours, and his voice was going. It was scheduled last precisely because everyone knew what it would do to him.

He drank milk, gargled, and did it in one take. A second take was attempted and was unusable, because there was nothing left.

That is why the record sounds the way it does. The tearing quality in the vocal is not a stylistic choice or a studio effect — it is a voice being destroyed in real time, captured because there was no alternative.

Both versions are correct. The Isleys' is a great arrangement performed well. The Beatles' is a document of physical extremity, which is a different and rarer thing.
facts: Lennon's voice gave out immediately afterward
It was done in one take because he could not sing another

06-04.title: Cecil Taylor turned the piano into percussion
06-04.story:
Taylor attacked the keyboard with clusters and forearms, treating it as 88 tuned drums rather than a melodic instrument.

The reconception is total. Conventional piano technique treats the instrument as a means of producing lines and harmonies; Taylor treated it as a percussion instrument that happens to have pitches, using tone clusters, forearm strikes, and extraordinary physical velocity to produce dense masses of sound rather than melodies.

He was conservatory trained, at the New England Conservatory, and had a thorough grounding in European modernism as well as jazz. The playing is not an absence of technique; it is an enormous amount of technique pointed somewhere unfamiliar.

Audiences left. Early performances in the fifties and sixties emptied rooms routinely, and he spent years working day jobs — including as a dishwasher — while making some of the most demanding music of the period.

His endurance was legendary. Solo performances could run over an hour without pause at a physical intensity closer to athletics than to recital playing.

He is one of the founding figures of free jazz alongside Ornette Coleman, and unlike Coleman he never made a concession toward accessibility in six decades.

He died in 2018, having been essentially uncompromising for longer than most careers last.
facts: He trained classically at conservatory
Audiences frequently walked out of early performances

06-05.title: Bill Withers recorded 'Grandma's Hands' in under two minutes
06-05.story:
Withers wrote about his grandmother's church in West Virginia. The song is barely 120 seconds long and needed nothing more.

The restraint is the craft. It is a series of images of one woman's hands — clapping in church, picking him up, warning him about the street — and each verse is a single memory delivered without commentary. There is no bridge, no key change, and no attempt to broaden it into a statement about grandmothers generally.

He resisted adding anything. The song says what it has to say and stops, which is a much harder decision than extending it.

Withers was in his early thirties and still working a factory job when he recorded it, and the writing throughout that first album has a plainness that came from not having spent years inside the music industry learning what songs are supposed to do.

Blackstreet's 'No Diggity' is built on it, using the guitar figure and Withers's voice, and it introduced the song to an audience two generations later.

The original runs about two minutes. Contemporary radio convention said a single needed roughly three, and Withers's response was that the song was finished.

He left the industry entirely in the mid-eighties and declined, for the rest of his life, to be persuaded back.
facts: Blackstreet later built 'No Diggity' on its bones
He resisted adding a bridge, saying it was finished

06-06.title: Prince Buster shaped the beat that became ska
06-06.story:
Buster instructed guitarists to accent the offbeat, flipping Jamaican R&B into ska and eventually rocksteady and reggae.

The instruction was specific and consequential. Jamaican musicians in the late fifties were largely playing American R&B, which accents beats two and four. Buster told his guitarist to play on the upbeat instead — the and between the beats — which inverts the rhythmic feel entirely and produces the chopping skank that defines ska.

Everything downstream follows from that single displacement. Ska slowed into rocksteady, rocksteady slowed further into reggae, and the offbeat guitar remained constant throughout.

Buster was also a sound system operator, and the clashes he staged against rivals — particularly Coxsone Dodd and Duke Reid — were public theatre with real stakes, involving exclusive dubplates, insult records aimed at opponents by name, and occasional violence.

His records were carried to Britain by Jamaican migrants and became foundational to mod and skinhead culture in the sixties, and then to the two-tone movement in the late seventies. The Specials, Madness, and the Beat rebuilt substantial parts of his catalogue — Madness took their name from one of his songs and recorded a tribute to him as their debut single.

He died in 2016.
facts: He staged sound-system clashes as public theatre
Two-tone bands in Britain rebuilt his catalogue

06-07.title: Prince changed his name to a symbol to escape a contract
06-07.story:
In a dispute with Warner Bros., Prince adopted an unpronounceable glyph and wrote 'slave' on his face at appearances.

The dispute was about ownership and pace. Prince recorded faster than Warner wanted to release — the label had a commercial interest in spacing albums out and protecting the value of each — and he did not own his master recordings, which meant the catalogue he had made belonged to someone else.

The symbol was a legal manoeuvre as much as a gesture. His contract obligated Prince to deliver albums; an artist with no pronounceable name and a different legal identity complicated the label's ability to market him and made the situation actively expensive.

Warner mailed floppy disks to the press containing a custom font so publications could reproduce the glyph. Most gave up and wrote 'the artist formerly known as Prince'.

Writing 'slave' on his cheek at public appearances was widely mocked at the time, including by people who thought a multi-millionaire had chosen an obscene comparison. The substantive point underneath — that standard recording contracts transferred ownership of an artist's life's work in perpetuity — was one the industry has since had to concede repeatedly.

He regained his masters in 2014. Artists renegotiating master ownership now are working ground he cleared at considerable reputational cost.
facts: Media resorted to calling him 'the artist formerly known as'
Floppy disks with the symbol font were mailed to press

06-08.title: Brooklyn's Kings Theatre reopening drew a Flatbush crowd
06-08.story:
After decades dark, the Flatbush palace reopened with a sold-out show, restoring a major venue to the neighborhood's doorstep.

The restoration took roughly four years and a budget in the region of ninety-five million dollars, funded through a mix of public money and private investment. The building had been closed since 1977 and had taken serious water damage, so a great deal of the ornamental plasterwork had to be recast from surviving fragments rather than repaired.

What reopened is one of the largest theatres in Brooklyn, seating around three thousand, roughly a mile from Cortelyou Road.

The practical effect on the neighbourhood was immediate. For nearly four decades, an arena- or theatre-scale act playing New York meant a trip to Manhattan or downtown Brooklyn, and Central Brooklyn audiences travelled to see their own. Kings reversed the direction.

The booking since has been notably broad — gospel, Caribbean and African acts, comedy, legacy soul, indie rock, orchestral programmes — which reflects an audience the touring industry had historically routed around rather than served.

There is a straightforward argument that restoring a 1929 movie palace is a nostalgic use of ninety-five million dollars. The counterargument is that the room is full, and that it is full of people who live nearby.
facts: Restoration took roughly four years
It is among the largest theaters in Brooklyn

06-09.title: Les Paul invented multitrack recording in his garage
06-09.story:
Frustrated by one-take recording, Paul rigged a system to layer parts, then built the solid-body electric guitar to reduce feedback.

Both inventions came from the same impatience. Recording in the forties meant a performance captured in one pass; if you wanted harmony you needed other musicians in the room. Paul wanted to play all the parts himself, so he built a system for recording onto disc and then onto tape while playing along with what was already there — sound on sound, which became multitrack.

He was doing this in a garage, years before any commercial studio offered it. His records with Mary Ford, with layered guitars and stacked vocals, sounded impossible to contemporaries because the technique did not exist anywhere else.

Ampex built him an eight-track machine in the fifties on his specification, which is essentially the origin of modern studio recording.

The solid-body guitar came from the same problem-solving. A hollow-body electric feeds back at volume because the body resonates; a solid plank does not. He built a prototype known as the Log and took it to Gibson, who declined, telling him it was a broomstick with a pickup. They changed their minds after Fender proved there was a market.

He played weekly in New York clubs into his nineties.
facts: He recorded harmonies with himself years before studios could
Manufacturers initially rejected his guitar design

06-10.title: 'Ain't No Half Steppin' announced Brooklyn's technical peak
06-10.story:
Big Daddy Kane's Bed-Stuy delivery combined speed, clarity and swing, setting a standard other rappers openly chased.

The technical content is the reason it still gets studied. Kane's delivery combines speed with articulation — most rappers lose one to get the other — and he places multisyllabic rhymes at irregular points in the bar rather than only at the end, which produces internal patterns the ear tracks without being able to predict.

The breath control is the part MCs mention most. Long passages run without an audible break at a tempo that should require one, and the phrasing swings against the beat rather than sitting on it, which is a jazz instinct applied to speech.
