He was also writing for other people. Biz Markie and Roxanne Shanté both used his material, and he was part of the Juice Crew, which put him in direct competition with the strongest technical rappers of the period on a weekly basis.

That competitive density is a large part of why the standard rose so fast in the late eighties. Everyone involved was hearing everyone else immediately.

Rappers who came after him in the same few Bed-Stuy blocks — Jay-Z most explicitly — have named him as the benchmark they were measuring against before they had recorded anything.
facts: He wrote for Biz Markie and Roxanne Shanté as well
His breath control is still studied by MCs

06-11.title: Which 'Superstar' wins: Delaney & Bonnie or the Carpenters?
06-11.story:
Originally a rough rock lament, the Carpenters' 1971 arrangement turned it into a lush, aching ballad with an oboe line.

The song's authorship is Bonnie Bramlett and Leon Russell, and the early versions — by Delaney & Bonnie, then Rita Coolidge and Bette Midler — treat it as a rock and soul lament, rougher and more direct.

Richard Carpenter reworked it substantially: changed harmony, slowed it, and built an orchestral arrangement around an oboe line that gives the whole record its particular ache. It is a genuinely sophisticated piece of arranging that most listeners experience as simply pretty, which is usually the sign of good work.

Karen Carpenter's vocal is the reason it lands. She sang it from a lyric sheet as a rough guide take, essentially reading it for the first time, and Richard kept that take because nothing subsequent matched it.

The song's subject is a groupie addressing a musician who does not remember her, which is considerably darker than the Carpenters' public image suggested and is part of why the record has aged better than its reputation.

Karen Carpenter died in 1983 of complications from anorexia nervosa, at thirty-two. Her death did a great deal to bring eating disorders into public discussion at a point when they were barely acknowledged.
facts: Richard Carpenter reworked the harmony substantially
Karen Carpenter sang the vocal from a rough scratch take that was kept

06-12.title: Nile Rodgers wrote 'Le Freak' after being turned away
06-12.story:
Refused entry to Studio 54, Rodgers and Edwards went home angry and wrote a chorus built on an expletive, later changed to 'freak out'.

They had been invited by Grace Jones and their names were not on the door. New Year's Eve, freezing, and the doormen would not let them in despite Chic being one of the biggest acts in the building's own soundtrack.

They went back to Rodgers's apartment, started playing, and built a groove with a chorus that was, in its original form, an instruction to the club involving a considerably ruder verb. They kept the melody and the rhythm and substituted 'freak out', which scans identically.

It became Atlantic Records' biggest-selling single, and it remained so for a very long time.

The musical content is Chic at their most efficient: Rodgers's muted guitar chucking, Bernard Edwards's melodic bass, Tony Thompson's drums, and almost nothing else. There is enormous space in the arrangement, which is why it still sounds modern.

The bassline has been sampled and interpolated repeatedly, most famously as the foundation of the Sugarhill Gang's follow-up work and across decades of dance records.

One of the most successful singles in history exists because two Black musicians were kept standing in the cold outside a nightclub.
facts: The original hook was considerably ruder
It became Atlantic Records' biggest-selling single

06-13.title: Tape delay was invented using two machines
06-13.story:
Engineers fed a signal from one tape head to another, creating slapback echo. Sun Studio's version defined early rock and roll vocals.

The mechanism is entirely physical. A tape machine has separate record and playback heads with a gap between them, so the playback head hears the signal a fraction of a second after it is recorded. Feed that delayed output back into the input and you get a repeating echo, with the delay time determined by the distance between the heads and the speed of the tape.

Sam Phillips used a second Ampex machine at Sun to produce the short, single-repeat version known as slapback, and it is all over the early Elvis Presley, Carl Perkins, and Johnny Cash recordings. It gives a voice presence and size without the wash of a reverb chamber, and it is a substantial part of what people mean by the Sun sound.

The delay could not be set arbitrarily. Changing it meant changing tape speed, which also changed pitch, so engineers worked within a narrow range of usable settings.

Purpose-built tape echo units followed — the Echoplex, the Roland Space Echo — and those became instruments in their own right, particularly in dub, where King Tubby and Lee Perry played the delay as a performance control rather than setting it and leaving it.
facts: Elvis's voice at Sun is drenched in it
The delay time depended on physical head spacing

06-14.title: 'The Message' proved rap could report the news
06-14.story:
Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five released a bleak social document at a time when rap was expected to be party music.

The expectation in 1982 was firm. Rap records were party records, and the commercial logic was that nobody would dance to a description of a collapsing neighbourhood. Most of the group agreed and did not want to record it.

Melle Mel delivers nearly all of it, and Grandmaster Flash barely appears despite the billing. The song was largely written by Duke Bootee, a Sugar Hill session musician, with Melle Mel contributing a verse he had used previously.

What it established was that the form could carry reportage. The lyric describes a specific set of conditions — debt, decay, violence, the absence of any exit — with a plainness that had no precedent on a rap record, and the closing scene of the album version is genuinely bleak.

It was a commercial success, which settled the argument about whether audiences would accept it.

Everything from Public Enemy to Nas to Kendrick Lamar runs through this record, and the internal resistance to making it is a useful reminder that the people inside a form are frequently the last to know what it can do.
facts: Most of the group disliked the song initially
Melle Mel delivers nearly all of it

06-15.title: Ditmas Park's block parties keep the sound-system tradition
06-15.story:
Summer street closures along Cortelyou and Rugby Road turned into speaker-stack parties, echoing Caribbean sound-system culture nearby.

The mechanics are bureaucratic and the results are not. A block association applies to the city for a street activity permit, the street closes for a day, and what fills it is determined entirely by who lives there. In this part of Brooklyn that has meant, reliably, speaker stacks and a generator.

The lineage is direct. Central Brooklyn holds one of the largest Caribbean populations outside the islands, and Jamaican sound system practice — the mobile rig, the operator, the bass pushed far past what indoor listening requires — arrived with the migration and never left. A Cortelyou block party is running the same format as a Kingston yard dance, adapted to a street permit.

The housing stock helps. Detached houses with front lawns and porches mean a block can absorb amplified music in a way a wall-to-wall tenement street cannot.

DJs still run generators for outdoor sets because there is no other reliable power, which is its own continuity with the tradition.

It is also, quietly, one of the few remaining occasions when an entire block is outside at the same time and has to negotiate volume, space, and each other in person.
facts: Permits are typically pulled by block associations
DJs still run generators for outdoor sets

06-16.title: Tupac studied ballet and Shakespeare
06-16.story:
Shakur trained at the Baltimore School for the Arts, performing in ballet and theatre before rapping professionally.

The training was serious. He studied acting, poetry, and dance at a competitive arts high school, performed Shakespeare, and danced the Mouse King in a production of The Nutcracker. He later described those years as the most formative of his life and said the exposure to people from entirely different backgrounds changed what he thought was possible.

He credited the acting training directly for his delivery. What separates his recorded vocals from most of his contemporaries is not technical rhyme construction but performance — dynamics, timing, and an ability to shift register within a verse that comes from stage work rather than from rapping.

His mother Afeni Shakur was a Black Panther who defended herself successfully in a major conspiracy trial while pregnant with him, which is the other half of the formation.

The contradiction between the arts-school background and the public persona was frequently pointed out and he never had much difficulty holding both.

He was murdered in Las Vegas in September 1996, at twenty-five. The case remains unresolved, and the volume of unreleased material he left behind means more albums were issued after his death than during his life.
facts: He played the Mouse King in The Nutcracker
He credited acting training for his delivery

06-17.title: The Linn drum machine used real recorded drums
06-17.story:
Roger Linn sampled actual drum hits instead of synthesizing them, giving eighties pop its crisp, oversized snare.

Every drum machine before it synthesized its sounds, which is why they were used as accompaniment devices for organists rather than as replacements for drummers. Linn's insight was to record actual drum hits to digital memory and trigger those, which meant a machine could sound like a kit for the first time.

The LM-1 also had programmable patterns and swing, so a producer could shift the timing off the grid slightly and get something that felt played rather than quantised.

It cost around five thousand dollars in 1980, roughly the price of a car, and only a few hundred were built. Its early users were consequently the people who could afford it, which is why a particular snare sound is all over expensive eighties pop.

Prince built a substantial part of his sound on it — the drums on much of his early-eighties work are LM-1, frequently with the pitch and decay pushed to extremes.

The successor, the LinnDrum, was cheaper and spread further. Between them they defined a decade's rhythm sound, and their gated, oversized snare is now instant shorthand for the period.
facts: Prince built much of his sound on the LM-1
It cost roughly as much as a car

06-18.title: Paul McCartney woke up with 'Yesterday' in his head
06-18.story:
McCartney dreamed the melody and spent weeks asking people if he had accidentally stolen it. Placeholder lyrics were 'scrambled eggs'.

He woke in a room at his girlfriend's family home with the tune complete in his head, went to a piano, and played it before he lost it. His immediate assumption was that it must be somebody else's — a melody that arrives fully formed feels like a memory rather than an invention — and he spent weeks playing it to people in the industry asking whether they recognised it.

Nobody did, so he kept it.

The placeholder lyric was 'scrambled eggs, oh my baby how I love your legs', which scans correctly and is the sort of thing that makes the finished song slightly harder to take seriously once you know it.

The recording is unusual for a Beatles track: McCartney alone with an acoustic guitar and a string quartet arranged by George Martin, with no other Beatle on it. Martin has said McCartney was initially resistant to the strings, worried it would sound like easy listening.

It is among the most covered songs ever written, with recorded versions running into the thousands.

McCartney has said he has never had another melody arrive that way, which is probably just as well.
facts: It is among the most covered songs ever written
He recorded it alone with a string quartet

06-19.title: Juneteenth and the blues' long road north
06-19.story:
Emancipation's spread carried musical traditions from the Deep South up through Memphis and Chicago, reshaping American popular music.

Juneteenth marks 19 June 1865, when Union troops reached Galveston, Texas, and enforced the Emancipation Proclamation — two and a half years after it had been issued. That gap is the point of the commemoration: freedom arriving late, and only where it could be enforced.

The musical consequence took decades and ran along the railway lines. The Great Migration moved roughly six million people out of the rural South between 1916 and 1970, and the music travelled with them — Delta blues up the Illinois Central to Memphis and Chicago, Texas blues west to California.

What changed on arrival was volume. Country blues was made for a porch or a small room and worked acoustically. Chicago clubs were loud, crowded, and full of competing noise, which required amplification, and amplification changed the music rather than simply enlarging it: distorted guitar, harmonica through a small overdriven amp, and a full rhythm section replacing a single player.

Muddy Waters is the clearest single example of the transition, recorded acoustically in Mississippi in 1941 and electrically in Chicago within a decade.

Everything from rock and roll to soul to hip-hop runs back through that migration.
facts: The Great Migration moved the blues to electric amplification
Chicago's louder clubs demanded volume country blues never needed

06-20.title: Brian Wilson built 'Pet Sounds' while the band toured
06-20.story:
Wilson stopped touring and recorded the album with session players, presenting finished tracks to the Beach Boys on their return.

He had stopped touring in 1964 after a panic attack on a flight, which turned out to be the most productive decision of his career. While the band worked the road, he had unlimited studio time in Los Angeles and access to the session players later known as the Wrecking Crew.

He built the album as a producer rather than as a bandleader — writing parts, directing musicians, and constructing arrangements piece by piece across many sessions. The band returned to finished instrumental tracks and were asked to sing on them.

Some of them resisted. Mike Love in particular was, by most accounts, unconvinced by material that abandoned the surf and car songs the group had been selling successfully.

The instrumentation is deliberately strange: bicycle bells, dog whistles, empty Coca-Cola bottles, theremin-like electro-theremin, and unconventional doublings that produce composite timbres you cannot identify.

It sold less well than its predecessors in America and enormously influenced everyone who heard it, including Paul McCartney, who has repeatedly said it prompted Sgt. Pepper.

Wilson's mental health deteriorated badly in the years afterward. He died in 2025.
facts: He used bicycle bells, dog whistles and empty bottles
Some bandmates initially resisted the material

06-21.title: 'Funky Worm' gave G-funk its whine
06-21.story:
The Ohio Players' high synthesizer squeal became the signature lead sound of West Coast hip-hop two decades later.

The original is a joke. The track is a comic novelty built around a character called the worm, and the high, wavering synthesizer lead — played on an Arp — was intended as a cartoonish effect rather than a musical statement.

Twenty years later Dr. Dre and his contemporaries lifted that timbre and made it the defining lead sound of West Coast hip-hop. It appears on N.W.A records, across The Chronic, and throughout Snoop Dogg's early work, usually played rather than sampled but unmistakably derived from the same source.

The reason it works in that context is that it occupies a frequency range nothing else in the mix uses. Under a heavy 808 or live-feeling bass and a mid-range vocal, a thin high whine cuts through without any competition, which is why G-funk arrangements sound so wide.

The Ohio Players were a serious funk band with a substantial catalogue, and being remembered principally for a comic synthesizer squeal is a strange fate.

It is a good example of how sampling culture reassigns value. The thing later producers wanted was the element the original band would have considered least important.
facts: Dr. Dre used the tone repeatedly
The original was meant as a comic effect

06-22.title: Which 'Valerie' wins: The Zutons or Amy Winehouse?
06-22.story:
The Zutons wrote it as indie rock. Mark Ronson and Amy Winehouse recut it as sixties soul, and that version eclipsed the original.

The Zutons' original is a Liverpool indie rock record — guitar-driven, mid-tempo, with a saxophone and a slightly ragged charm. It was a modest hit and is, on its own terms, a good song.

Ronson's rearrangement moves it wholesale into mid-sixties soul: a Motown-derived backbeat, horn section, tambourine, and an arrangement that sounds like it was cut at a Detroit session in 1966. Nothing in the melody changes.

Winehouse recorded the vocal quickly and largely live, and what she does with it is the reason the version took over. She sings behind the beat throughout, with a phrasing derived from jazz singers rather than pop ones, and treats the lyric conversationally rather than performing it.

That combination — modern songwriting, period arrangement, and a singer with a genuinely pre-rock sense of time — is the whole formula of Back to Black and of a wave of records that followed it.

Winehouse died in 2011, at twenty-seven, of alcohol poisoning after years of very public struggle that the British press covered as entertainment.

The Zutons' version is now the one people are surprised exists.
facts: Ronson built the arrangement around a Motown-style backbeat
Winehouse recorded her vocal quickly, largely live

06-23.title: Bessie Smith outsold nearly every artist of her era
06-23.story:
Smith's records sold in the hundreds of thousands to Black audiences largely ignored by the mainstream industry.

The commercial scale is the part that gets understated. Her records sold in the hundreds of thousands at a time when the industry had assumed no significant Black record-buying market existed, and her success — following Mamie Smith's 'Crazy Blues' in 1920 — is what created the race records category and the entire structure of Black popular recording that followed.

She toured in her own railroad car, which was both a display of success and a practical necessity: segregated travel across the South made ordinary touring dangerous and frequently impossible, and owning the car meant the company could sleep and move without depending on facilities that would not accept them.

The voice itself required no microphone. She recorded acoustically for much of her career and could fill a tent without amplification, with a power and precision of pitch that is audible even through the limitations of 1920s recording.

Her material was frank about sex, drinking, violence, and independence in ways that later decades became squeamish about.

She died in 1937 after a car accident in Mississippi. The long-repeated story that she was refused treatment at a whites-only hospital appears not to be accurate, though the circumstances of her death were shaped by segregation regardless.
facts: She toured in her own railroad car
Her success proved a market executives had denied existed

06-24.title: The Neve console became a producer's instrument
06-24.story:
Rupert Neve's circuitry added a warmth engineers still chase. Studios built entire reputations on owning one.

Neve designed to measurable specifications rather than to a sound. His stated aim was accuracy — low noise, wide bandwidth, minimal distortion — and the console's celebrated warmth is largely a by-product of the transformers and discrete class-A circuitry he used to achieve it. The harmonic content those components add is technically a departure from accuracy that happens to be flattering.

The 1073 preamp module in particular became so sought-after that individual units now sell for several thousand dollars each, and studios have been bought and stripped for their consoles.

What that produced is an unusual situation where a piece of infrastructure became a creative signature. Records were booked into specific rooms because of the desk, and engineers developed techniques built around its particular behaviour when driven hard.

Software emulations now model not just the design but specific physical units, down to serial numbers, because component tolerances mean two consoles off the same production line do not sound identical.

The underlying lesson is one the audio industry keeps relearning. Every generation's idea of clean becomes the next generation's idea of character, and the flaws engineers spent decades removing get carefully reinstated as plugins.
facts: Plugins now emulate specific serial numbers
Neve designed to a spec, not a sound, and got both

06-25.title: Michael Jackson died, and streaming spiked worldwide
06-25.story:
Jackson's death caused traffic surges that briefly destabilized major websites, an early sign of how music news moved online.

The load was genuinely unprecedented for a single news event. Google's search team initially interpreted the volume of queries as an automated attack and served error pages; Twitter went down; Wikipedia and several news sites buckled. AOL's instant messaging service failed for a period.

It was an early demonstration that the internet's capacity planning assumed distributed interest rather than the entire connected world wanting the same thing in the same ten minutes.

The commercial aftermath was equally striking. His catalogue sold in enormous quantities immediately, and he became for several years the highest-earning deceased performer by a wide margin.

Thriller remains the best-selling album ever released, and the sales figures for it have the odd property of being disputed largely upward.

Jackson died of acute propofol intoxication; his physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter.

The allegations of child sexual abuse made against him during his life and after his death have not gone away, and how to hold his work and those allegations together at once is a question the culture has handled poorly in both directions — alternately ignoring the accusations entirely and pretending the music never mattered.
facts: Some services mistook the traffic for an attack
'Thriller' remains the best-selling album ever

06-26.title: Sly Stone assembled America's first fully integrated band
06-26.story:
Sly and the Family Stone included Black and white members, men and women, all sharing lead vocals, unprecedented at the time.

The composition of the band was the argument. In 1967 popular music was segregated by convention at almost every level — audiences, radio formats, touring circuits, and the personnel of the bands themselves — and a group that was mixed by race and by gender, with lead vocals passed around rather than assigned to a frontman, was making a claim simply by walking on stage.

Cynthia Robinson on trumpet was one of very few women playing a lead horn in a major American band, and she was not decorative — she plays and shouts across the records constantly.

The music enacted the same idea. Everyone sings, the arrangements pass melodic responsibility between members mid-song, and the sound fuses soul, rock, gospel, and psychedelia without treating any of them as the home key.

Sly Stone had worked as a radio DJ and a staff producer before forming the band, which is part of why the records are so structurally assured.

It did not hold. Drug use, pressure from militants who objected to the white members, and Stone's deteriorating condition pulled the group apart within a few years, and There's a Riot Goin' On is the sound of that collapse.

Stone died in 2025.
facts: Trumpeter Cynthia Robinson was a rare female horn lead
The lineup was itself a political statement

06-27.title: 'Nautilus' became crate-diggers' holy grail
06-27.story:
Bob James's track hid a haunting synth figure that producers mined for decades, often unaware others had found it too.

James was a jazz keyboardist making accessible instrumental records for CTI, and 'Nautilus' closes an album otherwise full of considerably lighter material. It is slow, minor, and built on a synthesizer figure with an unsettled quality that has almost nothing in common with the rest of his catalogue.

That sound turned out to be perfect raw material. It is harmonically ambiguous enough to sit under anything, texturally distinctive enough to be recognisable, and slow enough to be sped up without artefacts.

Ghostface Killah, Slick Rick, Run-DMC, Eric B. & Rakim, and dozens of others built records on it, frequently within the same few years and without knowing others were working from the same source.

James has been unusually gracious about all of it, saying he is delighted by the second life and pointing out that a track buried at the end of a 1974 jazz-funk album would otherwise have been forgotten entirely.

That attitude is rarer than it should be. A number of jazz musicians whose work underpins hip-hop treated the borrowing as theft, which is legally defensible and has generally made them poorer company than the people who leaned into it.
facts: It anchors multiple hip-hop classics
James has said he is delighted by its second life

06-28.title: Gil Scott-Heron read poetry over congas
06-28.story:
'The Revolution Will Not Be Televised' was spoken word over percussion, an ancestor of rap that Scott-Heron resisted being called.

The first recorded version, on Small Talk at 125th and Lenox, is voice and congas and nothing else. A later version added a full band and is the one most people know, but the original makes the point more sharply: the words carry the entire piece and the percussion is a pulse rather than an accompaniment.

The text is a catalogue of advertising slogans, television personalities, and consumer imagery, arranged to make an argument about the difference between watching change and participating in it. It is genuinely funny in places, which people who quote the title tend to forget.

He resisted being called a father of rap, and the objection was substantive rather than snobbish. He located his work in a longer tradition — Langston Hughes, the Last Poets, blues, and jazz — and preferred the term bluesologist, a word he coined for himself.

He was also, by his own account, wary of being made into a founding ancestor for a commercial form he had complicated feelings about.

His later years involved addiction and imprisonment. The final album, made shortly before his death in 2011, is one of the bleakest and best things he did.
facts: He preferred the term 'bluesologist'
The first version used only congas and voice

06-29.title: Little Richard's 'Tutti Frutti' had to be rewritten on the spot
06-29.story:
The original lyrics were far too explicit for radio, so a local songwriter rewrote them during a lunch break at the session.

The session was going badly. Richard had been cutting conventional blues numbers at J&M in New Orleans and none of it was working, and during a break at a nearby club he sat at a piano and played the song as he actually performed it live — which was explicitly about gay sex and completely unreleasable in 1955.

Producer Bumps Blackwell recognised the energy immediately and brought in Dorothy LaBostrie, a local songwriter, who rewrote the lyric in roughly fifteen minutes over lunch. The result is nonsense about girls named Sue and Daisy, and the nonsense is precisely why it works — the words carry no meaning, so all the information is in the delivery.

The opening piano and the shouted syllables were kept exactly as first played.

What that record established is difficult to overstate: the pounding piano, the screamed vocal, and the sheer velocity became the template for rock and roll performance.

Pat Boone's sanitised cover outsold it, which was standard practice for white artists covering Black records at the time and is one of the clearer illustrations of how the money moved.

Richard was, throughout, considerably queerer than the record industry was willing to let him be.
facts: The rewrite took roughly 15 minutes
Richard's piano intro was kept exactly as first played

06-30.title: Brooklyn's Celebrate Brooklyn keeps free music alive
06-30.story:
The Prospect Park bandshell series has run for over four decades, one of the last major free festivals in New York.

It began in a city that was effectively broke. New York in 1979 had come through near-bankruptcy, park budgets had collapsed, and Prospect Park had a reputation that kept people out of it after dark. Free concerts at the bandshell were partly cultural programming and partly a deliberate attempt to give surrounding neighbourhoods a reason to reclaim the space.

More than four decades on it is among the longest-running free outdoor performance festivals in the country, and the booking has stayed genuinely broad — Afrobeat, salsa, indie rock, jazz, classical, hip-hop, and film screenings with live scores.

The bandshell's position at Prospect Park West and Ninth Street puts it within walking distance of Ditmas Park, Flatbush, Windsor Terrace, Park Slope, and Crown Heights, which is why the crowd looks like the borough rather than like one neighbourhood.

Most of the programme remains free, funded partly by a small number of ticketed benefit shows.

A good proportion of the artists who play it go on to headline paid rooms elsewhere in the city, which makes it one of the few places where you can see something significant before the ticket price catches up.
facts: It draws crowds from across Flatbush and Ditmas Park
Many artists play it before headlining paid venues

07-01.title: Stravinsky's premiere caused a riot
07-01.story:
'The Rite of Spring' provoked shouting and fistfights at its Paris debut. The dancers could not hear the orchestra over the noise.

The disturbance began early and escalated. Accounts describe shouting, whistling, objects thrown, and physical fights in the aisles, with the police called at some point during the performance. The noise became loud enough that the dancers could not hear the orchestra, and Nijinsky, the choreographer, stood in the wings shouting counts at them.

How much of it was the music and how much the choreography is still argued. Stravinsky's score is genuinely violent — irregular metre, brutal dissonance, a bassoon opening in a register at the top of its range — but Nijinsky's choreography was equally confrontational: turned-in feet, stamping, and a deliberate rejection of everything classical ballet had established.

There is also a reasonable case that a portion of the audience arrived expecting a scandal and supplied one.

The work was performed again shortly afterward without incident, and it is now standard repertoire, played by student orchestras and used in a Disney film.

What the episode preserves is a genuine cultural rupture point — a moment when an audience understood clearly that something had changed and objected in real time.
facts: The choreographer shouted counts from the wings
It is now standard repertoire worldwide

07-02.title: Which 'Hallelujah' wins: Cohen or Buckley?
07-02.story:
Leonard Cohen wrote around 80 verses and released a restrained gospel-tinged version. Jeff Buckley's 1994 reading, learned from John Cale's cover, made it a standard.

Cohen's writing process was famously agonising. He worked on the song for years and produced something in the region of eighty verses, and he described a low point spent on a hotel room floor in his underwear, banging his head, unable to finish it. The version he released in 1984 is restrained, organ-backed, and closer to a hymn than a ballad. His label initially refused to release the album it came from in the United States.

The chain of transmission matters. John Cale recorded a stripped-down piano version for a Cohen tribute album, selecting a different set of verses from the many Cohen sent him. Jeff Buckley learned the song from Cale's version rather than Cohen's, which is why the words most people know are Cale's edit.

Buckley's recording is essentially one electric guitar and a voice, largely captured live, and it treats the song as intimate and sexual rather than liturgical.

The song's subsequent ubiquity — talent shows, funerals, films — has worn it down considerably, which is a strange fate for something that took a decade to write and sat ignored for another.
facts: Cohen spent years writing it, reportedly banging his head on a hotel floor
Buckley's take is a single guitar and voice, recorded largely live

07-03.title: Bernie Worrell made the synthesizer funky
07-03.story:
Parliament-Funkadelic's keyboardist treated the Moog as a bass instrument, inventing the squelching low end that shaped G-funk two decades later.

The innovation was conceptual before it was technical. Synthesizers in the mid-seventies were treated as lead or texture instruments; Worrell used the Minimoog as a bass, playing lines with portamento and filter sweeps that a bass guitar physically cannot produce. The result is the sliding, rubbery low end on records like 'Flash Light', which is one of the most influential sounds in American popular music.

He was classically trained. He began piano at three, wrote a concerto as a child, and attended the New England Conservatory, which is not the background one assumes for the P-Funk keyboard chair — and it is precisely why the harmony on those records is more sophisticated than the party framing suggests.

Dr. Dre's nineties productions lean directly on this vocabulary. G-funk is essentially the P-Funk synth bass and lead-line language slowed down and given more space, and Worrell's playing is sampled and interpolated throughout it.

He later worked with Talking Heads, appearing prominently in Stop Making Sense, which put him in front of an entirely different audience.

He died in 2016. The financial arrangements around the P-Funk catalogue were contested for decades and he saw comparatively little from it.
facts: He was classically trained and wrote a concerto as a child
Dr. Dre's nineties productions lean directly on his vocabulary

07-04.title: Which 'Girls Just Want to Have Fun' wins: Hazard or Lauper?
07-04.story:
Robert Hazard wrote it from a man's perspective as a demo. Cyndi Lauper rewrote the meaning entirely, turning it into a feminist anthem.

Hazard's demo is sung by a man who is pleased that girls want to have fun, which is a different proposition entirely — the women in it are objects of the narrator's satisfaction rather than subjects of their own.

Lauper's initial reaction was refusal. She disliked the song and did not want to record it, and only agreed after reworking the lyric so that the perspective shifted to the women themselves. The changes are not extensive on the page and they relocate the song completely: it becomes a statement about autonomy made by the people it concerns.

The arrangement supports the reading. It is bright, fast, and slightly chaotic, and Lauper's vocal is deliberately unpolished in a way that reads as a person rather than a product.

The video did comparable work, casting her mother and featuring a visibly diverse cast at a point when MTV was not notable for either.

It is one of the clearest examples of a performer's interpretation constituting authorship. The notes are largely Hazard's. What the song means is Lauper's, and the meaning is the reason anyone still plays it.
facts: Lauper initially disliked the song and refused to record it
She rewrote lyrics to flip the point of view

07-05.title: The Ditmas Park porch concert circuit
07-05.story:
Neighbors around Cortelyou Road turned Victorian porches into micro-venues, hosting acoustic sets for audiences of thirty. The tradition continues each summer.

The format works because of the architecture. The blocks around Cortelyou were laid out around 1900 as freestanding wood-frame houses with deep front porches set close to the sidewalk — a design intended to encourage exactly this kind of semi-public sociability, a century before anyone thought to book a band on one.

A porch is a genuinely good small venue. It is raised, so sightlines work; it is covered, so weather is survivable; and the audience stands on a lawn and a sidewalk, which means passers-by become part of the crowd without having to decide to attend.

The scale is the appeal. Thirty people, no PA or a very small one, no ticket, and a hat passed. Nothing about it scales up, which is the point — it produces the kind of listening that a room of a thousand cannot.

Some porches host annual multi-act bills that have been running for years and are publicised almost entirely by word of mouth and neighbourhood mailing lists.

The lineage runs back through house-party culture across Flatbush and, further, to rent parties and stoop gatherings. Cortelyou's version is the same instinct with better woodwork.
facts: Some porches host annual multi-act bills
The format traces back to house-party culture across Flatbush

07-06.title: Coney Island's boardwalk had its own sound
07-06.story:
Amusement park organs, barkers and competing radios created a dense collage that New York songwriters mined for decades. The Tilyou family's Steeplechase organ was audible for blocks.

Band organs were engineering solutions to a specific problem. Before amplification was practical outdoors, a fairground needed music loud enough to carry over crowds, machinery, and the ocean, and the answer was a large mechanical organ driven by pneumatics and paper rolls, voiced deliberately bright and reedy so it would cut through. They are not subtle instruments because subtlety was never the brief.

Stack several of those against barkers working the sideshows, competing radios, the Cyclone, and the crowd itself and you get a genuinely dense sonic environment — one that a lot of New York songwriting has drawn on, consciously or not, as shorthand for a particular kind of summer.

The area gained a second layer later. Brighton Beach, immediately east along the same boardwalk, became home to a large Soviet and post-Soviet Jewish community from the 1970s, and its restaurants and clubs brought Russian and Ukrainian popular music into the same stretch of coastline.

Both layers are still audible on a hot Saturday, which makes the boardwalk one of the few places in the city where you can hear a hundred years of immigration in about a fifteen-minute walk.
facts: Band organs were built to cut through crowd noise without amplification
Brighton Beach's Russian clubs later added a second musical layer nearby

07-07.title: The 'Loud War' shrank music's dynamic range
07-07.story:
Mastering engineers began compressing records to sound louder than competitors on radio and CD changers. The side effect was flattened peaks and listening fatigue.

The mechanism is competitive and self-defeating. Louder registers as better on a first listen — a track that jumps out of a CD changer or a radio sequence gets attention — so labels pushed mastering engineers to raise average level. Since digital audio has a hard ceiling, the only way to get louder is to compress and limit the peaks, bringing everything closer to maximum.

Do that far enough and the waveform stops looking like music and starts looking like a solid block. The transients that make a snare hit feel like an impact are the first thing to go, and the result is a record that sounds impressive for thirty seconds and tiring after ten minutes.

Some nineties albums were remastered louder than their originals and are, by any technical measure, worse. A number of reissues have since been deliberately mastered quieter to undo it.

Streaming has largely defused the incentive. Platforms normalise playback loudness, so a heavily compressed track gets turned down to match everything else and arrives sounding smaller rather than bigger. The arms race stopped paying, which is a rare case of a technical standard fixing an aesthetic problem.
facts: Some nineties reissues are quieter than their originals by design
Streaming loudness normalization has since reduced the incentive

07-08.title: Nina Simone played Carnegie Hall, but not as she planned
07-08.story:
When Simone finally reached Carnegie Hall, she noted bitterly that she arrived as a pop singer, not the classical concert pianist she trained to be.

The ambition had been specific and lifelong. She trained from childhood toward a career as a concert pianist, her hometown raised money for her lessons, and she believed until her death that her rejection by the Curtis Institute was racial rather than musical. Reaching Carnegie Hall on somebody else's terms was not the vindication it looked like from outside.

She made the point on stage. Opening a set with a Bach prelude in front of an audience expecting popular song was a deliberate act of insistence about what she actually was, and her improvisations move through contrapuntal writing in a way no other performer in that context was attempting.

The same period pushed her decisively into civil rights work. 'Mississippi Goddam' was written in 1963 after the murder of Medgar Evers and the Birmingham church bombing, and it is furious in a way almost nothing on American radio was permitted to be.

The cost was concrete. Stations refused to play the record, some returned promotional copies broken, and bookings dried up. She was entirely clear-eyed that the position she took was expensive, and she took it anyway.
facts: She opened sets with Bach preludes to make the point
Her civil-rights songs cost her radio play and income

07-09.title: Leap day gave Gioachino Rossini a rare birthday
07-09.story:
Born on 29 February, Rossini joked he only aged once every four years. He retired from opera at 37 and spent decades writing small pieces and cooking.

The retirement is the genuinely strange part. Rossini was the most successful opera composer in Europe, had written roughly forty operas by his late thirties, and then stopped almost entirely after William Tell in 1829, living another thirty-nine years without producing another one. Explanations have included illness, exhaustion, wealth, and simple disinclination, and none of them fully account for it.

He wrote fast when he was writing. The Barber of Seville was completed in something like three weeks, and he was notorious for reusing overtures between operas when the deadline demanded it — the Barber's overture had already served two previous works.

What he did instead was cook and write small pieces. He was a serious gastronome, several dishes carry his name, and the late piano and vocal miniatures he produced for private performance were collected under the title Sins of Old Age. Several are named after food.

He died in 1868 and left the bulk of a substantial fortune to endow a music conservatory in his home town of Pesaro, which still operates.

By his own count he had lived about nineteen birthdays.
facts: He wrote 'The Barber of Seville' in about three weeks
He named several compositions after food

07-10.title: Elvis recorded his first single for his mother
07-10.story:
At 18, Presley paid Sun Studio's $4 fee to cut 'My Happiness' as a gift. Receptionist Marion Keisker secretly taped a copy because she liked his voice.

Sun ran a walk-in service where anyone could record a two-sided acetate for a few dollars, and it was a real business — the studio needed the income between sessions. Presley was one of dozens of amateurs who came through that year, and there was nothing about the arrangement that implied a career.

Keisker's decision to keep a copy is the pivot the whole story turns on. Her note, as she later recounted it, read: 'Good ballad singer. Hold.' Sam Phillips, who ran the studio, had been saying for some time that he was looking for a white singer who could deliver a Black feel — a remark that is usually quoted approvingly and is worth sitting with, since it describes the commercial logic that shaped American popular music for the next two decades.

Phillips called him back roughly a year later. The session that produced 'That's All Right' reportedly came out of a break, with Presley fooling around on an Arthur Crudup blues while the tape happened to be running.

Both turning points were accidents somebody chose to preserve. That is most of what the early history of recorded music consists of.
facts: Her note read: 'Good ballad singer. Hold.'
That saved tape led Sam Phillips to call him back a year later

07-11.title: Dolly Parton wrote two standards on the same day
07-11.story:
Parton has said she wrote 'Jolene' and 'I Will Always Love You' in a single writing session. One was about a bank teller flirting with her husband; the other about leaving her mentor.

The second song is the more consequential piece of business in country music history. It was written as a farewell to Porter Wagoner, whose television show had made Parton a star and whose partnership she was leaving to work on her own. She has described playing it to him as a way of explaining a decision he was resisting.

Elvis Presley wanted to record it. His manager, Colonel Tom Parker, made the standard demand of the era — half the publishing rights in exchange for the recording. Parton refused and kept the song, a decision she has said she cried over at the time.

Whitney Houston's 1992 version, from The Bodyguard, became one of the best-selling singles ever released. Because Parton had retained the writer's share, the royalties came to her.

'Jolene' has had a slower and stranger afterlife, covered across genres for fifty years, and it is built on an unusual premise: the narrator does not confront her rival so much as beg her, and openly concedes that the other woman is more beautiful. That refusal to posture is most of why it still lands.
facts: Elvis wanted to record 'I Will Always Love You' but his manager demanded publishing
She said no, and kept the rights that later made her a fortune

07-12.title: The Clash recorded 'London Calling' with a producer who threw chairs
07-12.story:
Guy Stevens motivated takes by swinging ladders and pouring wine on the piano. The chaos was intentional; he wanted performances, not perfection.

Stevens had a real track record — he had worked with Mott the Hoople and had an ear for the moment when a band stops thinking — and a serious drinking problem. His method involved doing whatever produced adrenaline in the room: throwing furniture, wrestling with band members mid-take, swinging a ladder near the players.

Engineer Bill Price handled the actual recording, and by most accounts the record exists because he kept the tape running and quietly captured usable takes while the theatre happened around him. The division of labour was unspoken and essential.

The album itself is the opposite of punk orthodoxy. Reggae, rockabilly, ska, jazz, and New Orleans R&B all appear across nineteen tracks, at a point when the genre's rules had hardened into something quite narrow. The band's willingness to ignore those rules is the reason the record outlived the scene it came from.

Paul Simonon, who plays the bass figure on the title track, had learned the instrument after joining the band. Stevens died in 1981. The Clash dedicated their next work to him.
facts: Engineer Bill Price quietly kept the tape rolling through the mayhem
The title track's bass was played by Paul Simonon, who learned bass in the band

07-13.title: Marilyn Monroe's birthday and the art of the breathy mic
07-13.story:
Close-mic crooning only became possible with sensitive condenser microphones, letting singers whisper instead of project.

Before electrical recording, a singer's job was partly athletic. Acoustic recording required enough volume to physically move a diaphragm, and live performance in a large room required filling it without amplification — which is why the popular singers of the early twentieth century sound like opera singers whether or not they were trained as such.

The condenser microphone changed the arithmetic entirely. Suddenly a whisper could be captured with detail, and singers could work at conversational volume with all the nuance that permits: breath, consonants, the slight break in a held note. Bing Crosby was the first major figure to build a style on it, and everything called crooning descends from that technical shift.

Monroe's singing voice is the extreme case. It has almost no projection and enormous intimacy, and it only functions as a recorded and amplified instrument. A hundred years earlier there would have been no way for it to exist professionally.

The broader point is that vocal style is downstream of microphone technology more often than of taste. Belting, crooning, close-mic rap delivery, and modern pop's heavily compressed intimacy are each responses to what the equipment of the period rewarded.
facts: Before electric mics, singers needed opera-level volume
The intimate vocal style is a technology story as much as a taste one

07-14.title: Les Paul invented multitrack recording in his garage
07-14.story:
Frustrated by one-take recording, Paul rigged a system to layer parts, then built the solid-body electric guitar to reduce feedback.

Both inventions came from the same impatience. Recording in the forties meant a performance captured in one pass; if you wanted harmony you needed other musicians in the room. Paul wanted to play all the parts himself, so he built a system for recording onto disc and then onto tape while playing along with what was already there — sound on sound, which became multitrack.

He was doing this in a garage, years before any commercial studio offered it. His records with Mary Ford, with layered guitars and stacked vocals, sounded impossible to contemporaries because the technique did not exist anywhere else.

Ampex built him an eight-track machine in the fifties on his specification, which is essentially the origin of modern studio recording.

The solid-body guitar came from the same problem-solving. A hollow-body electric feeds back at volume because the body resonates; a solid plank does not. He built a prototype known as the Log and took it to Gibson, who declined, telling him it was a broomstick with a pickup. They changed their minds after Fender proved there was a market.

He played weekly in New York clubs into his nineties.
facts: He recorded harmonies with himself years before studios could
Manufacturers initially rejected his guitar design

07-15.title: The Linn drum machine used real recorded drums
07-15.story:
Roger Linn sampled actual drum hits instead of synthesizing them, giving eighties pop its crisp, oversized snare.

Every drum machine before it synthesized its sounds, which is why they were used as accompaniment devices for organists rather than as replacements for drummers. Linn's insight was to record actual drum hits to digital memory and trigger those, which meant a machine could sound like a kit for the first time.

The LM-1 also had programmable patterns and swing, so a producer could shift the timing off the grid slightly and get something that felt played rather than quantised.

It cost around five thousand dollars in 1980, roughly the price of a car, and only a few hundred were built. Its early users were consequently the people who could afford it, which is why a particular snare sound is all over expensive eighties pop.

Prince built a substantial part of his sound on it — the drums on much of his early-eighties work are LM-1, frequently with the pitch and decay pushed to extremes.

The successor, the LinnDrum, was cheaper and spread further. Between them they defined a decade's rhythm sound, and their gated, oversized snare is now instant shorthand for the period.
facts: Prince built much of his sound on the LM-1
It cost roughly as much as a car

07-16.title: Michael Jackson died, and streaming spiked worldwide
07-16.story:
Jackson's death caused traffic surges that briefly destabilized major websites, an early sign of how music news moved online.

The load was genuinely unprecedented for a single news event. Google's search team initially interpreted the volume of queries as an automated attack and served error pages; Twitter went down; Wikipedia and several news sites buckled. AOL's instant messaging service failed for a period.

It was an early demonstration that the internet's capacity planning assumed distributed interest rather than the entire connected world wanting the same thing in the same ten minutes.

The commercial aftermath was equally striking. His catalogue sold in enormous quantities immediately, and he became for several years the highest-earning deceased performer by a wide margin.

Thriller remains the best-selling album ever released, and the sales figures for it have the odd property of being disputed largely upward.

Jackson died of acute propofol intoxication; his physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter.

The allegations of child sexual abuse made against him during his life and after his death have not gone away, and how to hold his work and those allegations together at once is a question the culture has handled poorly in both directions — alternately ignoring the accusations entirely and pretending the music never mattered.
facts: Some services mistook the traffic for an attack
'Thriller' remains the best-selling album ever

07-17.title: 'The Star-Spangled Banner' was set to a drinking song
07-17.story:
Francis Scott Key's poem was matched to 'To Anacreon in Heaven', a British social club tune notorious for its difficult octave-and-a-half range.

The Anacreontic Society was a gentlemen's musical club in London, and the song was its constitutional anthem — a genial celebration of wine and music named after the Greek poet Anacreon. Setting a patriotic American poem to a British club tune during a war against Britain is a piece of irony that the period seems not to have found troubling.

The range is the practical problem. The melody spans an octave and a half, which is comfortable for a trained singer and brutal for anyone else, and it puts its highest note on the phrase 'land of the free' — the exact moment when a stadium performance is most exposed. Almost every famous failure at a sporting event happens at that interval.

Key wrote the poem in 1814 after watching the bombardment of Fort McHenry, and it circulated widely for over a century in an unofficial capacity. It was used by the military from the 1890s but only became the official national anthem by act of Congress in 1931.

Other anthems were in contention, including 'America the Beautiful', which is considerably easier to sing and lost anyway.
facts: That range is why singers so often struggle with it
It became the official anthem only in 1931

07-18.title: Bobby McFerrin used no instruments at all
07-18.story:
'Don't Worry, Be Happy' is entirely voice and body percussion, multitracked. Listeners assumed they were hearing a full band.

Every sound on the record is McFerrin: the melody, the harmony parts, the bassline, and the percussion, which is his hand striking his own chest and body. There are no instruments and no samples. Most listeners at the time assumed they were hearing a small band with a whistling lead.

It was the first a cappella song to reach number one on the US chart, and it won record and song of the year at the Grammys, which for a track made entirely of one man's body is an unusual outcome.

The song's enormous ubiquity did him no favours artistically. He was a serious jazz vocalist with a technique — simultaneous melody and bass, rapid register jumps, improvisation across a full four-octave range — that almost nobody else possessed, and the hit flattened his public identity into a single cheerful chorus. He stopped performing it live for years.

His father, Robert McFerrin Sr., was the first Black man to sing with the Metropolitan Opera and dubbed Sidney Poitier's singing in Porgy and Bess.

McFerrin went on to conduct orchestras, which is roughly the opposite career move from the one the hit implied.
facts: Every sound including the bass is McFerrin's own voice
It was the first a cappella song to top the US chart

07-19.title: Wagner built a theater to control how his music was heard
07-19.story:
Frustrated by noisy houses, Wagner designed Bayreuth with a hidden orchestra pit and a darkened hall, inventing conventions concert audiences still follow.

Opera houses of the period were social venues. The auditorium stayed lit, people talked, moved between boxes, and treated the performance as a backdrop. Wagner regarded this as intolerable and built his own theatre at Bayreuth to eliminate it.

Two of his solutions became universal. Darkening the auditorium so the audience cannot see each other was considered radical and slightly hostile; it forces attention onto the stage and effectively ends conversation. And the sunken, covered orchestra pit hides the players entirely, which removes the visual distraction and blends the instrumental sound into a single mass before it reaches the audience — Bayreuth's pit produces a warmth that cannot be reproduced in a conventional house.

The seating was also unusual: a single raked fan of seats with no boxes, which flattened the social hierarchy that Italian opera house design encoded architecturally.

Every convention of concert etiquette people now treat as natural — lights down, silence, applause only at the end — descends substantially from one composer's irritation.

Wagner's antisemitism was explicit, published, and vicious, and the Bayreuth festival's later relationship with the Nazi regime was close. Both things sit in the same building.
facts: Darkening the auditorium was considered radical
The sunken pit blends the orchestra into a single sound

07-20.title: Mariah Carey co-wrote nearly everything she sang
07-20.story:
Unusual for a young pop signing, Carey held writing credits from her debut, giving her long-term control of her catalogue.

The standard arrangement for a young pop artist is to sing material written by others, which means the performer earns from records and touring while the writers earn from the songs — an income stream that keeps paying long after a career peaks. Carey held co-writing credits from the beginning, which is the reason her position decades later is what it is.

The demo reached Tommy Mottola, then head of Columbia, at a party, essentially by chance. He signed her, married her, and the professional and personal entanglement went badly.

Her vocal signature is the whistle register — the range above the normal soprano top, produced differently from ordinary singing and accessible to very few people. She used it as a compositional element rather than a stunt, writing lines that go there deliberately.

The other durable thing she did was help normalise rap features on pop records. The remix culture around her mid-nineties singles, pairing her with hip-hop artists, was not standard practice at the time and became so.

'All I Want for Christmas Is You', which she co-wrote, returns to the chart every December and has become one of the most valuable copyrights in popular music.
facts: She uses the whistle register, a rare vocal extreme
Her demo reached a label head at a party by chance

07-21.title: 'Sing Sing' delivered the drums for a hip-hop decade
07-21.story:
Gaz's 'Sing Sing' and its cousins supplied breaks that New York DJs guarded like secrets, soaking labels off records to hide titles.

The secrecy was competitive and total. A DJ's value at a block party rested on having breaks nobody else could identify, so records were carried in blank sleeves and their labels were soaked off in water or scratched into illegibility. Rivals would push toward the turntables during a set specifically to read a label, and getting close enough was a genuine victory.

That culture is the direct origin of crate digging as a discipline. Finding a usable break meant listening through entire albums of unpromising material for a few seconds of drums, in thrift stores, church sales, and the bargain bins of shops that had no idea what they were holding.

Break compilations began appearing in the eighties — bootleg records collecting the useful passages in one place — which democratised access and infuriated the DJs who had done the searching.

What the practice produced was an enormous act of collective musical archaeology. Records that had failed commercially and been forgotten were rediscovered, recontextualised, and given a second life entirely detached from their original purpose.

Most of the musicians who played on them never knew.
facts: DJs soaked or scratched off labels to protect their sources
Digging culture grew directly from that secrecy

07-22.title: The Winstons' break has its own documentary
07-22.story:
Decades after 'Amen, Brother', filmmakers traced how six seconds spawned entire scenes without the band's knowledge or payment.

Nate Harrison's 2004 video essay Can I Get an Amen? is the best-known account, and it makes an argument beyond the anecdote: that copyright as constructed does not recognise the thing that was actually valuable. Gregory Coleman's performance — the specific way he played those bars — is not itself protected in a way that generated any income for him, while the underlying composition and the recording sit with rights holders who had no part in it.

The scale of the uncompensated use is difficult to overstate. Jungle and drum and bass are built on it essentially wholesale, Aphex Twin and Squarepusher constructed careers partly on manipulating it, and it appears across rave, hip-hop, pop, and advertising.

Richard Spencer, the Winstons' leader, held the copyright and never pursued enforcement, which would have been ruinously expensive and legally uncertain across decades and jurisdictions.

A UK crowdfunding campaign in 2015 raised a modest amount and handed it to him — an entirely voluntary gesture from producers who felt the debt, with no legal basis whatsoever.

Coleman died homeless in 2006, having received nothing.
facts: Copyright never protected the drummer's performance itself
Public fundraising eventually delivered some belated compensation

07-23.title: Bach's music was rescued by a butcher's wrapping paper
07-23.story:
Legend holds Mendelssohn found Bach manuscripts used as packing material, sparking the revival that restored Bach to the canon.

The wrapping paper story is almost certainly embellished — versions of it attach to several composers and the documentary basis is thin. What is solid is that Bach's music had substantially fallen out of performance after his death in 1750, that he was remembered primarily as an organist and a technician rather than a composer, and that a great deal of the manuscript material sat unpublished and unperformed.

Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of the St Matthew Passion in Berlin is the event that changed it. He was twenty, he cut and reorchestrated the work considerably to suit the forces and tastes of the time, and the performance was a public sensation. It is generally treated as the beginning of the Bach revival.

The broader point is uncomfortable. A composer now regarded as foundational to Western music spent roughly eighty years in near-obscurity, and his return depended on a wealthy, well-connected young musician deciding to take the trouble.

What else did not get a Mendelssohn is unanswerable, which is precisely the problem with canons. They record what survived, not what was best.
facts: He staged the St Matthew Passion after 100 years of neglect
Bach was known mainly as an organist in his lifetime

07-24.title: Gladys Knight had the first 'Grapevine' hit, then lost it
07-24.story:
Gladys Knight and the Pips charted with 'I Heard It Through the Grapevine' before Marvin Gaye's slower version eclipsed it entirely.

Gaye actually recorded it first, in early 1967. Motown's quality control committee — a real internal body that voted on which records the label released — rejected it, and the song was given to Gladys Knight and the Pips, whose faster, gospel-driven version went to number two.

Gaye's take sat on the shelf for over a year and was eventually released as an album track. Radio programmers found it themselves and began playing it, and the demand became large enough that Motown had no choice but to issue it as a single.

It became the label's biggest-selling record to that point.

The two versions are a good demonstration of what tempo does to meaning. Knight's is defiant and propulsive — a person confronting a betrayal with energy. Gaye's is slow, sparse, and paranoid, and the arrangement leaves so much space that the vocal sounds genuinely isolated.

The song was written by Norman Whitfield and Barrett Strong, and Whitfield had pushed hard for the Gaye version against the committee's judgement. He was right, and the committee's process — which normally worked well — produced one of the label's clearest misjudgements.
facts: Motown shelved Gaye's take for over a year
Gaye's version became the label's biggest-selling single to that point

07-25.title: The Amen break is six seconds long and built three genres
07-25.story:
Chopped and sped up, the Winstons' break became the engine of jungle, drum and bass and UK hardcore, often at double its original tempo.

What British producers did with it in the early nineties went well beyond looping. The break was sliced into its individual drum hits and reassembled into entirely new patterns, then time-stretched to tempos around 160 to 180 beats per minute — roughly double the original — while keeping the pitch usable. That editing process is the actual compositional technique of jungle, and it required the sampler to be treated as an instrument rather than a playback device.

The result is a genre in which almost every record is built from the same six seconds and almost none of them sound alike.

Its reach extends far past dance music. It appears on N.W.A's Straight Outta Compton, the Prodigy's 'Firestarter', an Oasis single, television idents, and an enormous volume of advertising.

Nobody in the Winstons was ever paid for any of it. Richard Spencer, the band's leader and the copyright holder, was aware and had no practical route to enforcement.

A crowdfunding campaign in the UK raised a modest sum for him in 2015 — a voluntary gesture from producers rather than anything the industry required.
facts: Producers slice it into individual hits and rebuild new patterns
A crowdfunding campaign later raised money for the surviving band member

hits: Oasis - D'You Know What I Mean?

07-26.title: Carole King wrote hits in Brooklyn before singing them
07-26.story:
Born in Manhattan and raised in Brooklyn, King wrote dozens of standards with Gerry Goffin before 'Tapestry' made her a performer.

She attended James Madison High School in Brooklyn and was writing professionally as a teenager. 'Will You Love Me Tomorrow', written with Gerry Goffin when she was around seventeen, became the first number one by a Black girl group when the Shirelles recorded it — and it is a remarkably adult piece of writing about the morning after, which is not what the market expected from a teenager in 1960.

The Goffin–King partnership produced an extraordinary run: 'The Loco-Motion', 'Up on the Roof', '(You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman', 'Pleasant Valley Sunday'. She wrote the music, he wrote the lyrics, and they worked inside the Brill Building system alongside a floor of direct competitors.

The move to performing came after the marriage ended and after the industry had shifted toward artists writing their own material. Tapestry, in 1971, was one of the best-selling albums of the decade and reframed her entirely — the same songs, sung by the person who wrote them, at a piano.

Her version of 'A Natural Woman' arrived four years after Aretha Franklin's, which is an unusual direction of travel.
facts: She attended James Madison High School in Brooklyn
'Will You Love Me Tomorrow' was written when she was 17

07-27.title: Prince died, leaving a vault of unreleased music
07-27.story:
Prince recorded relentlessly, storing thousands of unreleased tracks in a bank-style vault at Paisley Park. Estimates suggest decades of material.

The vault is literal — a climate-controlled room with a bank-style door at Paisley Park, containing tapes going back to the seventies. Estimates of its contents vary wildly, but people who have been inside describe enough finished and near-finished material to release albums for decades.

The working method explains the volume. He recorded alone through the night, playing every part and frequently engineering himself, and he did it continuously for forty years. Finished songs were shelved not because they were weak but because he had already moved on.

He also gave enormous amounts away. 'Nothing Compares 2 U', 'Manic Monday', and 'I Feel for You' were written by him and became hits for other people, in some cases before most listeners knew who had written them.

He died in April 2016 of an accidental fentanyl overdose, having been treated for chronic hip pain for years, and left no will — which produced a long and expensive estate dispute before any of the vault material could be released.

The posthumous releases have been careful. Whether he would have sanctioned any of them is unknowable and was, throughout his life, the thing he cared most about controlling.
facts: He often recorded alone overnight, engineering himself
Some vault songs date to the seventies

07-28.title: Duke Ellington wrote for specific players, not instruments
07-28.story:
Ellington composed around individual musicians' quirks, writing parts only they could play. Replacing a member meant rewriting the music.

This is the thing that separates him from every other composer of comparable stature. A conventional score specifies trumpet; Ellington's specified Cootie Williams, or Bubber Miley, or Johnny Hodges — and the part exploited that particular player's tone, growl technique, or way of bending a note. He described his orchestra as his instrument, and he meant it literally.

The consequence is that the band was not replaceable. When a member left, the music written for them either left with him or had to be rewritten, and Ellington's players consequently stayed for decades, which is unheard of in a business where sidemen rotate constantly.

It also means the recordings are the compositions in a way that written scores are not. Later performances by other orchestras are, unavoidably, arrangements of something that was never fully notated.

He composed constantly and largely on the move — on trains between engagements, in hotel rooms, on the back of whatever paper was available — across a career spanning fifty years and thousands of pieces.

Billy Strayhorn was his writing partner for nearly three decades, and the division of authorship between them remains genuinely difficult to untangle.
facts: He called his orchestra his real instrument
He wrote on trains between gigs for decades

07-29.title: The Beastie Boys started as a Brooklyn hardcore band
07-29.story:
Before rapping, the Beastie Boys played fast hardcore punk around New York. Their pivot to hip-hop began as a joke track that got better reactions than their punk set.

The first release was Polly Wog Stew, a hardcore EP, and the band operated inside the same downtown and outer-borough punk circuit as everyone else playing that music in the early eighties. Kate Schellenbach, later of Luscious Jackson, played drums.

The joke track was 'Cooky Puss', built around a prank phone call to a Carvel ice cream shop over a beat. It got played in clubs, it got a reaction the punk material was not getting, and the band followed the reaction. Rick Rubin, then producing out of an NYU dorm room, became the connection into hip-hop proper.

The transition was not smooth or particularly principled at the time. Licensed to Ill sold enormously and leaned on a frat-party persona the band spent much of the following decade repudiating, publicly and repeatedly.

What is genuinely unusual is that they kept playing instruments. By Check Your Head they were performing as a band again, and the later records combine live playing, sampling, and rapping in a way almost nobody else attempted. The punk years turned out not to be a phase they left behind.
facts: Their first release was a hardcore EP, not a rap record
They kept playing instruments themselves long after going platinum

07-30.title: Handel wrote 'Messiah' in 24 days
07-30.story:
Working almost without sleep, Handel completed the 259-page score in just over three weeks. A servant reported finding him weeping at his desk.

The speed is less miraculous than it sounds, and more impressive for a different reason. Handel, like most composers of the period, reused material freely — several movements adapt his own earlier Italian secular works — and he wrote in a highly systematised style where a great deal could be produced quickly by a fluent professional. What is remarkable is not that he wrote fast but that he wrote this fast and produced something that has not left the repertoire in nearly three centuries.

His circumstances mattered. Italian opera, the form he had built his career on, was collapsing commercially in London, and he was in serious financial difficulty. The English-language oratorio was a pivot toward a cheaper form with a broader audience and no staging costs.

It premiered in Dublin in 1742 as a charity performance, not in London. Demand was high enough that the organisers asked ladies to come without hooped skirts and gentlemen without swords so more people could be fitted into the hall.

The tradition of standing for the Hallelujah chorus is attributed to George II, though there is no contemporary evidence he was even present.
facts: It premiered in Dublin, not London
Audiences were asked to leave hoops and swords at home to fit more people in

07-31.title: Kurt Cobain was born, and later hid melodies in noise
07-31.story:
Cobain's writing method paired sweet pop melody with deliberately abrasive tone, a tension he credited to loving both the Beatles and Black Flag.

The structural signature is the quiet-loud-quiet dynamic, which Nirvana took fairly directly from the Pixies — Cobain said as much, repeatedly and without embarrassment. A verse played clean and restrained, a chorus that arrives at full distortion, and the contrast doing the emotional work that an arrangement would otherwise have to build gradually.

Underneath the noise, the songs are conventionally melodic. Strip the distortion from most of Nevermind and what remains is pop writing in a fairly traditional mould, which is precisely why it crossed over so completely.

Cobain disliked the album's sound. Butch Vig produced and Andy Wallace mixed it into something considerably more polished than the band had wanted, and Cobain complained publicly about the gloss almost immediately — In Utero, with Steve Albini, was the corrective.

His lyrics were frequently written minutes before the vocal take, assembled from notebooks rather than composed as arguments, which is why they resist interpretation and why interpreting them anyway became a cottage industry.

He died by suicide in April 1994, at twenty-seven. If this is a difficult subject for you personally, it is worth talking to someone you trust.
facts: 'Nevermind' was mixed to sound more polished than the band wanted
He wrote lyrics minutes before recording many vocals

08-01.title: The Moog synthesizer needed a hit to be taken seriously
08-01.story:
Wendy Carlos's 'Switched-On Bach' proved the Moog could make music, not just noise. It became one of the best-selling classical records ever.

The instrument had been available for a few years and was largely regarded as a laboratory curiosity or a source of sound effects. Robert Moog's modular system was difficult to use, unstable in tuning, and had no obvious repertoire, and the electronic music being made with comparable equipment was largely academic and forbidding.

Carlos's choice of Bach was strategic. Bach's writing is contrapuntal, precisely notated, and instrumentally neutral — it has been transcribed for every ensemble imaginable for two centuries — so realising it electronically was a demonstration rather than a provocation.

The labour involved was enormous. The Moog was monophonic, playing one note at a time, so every voice in a fugue had to be recorded separately and layered, with tuning drifting between passes and requiring constant correction. Carlos worked with Rachel Elkind on the production across many months.

It sold in the hundreds of thousands and became one of the best-selling classical records ever released, which put the synthesizer in front of musicians who had dismissed it.

Carlos went on to score A Clockwork Orange and Tron, and is a trans woman who came out publicly in 1979, at considerable personal cost.
facts: Each note had to be played and layered one at a time
The instrument was monophonic, so chords required many passes

08-02.title: The piano on 'Layla' was never meant to be there
08-02.story:
Drummer Jim Gordon was caught playing a private piano melody during downtime. Eric Clapton heard it through the studio glass and insisted it become the song's second half.

The result is one of the strangest structures in rock radio. 'Layla' is effectively two separate pieces bolted together: a fast, desperate blues-rock song built on Duane Allman's slide guitar figure, followed by a long, slow, largely instrumental piano coda that shares no material with what precedes it. Nothing about the arrangement prepares you for the transition.

The coda was recorded separately, some weeks after the main track, and joined to it with a tape splice rather than performed as one piece. The two halves sit at different tempos and in different emotional registers, and the join is audible if you listen for it.

Authorship of the piano theme has been disputed for decades, with claims that Gordon adapted it from a piece written by Rita Coolidge. Gordon received a co-writing credit on the song.

Radio initially treated the length as a problem and often played an edit ending before the coda. Over time the full version won, which is the more interesting outcome — a seven-minute record with an unexplained second movement became one of the most requested songs in the format.
facts: The coda was recorded months after the main track
The two halves were spliced together with tape, not re-performed

08-03.title: Stevie Wonder played nearly every instrument on 'Innervisions'
08-03.story:
Wonder recorded drums, keys, bass and harmonica himself, layering parts alone in the studio through the night. Engineers worked in shifts to keep up with him.

The autonomy was contractual before it was creative. On turning twenty-one, Wonder let his Motown contract lapse, formed his own publishing company, and renegotiated for full artistic control — an almost unheard-of position for an artist the label had managed since childhood. The run of albums that followed exists because of that legal manoeuvre.

His principal instrument on these records is the clavinet, an electric keyboard with a plucked, percussive attack that behaves more like a rhythm guitar than a piano. He paired it with the ARP and Moog synthesizers, working with the engineers Robert Margouleff and Malcolm Cecil, who had built a large modular system and effectively functioned as translators between Wonder's ideas and the machines.
