Every song is counted in identically — one-two-three-four — which functioned as a structural device as much as a count-off.

What made it influential was the demonstration rather than the innovation. The record proved that a band with limited technique, no budget, and no studio access could make something that sounded finished, which is the message that reached kids in Britain and produced the entire first wave of UK punk within about eighteen months.

The band never had a hit single and never sold in significant numbers during its existence. Its influence is wildly out of proportion to its commercial performance, which is true of remarkably few records.
facts: They counted off every song identically
The whole album was recorded in about a week

09-27.title: The Wrecking Crew played on records credited to bands
09-27.story:
A pool of Los Angeles session musicians performed on hits attributed to famous groups. Many listeners never knew.

The arrangement was standard practice and largely unspoken. A band would be signed on the strength of its singer and image, and when it came time to record, producers brought in session players who could deliver a usable take in two passes rather than twenty. The band's name went on the sleeve.

The pool included Carol Kaye, Hal Blaine, Tommy Tedesco, Glen Campbell, and Leon Russell among many others, and their playing appears on an enormous share of the era's American hits — Beach Boys records, Phil Spector productions, the Monkees, television themes, film scores.

Carol Kaye's bass playing in particular is on hundreds of records people would attribute to someone else, and she was one of very few women working at that level in any studio.

Some bands genuinely did not know until the record came out, and a few learned their own parts afterward in order to perform them live.

The practice is less hidden now but has not stopped. What changed is the disclosure norm — credits are more complete, and the assumption that the people pictured played the notes has quietly been abandoned.
facts: Carol Kaye played bass on hundreds of well-known records
Some bands only learned their own parts after release

09-28.title: 'Sunshine of Your Love' came from a bass riff heard at a gig
09-28.story:
Jack Bruce wrote the riff after seeing Jimi Hendrix play live and going home to his bass at dawn.

Cream had gone to see Hendrix at a London club, and Bruce came away rattled. By his account he went home in the early hours, picked up a double bass, and worked out the descending figure that opens the song more or less immediately — a direct response to having watched someone reset the standard for what a guitarist could do.

The riff is unusual in that it is a bass line the guitar doubles rather than a guitar riff with bass underneath, which is why it sits so low and heavy.

Ginger Baker's drum part is the other distinctive element. Rather than marking the backbeat, he plays a tom pattern across the beat that he described as drawing on Native American rhythms, and the effect is that the song does not push forward so much as circle.

The band nearly discarded it. Eric Clapton in particular reportedly thought it too simple, and it took Ahmet Ertegun at Atlantic to insist it was a single.

It became Cream's biggest American hit and one of the most recognisable riffs in rock, which is a reasonable return on a sleepless night.
facts: Ginger Baker's tom pattern was inspired by Native American rhythms
The band nearly rejected it as too simple

09-29.title: Which 'Nothing Compares 2 U' wins: Prince or Sinéad?
09-29.story:
Prince wrote it for his side project The Family. Sinéad O'Connor's 1990 version, with its single-shot video, became definitive.

The Family's original is a full band arrangement with saxophone, buried on an album by a Prince side project that lasted one record. Almost nobody heard it, and Prince rarely performed the song himself until after O'Connor's version succeeded.

Her reading strips it to a sparse arrangement and a vocal that moves from restrained to broken over four minutes. Producer Nellee Hooper's arrangement leaves an enormous amount of space, which puts all the weight on the performance.

The video is close to a single continuous shot of her face, and the tears near the end were reportedly not planned — she has said she was thinking about her mother, who had died in 1985. That accident is a large part of why the record landed the way it did.

O'Connor's relationship with fame afterward was adversarial and principled. Her 1992 protest against the Catholic Church on live television cost her enormously at the time and looks quite different now.

She died in 2023. Her account of Prince's own behaviour toward her was, by her telling, frightening — the two never had a comfortable relationship over a song that made them both.
facts: Her tears in the video were reportedly unplanned
Prince rarely performed it before her version succeeded

09-30.title: Bill Withers was making toilet seats for airplanes
09-30.story:
Withers kept his factory job while recording 'Ain't No Sunshine', assuming music would not last. The famous repeated 'I know' was a placeholder.

He was thirty-two, had spent nine years in the Navy, and was working at a factory making aircraft lavatory fittings. He recorded his first album while still employed there, and photographs from the period show him at the studio holding his lunchbox, because he was going to work afterward.

The caution was rational. He had watched the industry chew through people and had no reason to believe he would be an exception, and he kept the job until the record was demonstrably working.

The repeated 'I know' — twenty-six times in a row — was a placeholder. He intended to write a proper verse there and was told by the people in the room, including Booker T. Jones, to leave it. It is now the most memorable thing in the song, and it works because the repetition does something a lyric could not: it enacts the obsessiveness the words are describing.

He left the industry in the mid-eighties after protracted conflict with his label about creative control, and simply stopped. He gave interviews occasionally and declined, for decades, to come back.

He died in 2020.
facts: He meant to write real lyrics there but was told to keep it
He brought his lunchbox to the studio

10-01.title: Miles Davis plugged in and lost half his audience
10-01.story:
'Bitches Brew' used electric instruments and studio editing, alienating purists while inventing fusion.

The electric instruments were only half of it. The more radical decision was structural: producer Teo Macero recorded long, loosely directed sessions and then assembled the album afterward with tape splices, looping passages, repeating sections, and constructing pieces that were never performed continuously by anyone.

That is a rock and pop production method applied to jazz, and to a substantial part of the jazz audience it was a betrayal of the form's founding principle — that a recording documents musicians playing.

Davis was explicit about his motivation. He had watched Sly Stone and Jimi Hendrix reach audiences that jazz was losing, and he had no interest in curating a museum.

The personnel is remarkable in hindsight: Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock, John McLaughlin, Joe Zawinul, Jack DeJohnette. Nearly all of them went on to lead the fusion movement the album started.

It sold better than any jazz record he had made and cost him a substantial part of his existing audience.

He did this repeatedly across his career — bebop, cool, modal, fusion — and each time the people who had followed him to the last position objected to the next.
facts: Producer Teo Macero spliced the tapes like a film editor
Long passages were assembled, not performed continuously

10-02.title: Which 'Respect' wins: Otis or Aretha?
10-02.story:
Otis Redding wrote it in 1965 as a working man's plea. Aretha Franklin rebuilt it in 1967 as a demand, adding the spelling hook and her sisters' backing vocals.

The two versions are worth hearing back to back because almost nothing changes on paper. Same title, largely the same words, similar tempo. Redding's is a man coming home from work asking to be treated properly in his own house — the tone is tired and slightly pleading, and the arrangement pushes forward like someone making a case.

Franklin's inverts the power relationship completely. The narrator is not asking. She is stating terms, and the spelled-out hook — invented in the studio with her sisters Carolyn and Erma — functions as an instruction rather than a chorus.

The arrangement does its share. King Curtis's saxophone solo quotes 'When Something Is Wrong with My Baby', the rhythm section drives rather than swings, and the whole thing was built quickly at Atlantic with Jerry Wexler and the Muscle Shoals players.

Redding took it well and appears to have found it funny, joking at Monterey that the girl had taken his song away from him.

Most covers disappear behind the original. This is one of the few cases where the second version became the definitive one, and the first became the interesting footnote.
facts: Redding joked she had stolen the song for good
Aretha's version was cut in a single afternoon session

10-03.title: 'Under Pressure' was a jam nobody planned
10-03.story:
Bowie and Queen were in the same Swiss studio and started improvising. The famous bassline came from John Deacon noodling during a break.

The two acts were working at Mountain Studios in Montreux at the same time, and what began as Bowie dropping in to add backing vocals to something else turned into an all-day improvisation. Neither party arrived with a song.

The origin of the bassline is genuinely disputed. Most accounts credit John Deacon playing it during a break; Brian May has suggested Bowie changed it; Deacon has given differing versions over the years. The likeliest explanation is that nobody was paying attention at the moment it happened because nobody knew it mattered yet.

The vocal was built by a method Bowie proposed: each singer went into the booth without hearing what the other had done, sang over the track, and the results were combined. That is why the two voices overlap and interrupt rather than trading verses politely.

Both parties later expressed reservations about the mix, having run out of patience by the end of the session.

Vanilla Ice used the bassline on 'Ice Ice Baby' in 1990, initially claimed it was different because of an added note, and eventually settled with credit and payment.
facts: Accounts differ on who actually invented the riff
Vanilla Ice later used it and initially denied the resemblance

10-04.title: The producer who never let artists hear playback
10-04.story:
Phil Spector often refused to let performers hear the full mix, keeping the arrangement in his head so no one could argue with it.

The control was total by design. Sessions at Gold Star ran for hours with dozens of musicians playing doubled and tripled parts, and the only person who knew what the finished record would sound like was Spector. Singers frequently cut vocals without hearing the assembled arrangement, which removed any basis on which they could object to it.

That method produced records of genuine power and a working environment that was, by many first-hand accounts, controlling and frightening well before it became criminal.

Darlene Love is the clearest case. Her voice is on records credited to the Crystals and to Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, and Spector released her performances under whichever group name suited him commercially. She spent years in litigation over royalties and credit and was at one point cleaning houses while hearing her own uncredited voice on the radio at Christmas.

Spector was convicted of the second-degree murder of Lana Clarkson in 2009 and died in prison in 2021.

The records remain in the canon. The people who made them were treated as raw material by a man whose method depended on them not knowing what they were making.
facts: Sessions ran for hours with dozens of players
Darlene Love's voice appeared on records credited to other groups

10-05.title: Grandmaster Flash built his mixer by hand
10-05.story:
Trained in electronics, Flash rigged a crossfader and cue system so he could hear the next record before the crowd did.

The problem he was solving was precise. Kool Herc's technique required switching between two copies of a record at exactly the right moment, and there was no way to check where the second record was without the audience hearing it. Herc did it by eye and by feel, and it was frequently approximate.

Flash had studied electronics at a vocational school, and he wired a preview system — a single-pole double-throw switch feeding a headphone amp — that let him cue the second turntable silently. Parts were salvaged from junked stereos and car audio.

That single capability is the foundation of everything DJs do now. Being able to hear the next record before the crowd is what makes accurate beat-matching possible, and once it was possible, mixing became a craft with a technical standard rather than an approximation.

He built the rest of the vocabulary on top of it: backspinning, punch phrasing, and the clock theory of marking a record so he could find a specific point instantly.

The crossfader as a standard feature on DJ mixers exists because manufacturers eventually copied what he and his contemporaries had already built for themselves.
facts: He soldered parts salvaged from junked stereos
That preview capability made beat-matching possible

10-06.title: Erasmus Hall in Flatbush produced two American icons
10-06.story:
Barbra Streisand and Neil Diamond both sang in the chorus at Erasmus Hall High School on Flatbush Avenue, a short walk from Cortelyou Road. They barely knew each other then.

Erasmus Hall is the oldest secondary school in New York State, founded in 1786 when Flatbush was a Dutch farming village, and the original wooden academy building still stands in the courtyard of the Gothic quadrangle that grew up around it. For most of the twentieth century it was an enormous public high school serving a neighbourhood in constant demographic change, and its alumni list is correspondingly improbable.

Streisand and Diamond overlapped in the choral club without any particular sense of each other. Both have described the connection as a footnote they only found interesting decades later, when they recorded 'You Don't Bring Me Flowers' as a duet in 1978 — a record that reached number one and was itself something of an accident, assembled after a radio programmer spliced their separate solo versions together and listeners demanded the real thing.

The school's cultural output extends well beyond them: Clive Davis, who would sign Bruce Springsteen and Whitney Houston, came through the same building, as did a long list of writers, athletes, and chess players.

It is a useful reminder of what a functioning neighbourhood school produced when the neighbourhood was dense, mixed, and the school was properly funded.
facts: They later recorded the duet 'You Don't Bring Me Flowers' in 1978
Clive Davis, who signed Springsteen and Whitney Houston, also went to Erasmus

10-07.title: The Beatles played Ed Sullivan to 73 million people
10-07.story:
Broadcast from CBS Studio 50 in Manhattan, the performance was watched by roughly 40 percent of America. Crime rates that hour reportedly dipped.

The booking came out of an accident of timing. Sullivan had been at Heathrow in late 1963 and witnessed the crowd chaos around the band's return from Sweden, and he booked them on the strength of the scene rather than the music, which he had not particularly heard.

The scale of the audience was a function of a media environment that no longer exists. Three networks, one time slot, and no way to watch later meant a single broadcast could genuinely reach forty percent of a country at once. Nothing since has been able to concentrate attention that way, which is why the moment gets treated as a turning point rather than a television booking.

The studio had roughly seven hundred seats and received something in the region of fifty thousand ticket requests.

The often-repeated claim about crime dropping during the broadcast is anecdotal and has never been properly substantiated, but it survives because it captures something true about the concentration involved.

The practical consequence was immediate. Within months American labels were signing British guitar bands indiscriminately, and the balance of trade in popular music reversed for the better part of a decade.
facts: The studio received 50,000 ticket requests for 700 seats
Sullivan had booked them after seeing fan chaos at Heathrow

10-08.title: Autotune was invented by an oil industry engineer
10-08.story:
Andy Hildebrand used seismic data math, designed to find oil underground, to detect and correct pitch. He built it as a subtle repair tool.

Hildebrand's previous work involved sending sound waves into the ground and analysing the reflections to map geological structures — a problem of extracting periodic signal from noise. Pitch detection in a human voice is mathematically the same problem, and he realised the autocorrelation techniques transferred directly.

The intended use was invisible repair: nudge a slightly flat note into tune so a good vocal take with one bad syllable does not have to be re-recorded. Used gently it is undetectable, and it has been used gently on a very large proportion of commercial records since.

The famous sound is a misuse. The plugin has a retune speed control, and setting it to its fastest value forces the voice to snap instantly between exact pitches rather than gliding, producing the stepped robotic effect. Hildebrand has said he included the extreme setting as a joke and never expected anyone to use it.

Cher's 'Believe' put it on the radio in 1998, the producers initially claimed it was a vocoder, and T-Pain later built an entire vocal identity on it.

It is now among the most consequential audio tools ever written, and it exists because someone was looking for oil.
facts: Cher's 'Believe' used the extreme setting the inventor called a joke
Hildebrand said he never expected anyone to use it that way

10-09.title: George Harrison's sitar lesson changed rock
10-09.story:
Harrison studied under Ravi Shankar, who insisted he learn properly rather than use the instrument as decoration. Indian modes then filtered into Western pop.

Shankar was a serious classical musician with no particular interest in Western pop and, by his own account, no clear idea who the Beatles were when they were introduced. His condition for teaching was that Harrison approach the instrument as a discipline — sitting properly, learning scales and rhythmic cycles — rather than treating it as an exotic sound to layer onto a rock record.

Harrison had already used sitar decoratively on 'Norwegian Wood', which he later described as fairly rudimentary. The study that followed produced something different: 'Within You Without You' is built on Indian classical structure, features no other Beatle, and uses tabla and dilruba players rather than the band.

The wider consequence was a vocabulary shift. Drones, modal scales that do not resolve the way Western harmony does, and long non-developmental forms entered rock and stayed, feeding directly into psychedelia and later into minimalism's popular reception.

It also opened a long and complicated conversation about appropriation that has not closed. Shankar himself was ambivalent, welcoming the attention to Indian music and frequently exasperated by audiences who treated a centuries-old tradition as a lifestyle accessory.
facts: Shankar initially had no idea who the Beatles were
'Within You Without You' features no other Beatle

10-10.title: Why Motown mixed its records on a car speaker
10-10.story:
Berry Gordy kept a cheap car-dashboard speaker wired into the Hitsville control room. If a mix didn't hit on that tinny cone, it went back, because that's where America actually heard music.

The logic was ruthless and correct. In the early sixties most people encountered a new record either on a car radio or on a portable transistor set, and both reproduced almost nothing below about 150 hertz. A mix that sounded enormous on studio monitors could vanish entirely on the equipment the audience owned. Gordy's speaker was a reality check disguised as a piece of junk.

What it produced was a house sound built around the middle of the frequency range. Motown records push vocals, tambourine, hand claps, and upper-register piano hard, and the bass — played by James Jamerson, one of the most inventive musicians of the century — is arranged so its melodic movement survives even when the low end does not.

The practice also explains the compression. Motown mixes are dense and loud in a way that cuts through AM static, because a record competing with engine noise and interference does not get a second chance.

Engineers elsewhere adopted the same idea and still use it. Almost every professional studio keeps one deliberately mediocre speaker, and the question it answers has not changed: does this hold up on the thing people actually own?
facts: Engineers called the test 'the Detroit ear'
Motown also boosted mid-range so songs cut through AM radio static

10-11.title: Why disco records used real strings and a metronome
10-11.story:
Philadelphia producers paired full orchestras with a rigid four-on-the-floor kick so DJs could beat-match by hand. The click track was the secret that made mixing possible.

Before this, dance records drifted. Live drummers speed up and slow down by a few beats per minute across a take, which is musically expressive and makes it effectively impossible to blend two records without the beats sliding apart. A DJ working with turntables and no pitch control had to cut between songs rather than mix through them.

Recording to a click fixed the tempo for the length of the track, and once tempo was stable a DJ could match one record to another and hold the blend indefinitely. That single technical change is what made continuous dancing — and therefore the extended club night as we understand it — possible.

The Philadelphia sound layered that mechanical foundation with the opposite: full string sections, horns, harp, and vibes, arranged by people trained in orchestral writing. The contrast between a metronomic kick and lush live orchestration is the defining texture of the era.

Labels began printing the tempo on record labels as a service to DJs, and a large share of the catalogue sits within a few beats of 120 per minute — close enough that almost any two records could be mixed together.
facts: Engineers printed the tempo on the record label for DJs
This is why so many disco 12-inches sit near 120 beats per minute

10-12.title: Prince played 27 instruments on his debut
10-12.story:
Warner Bros. doubted a 19-year-old could produce himself, so Prince recorded a demo playing every part. He got full creative control, almost unheard of for a new artist.

The demonstration was the negotiation. Label executives wanted an established producer attached; Prince's response was to go into the studio and produce a recording alone that made the question moot. The resulting contract gave him production control and a substantial advance at an age when most signings get neither.

The instrument count on For You is listed on the sleeve, and it covers guitars, bass, every keyboard in the room, drums, percussion, and a long list of incidental instruments. He recorded it in roughly five weeks, working the same way he would for the next four decades: laying down drums first, then bass, then building upward alone.

That method is audible in the results. One-person recordings tend to have an unusual rhythmic character, because the parts are not responding to each other in real time — they are responding to a single internal sense of time, layered.

The control he won at nineteen is what made everything afterward possible, and it is also what made his later fight with Warner over ownership of his masters so bitter. He had understood from the start that the contract was the instrument that mattered most.
facts: He reportedly recorded the album in about five weeks
His contract made him one of the youngest self-producing artists on a major label

10-13.title: Robert Johnson recorded facing the corner of a room
10-13.story:
In a San Antonio hotel room, Johnson played into the corner. For years it was called superstition; engineers now note it created natural bass reinforcement.

The sessions took place in a makeshift studio set up in a hotel, which was normal for field recording in the thirties — a producer travelled with equipment and recorded whoever was available in whatever room could be rented. Johnson recorded twenty-nine songs across two sets of sessions, in San Antonio and later Dallas, and that is the entire surviving catalogue.

The corner story was long told as evidence of shyness or of the occult mythology that accumulated around him. The acoustic explanation is more mundane and more interesting: a corner reinforces low frequencies and reflects sound back toward the player, so it functions as both a bass boost and a monitor. Musicians still use corners for exactly this.

The mythology around Johnson — the deal at the crossroads, the poisoned whiskey, the unmarked grave — took hold largely because so little was documented. Two verified photographs exist. Basic biographical facts were established only decades after his death.

What is not in question is the playing. The recordings suggest a guitarist maintaining bass, rhythm, and melody simultaneously with a precision that has kept musicians arguing about the technique for eighty years.
facts: Only 29 songs of his survive
The corner technique is a real acoustic trick still used today

10-14.title: Bill Withers recorded 'Grandma's Hands' in under two minutes
10-14.story:
Withers wrote about his grandmother's church in West Virginia. The song is barely 120 seconds long and needed nothing more.

The restraint is the craft. It is a series of images of one woman's hands — clapping in church, picking him up, warning him about the street — and each verse is a single memory delivered without commentary. There is no bridge, no key change, and no attempt to broaden it into a statement about grandmothers generally.

He resisted adding anything. The song says what it has to say and stops, which is a much harder decision than extending it.

Withers was in his early thirties and still working a factory job when he recorded it, and the writing throughout that first album has a plainness that came from not having spent years inside the music industry learning what songs are supposed to do.

Blackstreet's 'No Diggity' is built on it, using the guitar figure and Withers's voice, and it introduced the song to an audience two generations later.

The original runs about two minutes. Contemporary radio convention said a single needed roughly three, and Withers's response was that the song was finished.

He left the industry entirely in the mid-eighties and declined, for the rest of his life, to be persuaded back.
facts: Blackstreet later built 'No Diggity' on its bones
He resisted adding a bridge, saying it was finished

10-15.title: Tape delay was invented using two machines
10-15.story:
Engineers fed a signal from one tape head to another, creating slapback echo. Sun Studio's version defined early rock and roll vocals.

The mechanism is entirely physical. A tape machine has separate record and playback heads with a gap between them, so the playback head hears the signal a fraction of a second after it is recorded. Feed that delayed output back into the input and you get a repeating echo, with the delay time determined by the distance between the heads and the speed of the tape.

Sam Phillips used a second Ampex machine at Sun to produce the short, single-repeat version known as slapback, and it is all over the early Elvis Presley, Carl Perkins, and Johnny Cash recordings. It gives a voice presence and size without the wash of a reverb chamber, and it is a substantial part of what people mean by the Sun sound.

The delay could not be set arbitrarily. Changing it meant changing tape speed, which also changed pitch, so engineers worked within a narrow range of usable settings.

Purpose-built tape echo units followed — the Echoplex, the Roland Space Echo — and those became instruments in their own right, particularly in dub, where King Tubby and Lee Perry played the delay as a performance control rather than setting it and leaving it.
facts: Elvis's voice at Sun is drenched in it
The delay time depended on physical head spacing

10-16.title: 'Funky Worm' gave G-funk its whine
10-16.story:
The Ohio Players' high synthesizer squeal became the signature lead sound of West Coast hip-hop two decades later.

The original is a joke. The track is a comic novelty built around a character called the worm, and the high, wavering synthesizer lead — played on an Arp — was intended as a cartoonish effect rather than a musical statement.

Twenty years later Dr. Dre and his contemporaries lifted that timbre and made it the defining lead sound of West Coast hip-hop. It appears on N.W.A records, across The Chronic, and throughout Snoop Dogg's early work, usually played rather than sampled but unmistakably derived from the same source.

The reason it works in that context is that it occupies a frequency range nothing else in the mix uses. Under a heavy 808 or live-feeling bass and a mid-range vocal, a thin high whine cuts through without any competition, which is why G-funk arrangements sound so wide.

The Ohio Players were a serious funk band with a substantial catalogue, and being remembered principally for a comic synthesizer squeal is a strange fate.

It is a good example of how sampling culture reassigns value. The thing later producers wanted was the element the original band would have considered least important.
facts: Dr. Dre used the tone repeatedly
The original was meant as a comic effect

10-17.title: Little Richard's 'Tutti Frutti' had to be rewritten on the spot
10-17.story:
The original lyrics were far too explicit for radio, so a local songwriter rewrote them during a lunch break at the session.

The session was going badly. Richard had been cutting conventional blues numbers at J&M in New Orleans and none of it was working, and during a break at a nearby club he sat at a piano and played the song as he actually performed it live — which was explicitly about gay sex and completely unreleasable in 1955.

Producer Bumps Blackwell recognised the energy immediately and brought in Dorothy LaBostrie, a local songwriter, who rewrote the lyric in roughly fifteen minutes over lunch. The result is nonsense about girls named Sue and Daisy, and the nonsense is precisely why it works — the words carry no meaning, so all the information is in the delivery.

The opening piano and the shouted syllables were kept exactly as first played.

What that record established is difficult to overstate: the pounding piano, the screamed vocal, and the sheer velocity became the template for rock and roll performance.

Pat Boone's sanitised cover outsold it, which was standard practice for white artists covering Black records at the time and is one of the clearer illustrations of how the money moved.

Richard was, throughout, considerably queerer than the record industry was willing to let him be.
facts: The rewrite took roughly 15 minutes
Richard's piano intro was kept exactly as first played

10-18.title: Maurice Ravel wrote 'Boléro' as an experiment in repetition
10-18.story:
Ravel called it 'orchestral tissue without music', a single melody repeated with growing instrumentation and no development. He was surprised it became famous.

The structure is almost aggressively simple. One melody, stated eighteen times, over an unchanging snare drum pattern that runs the entire fifteen-odd minutes, with a single key change near the end. There is no development, no counter-subject, no departure. The only thing that changes is orchestration and volume.

That makes it a piece about timbre rather than about music in the conventional sense — which is precisely what Ravel meant by his dismissive description of it. He was demonstrating that colour alone could sustain a listener's attention for a quarter of an hour, and he appears to have regarded the demonstration as a technical exercise rather than a masterpiece.

The orchestration is genuinely virtuosic. Instruments are combined in unusual pairings to produce composite tones, including a passage where a horn, celesta, and piccolos are voiced to imitate the harmonics of an organ.

The snare player has one of the least enviable jobs in the repertoire: the same two-bar rhythm, unbroken, for the entire piece, with the tempo and dynamic control that everything else depends on.

It became the most performed and most lucrative work he ever wrote, to his visible irritation.
facts: The snare drum plays the same rhythm for roughly 15 minutes
He reportedly said the piece contained 'no music in it whatsoever'

10-19.title: Sister Rosetta Tharpe played electric guitar before Chuck Berry
10-19.story:
Tharpe's distorted gospel guitar and showmanship directly shaped rock and roll. Berry, Presley and Little Richard all cited her.

She was playing solid-body and hollow-body electric guitar with heavy distortion in the 1930s and 1940s, in churches and on the gospel circuit, with a technique built on bent notes, aggressive attack, and single-string soloing. Everything people describe as the invention of rock guitar in the mid-fifties is already present in her recordings a decade earlier.

'Strange Things Happening Every Day', recorded in 1944, is on many people's shortlist for the first rock and roll record, and it charted on the race records chart at a time when gospel almost never crossed over.

Her position was uncomfortable throughout. Churches objected to a woman playing secular-sounding electric guitar and performing in nightclubs; the secular world did not fully claim her either. She was recording gospel and performing in clubs simultaneously, which satisfied nobody's categories.

Chuck Berry, Elvis Presley, Little Richard, and Johnny Cash all cited her directly. Berry in particular has been quoted saying his career was essentially one long Rosetta Tharpe impression.

She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018, forty-five years after her death and long after everyone she influenced.
facts: She played a solid-body electric in churches, scandalizing congregations
She was inducted into the Rock Hall only in 2018

10-20.title: 'Billie Jean' nearly lost its famous intro
10-20.story:
Michael Jackson built the song around a bassline he refused to shorten. Quincy Jones wanted the 29-second intro cut down; Jackson insisted it stay because, in his words, it made him want to dance.

The argument was a real one and Jones lost it. Twenty-nine seconds of drums and bass before a vocal enters is an eternity by radio convention, and a producer's instinct is to get to the hook. Jackson's counterargument was simply that the groove was the hook, and that he wanted to dance to it before anyone sang anything.

He was right. The intro is one of the most recognisable passages in pop, identifiable within about two bars, and it works precisely because it is allowed to establish itself without interruption.

The production detail around it is obsessive. Jackson reportedly recorded the lead vocal partly through a cardboard tube to alter the tone, and Bruce Swedien mixed the track something in the region of ninety times before Jones approved a version — they eventually went back to an early mix.

A drum riser was built specifically for the song to get the kick and snare sound they wanted.

The result is a record with very few elements, each of them exhaustively worked. Almost nothing is happening, and every part of it took months.
facts: Jackson reportedly recorded the lead vocal through a cardboard tube for tone
The song was mixed roughly 90 times before Jones approved a take

10-21.title: The Wrecking Crew played on records credited to bands
10-21.story:
A pool of Los Angeles session musicians performed on hits attributed to famous groups. Many listeners never knew.

The arrangement was standard practice and largely unspoken. A band would be signed on the strength of its singer and image, and when it came time to record, producers brought in session players who could deliver a usable take in two passes rather than twenty. The band's name went on the sleeve.

The pool included Carol Kaye, Hal Blaine, Tommy Tedesco, Glen Campbell, and Leon Russell among many others, and their playing appears on an enormous share of the era's American hits — Beach Boys records, Phil Spector productions, the Monkees, television themes, film scores.

Carol Kaye's bass playing in particular is on hundreds of records people would attribute to someone else, and she was one of very few women working at that level in any studio.

Some bands genuinely did not know until the record came out, and a few learned their own parts afterward in order to perform them live.

The practice is less hidden now but has not stopped. What changed is the disclosure norm — credits are more complete, and the assumption that the people pictured played the notes has quietly been abandoned.
facts: Carol Kaye played bass on hundreds of well-known records
Some bands only learned their own parts after release

10-22.title: 'Sunshine of Your Love' came from a bass riff heard at a gig
10-22.story:
Jack Bruce wrote the riff after seeing Jimi Hendrix play live and going home to his bass at dawn.

Cream had gone to see Hendrix at a London club, and Bruce came away rattled. By his account he went home in the early hours, picked up a double bass, and worked out the descending figure that opens the song more or less immediately — a direct response to having watched someone reset the standard for what a guitarist could do.

The riff is unusual in that it is a bass line the guitar doubles rather than a guitar riff with bass underneath, which is why it sits so low and heavy.

Ginger Baker's drum part is the other distinctive element. Rather than marking the backbeat, he plays a tom pattern across the beat that he described as drawing on Native American rhythms, and the effect is that the song does not push forward so much as circle.

The band nearly discarded it. Eric Clapton in particular reportedly thought it too simple, and it took Ahmet Ertegun at Atlantic to insist it was a single.

It became Cream's biggest American hit and one of the most recognisable riffs in rock, which is a reasonable return on a sleepless night.
facts: Ginger Baker's tom pattern was inspired by Native American rhythms
The band nearly rejected it as too simple

10-23.title: Which 'Nothing Compares 2 U' wins: Prince or Sinéad?
10-23.story:
Prince wrote it for his side project The Family. Sinéad O'Connor's 1990 version, with its single-shot video, became definitive.

The Family's original is a full band arrangement with saxophone, buried on an album by a Prince side project that lasted one record. Almost nobody heard it, and Prince rarely performed the song himself until after O'Connor's version succeeded.

Her reading strips it to a sparse arrangement and a vocal that moves from restrained to broken over four minutes. Producer Nellee Hooper's arrangement leaves an enormous amount of space, which puts all the weight on the performance.

The video is close to a single continuous shot of her face, and the tears near the end were reportedly not planned — she has said she was thinking about her mother, who had died in 1985. That accident is a large part of why the record landed the way it did.

O'Connor's relationship with fame afterward was adversarial and principled. Her 1992 protest against the Catholic Church on live television cost her enormously at the time and looks quite different now.

She died in 2023. Her account of Prince's own behaviour toward her was, by her telling, frightening — the two never had a comfortable relationship over a song that made them both.
facts: Her tears in the video were reportedly unplanned
Prince rarely performed it before her version succeeded

10-24.title: Bill Withers was making toilet seats for airplanes
10-24.story:
Withers kept his factory job while recording 'Ain't No Sunshine', assuming music would not last. The famous repeated 'I know' was a placeholder.

He was thirty-two, had spent nine years in the Navy, and was working at a factory making aircraft lavatory fittings. He recorded his first album while still employed there, and photographs from the period show him at the studio holding his lunchbox, because he was going to work afterward.

The caution was rational. He had watched the industry chew through people and had no reason to believe he would be an exception, and he kept the job until the record was demonstrably working.

The repeated 'I know' — twenty-six times in a row — was a placeholder. He intended to write a proper verse there and was told by the people in the room, including Booker T. Jones, to leave it. It is now the most memorable thing in the song, and it works because the repetition does something a lyric could not: it enacts the obsessiveness the words are describing.

He left the industry in the mid-eighties after protracted conflict with his label about creative control, and simply stopped. He gave interviews occasionally and declined, for decades, to come back.

He died in 2020.
facts: He meant to write real lyrics there but was told to keep it
He brought his lunchbox to the studio

10-25.title: Miles Davis plugged in and lost half his audience
10-25.story:
'Bitches Brew' used electric instruments and studio editing, alienating purists while inventing fusion.

The electric instruments were only half of it. The more radical decision was structural: producer Teo Macero recorded long, loosely directed sessions and then assembled the album afterward with tape splices, looping passages, repeating sections, and constructing pieces that were never performed continuously by anyone.

That is a rock and pop production method applied to jazz, and to a substantial part of the jazz audience it was a betrayal of the form's founding principle — that a recording documents musicians playing.

Davis was explicit about his motivation. He had watched Sly Stone and Jimi Hendrix reach audiences that jazz was losing, and he had no interest in curating a museum.

The personnel is remarkable in hindsight: Wayne Shorter, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock, John McLaughlin, Joe Zawinul, Jack DeJohnette. Nearly all of them went on to lead the fusion movement the album started.

It sold better than any jazz record he had made and cost him a substantial part of his existing audience.

He did this repeatedly across his career — bebop, cool, modal, fusion — and each time the people who had followed him to the last position objected to the next.
facts: Producer Teo Macero spliced the tapes like a film editor
Long passages were assembled, not performed continuously

10-26.title: Which 'Respect' wins: Otis or Aretha?
10-26.story:
Otis Redding wrote it in 1965 as a working man's plea. Aretha Franklin rebuilt it in 1967 as a demand, adding the spelling hook and her sisters' backing vocals.

The two versions are worth hearing back to back because almost nothing changes on paper. Same title, largely the same words, similar tempo. Redding's is a man coming home from work asking to be treated properly in his own house — the tone is tired and slightly pleading, and the arrangement pushes forward like someone making a case.

Franklin's inverts the power relationship completely. The narrator is not asking. She is stating terms, and the spelled-out hook — invented in the studio with her sisters Carolyn and Erma — functions as an instruction rather than a chorus.

The arrangement does its share. King Curtis's saxophone solo quotes 'When Something Is Wrong with My Baby', the rhythm section drives rather than swings, and the whole thing was built quickly at Atlantic with Jerry Wexler and the Muscle Shoals players.

Redding took it well and appears to have found it funny, joking at Monterey that the girl had taken his song away from him.

Most covers disappear behind the original. This is one of the few cases where the second version became the definitive one, and the first became the interesting footnote.
facts: Redding joked she had stolen the song for good
Aretha's version was cut in a single afternoon session

10-27.title: 'Under Pressure' was a jam nobody planned
10-27.story:
Bowie and Queen were in the same Swiss studio and started improvising. The famous bassline came from John Deacon noodling during a break.

The two acts were working at Mountain Studios in Montreux at the same time, and what began as Bowie dropping in to add backing vocals to something else turned into an all-day improvisation. Neither party arrived with a song.

The origin of the bassline is genuinely disputed. Most accounts credit John Deacon playing it during a break; Brian May has suggested Bowie changed it; Deacon has given differing versions over the years. The likeliest explanation is that nobody was paying attention at the moment it happened because nobody knew it mattered yet.

The vocal was built by a method Bowie proposed: each singer went into the booth without hearing what the other had done, sang over the track, and the results were combined. That is why the two voices overlap and interrupt rather than trading verses politely.

Both parties later expressed reservations about the mix, having run out of patience by the end of the session.

Vanilla Ice used the bassline on 'Ice Ice Baby' in 1990, initially claimed it was different because of an added note, and eventually settled with credit and payment.
facts: Accounts differ on who actually invented the riff
Vanilla Ice later used it and initially denied the resemblance

10-28.title: The producer who never let artists hear playback
10-28.story:
Phil Spector often refused to let performers hear the full mix, keeping the arrangement in his head so no one could argue with it.

The control was total by design. Sessions at Gold Star ran for hours with dozens of musicians playing doubled and tripled parts, and the only person who knew what the finished record would sound like was Spector. Singers frequently cut vocals without hearing the assembled arrangement, which removed any basis on which they could object to it.

That method produced records of genuine power and a working environment that was, by many first-hand accounts, controlling and frightening well before it became criminal.

Darlene Love is the clearest case. Her voice is on records credited to the Crystals and to Bob B. Soxx and the Blue Jeans, and Spector released her performances under whichever group name suited him commercially. She spent years in litigation over royalties and credit and was at one point cleaning houses while hearing her own uncredited voice on the radio at Christmas.

Spector was convicted of the second-degree murder of Lana Clarkson in 2009 and died in prison in 2021.

The records remain in the canon. The people who made them were treated as raw material by a man whose method depended on them not knowing what they were making.
facts: Sessions ran for hours with dozens of players
Darlene Love's voice appeared on records credited to other groups

10-29.title: Grandmaster Flash built his mixer by hand
10-29.story:
Trained in electronics, Flash rigged a crossfader and cue system so he could hear the next record before the crowd did.

The problem he was solving was precise. Kool Herc's technique required switching between two copies of a record at exactly the right moment, and there was no way to check where the second record was without the audience hearing it. Herc did it by eye and by feel, and it was frequently approximate.

Flash had studied electronics at a vocational school, and he wired a preview system — a single-pole double-throw switch feeding a headphone amp — that let him cue the second turntable silently. Parts were salvaged from junked stereos and car audio.

That single capability is the foundation of everything DJs do now. Being able to hear the next record before the crowd is what makes accurate beat-matching possible, and once it was possible, mixing became a craft with a technical standard rather than an approximation.

He built the rest of the vocabulary on top of it: backspinning, punch phrasing, and the clock theory of marking a record so he could find a specific point instantly.

The crossfader as a standard feature on DJ mixers exists because manufacturers eventually copied what he and his contemporaries had already built for themselves.
facts: He soldered parts salvaged from junked stereos
That preview capability made beat-matching possible

10-30.title: Erasmus Hall in Flatbush produced two American icons
10-30.story:
Barbra Streisand and Neil Diamond both sang in the chorus at Erasmus Hall High School on Flatbush Avenue, a short walk from Cortelyou Road. They barely knew each other then.

Erasmus Hall is the oldest secondary school in New York State, founded in 1786 when Flatbush was a Dutch farming village, and the original wooden academy building still stands in the courtyard of the Gothic quadrangle that grew up around it. For most of the twentieth century it was an enormous public high school serving a neighbourhood in constant demographic change, and its alumni list is correspondingly improbable.

Streisand and Diamond overlapped in the choral club without any particular sense of each other. Both have described the connection as a footnote they only found interesting decades later, when they recorded 'You Don't Bring Me Flowers' as a duet in 1978 — a record that reached number one and was itself something of an accident, assembled after a radio programmer spliced their separate solo versions together and listeners demanded the real thing.

The school's cultural output extends well beyond them: Clive Davis, who would sign Bruce Springsteen and Whitney Houston, came through the same building, as did a long list of writers, athletes, and chess players.

It is a useful reminder of what a functioning neighbourhood school produced when the neighbourhood was dense, mixed, and the school was properly funded.
facts: They later recorded the duet 'You Don't Bring Me Flowers' in 1978
Clive Davis, who signed Springsteen and Whitney Houston, also went to Erasmus

10-31.title: The Beatles played Ed Sullivan to 73 million people
10-31.story:
Broadcast from CBS Studio 50 in Manhattan, the performance was watched by roughly 40 percent of America. Crime rates that hour reportedly dipped.

The booking came out of an accident of timing. Sullivan had been at Heathrow in late 1963 and witnessed the crowd chaos around the band's return from Sweden, and he booked them on the strength of the scene rather than the music, which he had not particularly heard.

The scale of the audience was a function of a media environment that no longer exists. Three networks, one time slot, and no way to watch later meant a single broadcast could genuinely reach forty percent of a country at once. Nothing since has been able to concentrate attention that way, which is why the moment gets treated as a turning point rather than a television booking.

The studio had roughly seven hundred seats and received something in the region of fifty thousand ticket requests.

The often-repeated claim about crime dropping during the broadcast is anecdotal and has never been properly substantiated, but it survives because it captures something true about the concentration involved.

The practical consequence was immediate. Within months American labels were signing British guitar bands indiscriminately, and the balance of trade in popular music reversed for the better part of a decade.
facts: The studio received 50,000 ticket requests for 700 seats
Sullivan had booked them after seeing fan chaos at Heathrow

11-01.title: Autotune was invented by an oil industry engineer
11-01.story:
Andy Hildebrand used seismic data math, designed to find oil underground, to detect and correct pitch. He built it as a subtle repair tool.

Hildebrand's previous work involved sending sound waves into the ground and analysing the reflections to map geological structures — a problem of extracting periodic signal from noise. Pitch detection in a human voice is mathematically the same problem, and he realised the autocorrelation techniques transferred directly.

The intended use was invisible repair: nudge a slightly flat note into tune so a good vocal take with one bad syllable does not have to be re-recorded. Used gently it is undetectable, and it has been used gently on a very large proportion of commercial records since.

The famous sound is a misuse. The plugin has a retune speed control, and setting it to its fastest value forces the voice to snap instantly between exact pitches rather than gliding, producing the stepped robotic effect. Hildebrand has said he included the extreme setting as a joke and never expected anyone to use it.

Cher's 'Believe' put it on the radio in 1998, the producers initially claimed it was a vocoder, and T-Pain later built an entire vocal identity on it.

It is now among the most consequential audio tools ever written, and it exists because someone was looking for oil.
facts: Cher's 'Believe' used the extreme setting the inventor called a joke
Hildebrand said he never expected anyone to use it that way

11-02.title: George Harrison's sitar lesson changed rock
11-02.story:
Harrison studied under Ravi Shankar, who insisted he learn properly rather than use the instrument as decoration. Indian modes then filtered into Western pop.

Shankar was a serious classical musician with no particular interest in Western pop and, by his own account, no clear idea who the Beatles were when they were introduced. His condition for teaching was that Harrison approach the instrument as a discipline — sitting properly, learning scales and rhythmic cycles — rather than treating it as an exotic sound to layer onto a rock record.

Harrison had already used sitar decoratively on 'Norwegian Wood', which he later described as fairly rudimentary. The study that followed produced something different: 'Within You Without You' is built on Indian classical structure, features no other Beatle, and uses tabla and dilruba players rather than the band.

The wider consequence was a vocabulary shift. Drones, modal scales that do not resolve the way Western harmony does, and long non-developmental forms entered rock and stayed, feeding directly into psychedelia and later into minimalism's popular reception.

It also opened a long and complicated conversation about appropriation that has not closed. Shankar himself was ambivalent, welcoming the attention to Indian music and frequently exasperated by audiences who treated a centuries-old tradition as a lifestyle accessory.
facts: Shankar initially had no idea who the Beatles were
'Within You Without You' features no other Beatle

11-03.title: Prince's 'Kiss' was a giveaway he took back
11-03.story:
Prince cut a rough acoustic demo and handed it to the funk band Mazarati. Producer David Z stripped it to a dry drum machine, chopped the vocals into stabs and added the falsetto arrangement — and when Prince heard it he took the song back.

The demo was a minute-long acoustic blues sketch, given away casually to a band on his own label because he had no use for it. What David Z did with it amounts to a rewrite by arrangement: he removed the bass entirely, built a bone-dry drum machine pattern with almost no reverb, chopped the backing vocals into rhythmic stabs, and had the vocals sung in falsetto.

The absence of a bassline is the record's defining feature and the reason it sounds like nothing around it. A funk record without low end should not work, and the space where the bass would be is what gives the guitar and the vocal their snap.

Prince heard the finished track, recognised what had happened, and reclaimed the song. Mazarati's backing vocals stayed on his version, which is the compensation they got.

Warner Bros. thought it was too sparse to release as a single and said so. It went to number one.

It is one of the clearest cases in pop of the arrangement, rather than the writing, being the thing that made a song.
facts: Mazarati's backing vocals stayed on the finished Prince record
Warner Bros. initially called it too sparse to be a single; it went to number one

11-04.title: The bassline Paul McCartney built from a mistake
11-04.story:
On 'Paperback Writer', McCartney wanted a bass so loud it would rattle radios. Engineer Ken Townsend rigged a loudspeaker as a microphone to capture the low end, a trick no one had tried.

The physics are simple and slightly absurd. A loudspeaker and a dynamic microphone are the same device running in opposite directions — a diaphragm attached to a coil in a magnetic field. Wire a speaker backwards and it works as a very large, very insensitive microphone with an enormous low-frequency response, which is exactly what a bass cabinet needs and no standard studio microphone could provide.

The motivation was competitive. The Beatles had been listening to American records, particularly Motown and Stax, and were frustrated that their own singles sounded thin by comparison. EMI's engineering rulebook set strict limits on recording levels, largely to protect the cutting lathe, and the band spent much of 1966 finding ways around them.

That pressure produced an unusual amount of invention in a short period: artificial double tracking, backwards guitar, varispeed, tape loops, and the closer microphone placement that gives Revolver its immediacy.

The broader point is that most studio innovation is a workaround. Someone wants a sound the equipment will not produce, and the solution becomes standard practice a few years later.
facts: EMI's rulebook technically forbade the setup
The result was the loudest bass ever pressed to a Beatles single to that point

11-05.title: Brian Eno wrote rules on cards to break writer's block
11-05.story:
Frustrated in the studio, Eno printed 'Oblique Strategies' — cards with instructions like 'Honour thy error as a hidden intention'. Musicians drew one when stuck.

He developed the deck with the painter Peter Schmidt, who had independently been keeping a similar set of written prompts. The two discovered their lists overlapped substantially and combined them into a printed edition, which has been revised several times since.

The cards are deliberately oblique rather than helpful. 'Use an old idea.' 'Change instrument roles.' 'What would your closest friend do?' 'Do nothing for as long as possible.' The point is not that any individual instruction is wise; it is that a random constraint forces a decision, and a decision — even an arbitrary one — breaks the loop of a room full of people relitigating the same choice.

Eno used the deck heavily during his work with David Bowie on the Berlin albums, where several of the more unusual production choices came directly from a drawn card, and it circulated widely among producers afterward.

The underlying idea is older than the cards and has been rediscovered repeatedly: constraint generates invention more reliably than freedom does. A studio with unlimited options and unlimited time produces less interesting work than one with a deadline and a broken piece of equipment.
facts: Bowie used the deck heavily during the Berlin albums
One card simply reads 'Do nothing for as long as possible'

11-06.title: 'I Feel Love' was built almost entirely from a Moog
11-06.story:
Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte built the backing track for Donna Summer at Munich's Musicland using a Moog modular synthesizer instead of a band. The machine drifted out of tune constantly, so the part was captured in short bursts and edited together.

The difficulty was not incidental. Analogue oscillators drift with temperature, and a modular Moog left running would go audibly out of tune within minutes, so the pulsing sixteenth-note bass sequence that defines the record had to be recorded in short usable sections and spliced. Engineer Robby Wedel worked out a way to sync the sequencer to tape — using a click derived from the Moog's own clock — which is what allowed the sequence to hold time across the length of a song at all.

Everything on the track except Summer's voice and a kick drum is synthesized. There is no band.

That matters because it demonstrated an entirely machine-generated dance record could carry a hit vocal, which nobody had shown. The relentless, unvarying pulse is doing something a drummer cannot: it does not breathe, and the lack of human fluctuation is precisely what makes it hypnotic.

Brian Eno's reaction is the most-quoted response in dance music history — he reportedly burst into the studio where he was working with Bowie and announced that this record would change club music for the next fifteen years. He was conservative by about thirty.
facts: Engineer Robby Wedel synced the Moog to tape so the sequence could hold time at all
Brian Eno reportedly told Bowie the record would change club music for the next fifteen years

11-07.title: Why 'Bohemian Rhapsody' took three weeks of overdubs
11-07.story:
Queen layered their vocal harmonies up to 180 times, bouncing tape so often it wore thin. Held to the light, the master was nearly transparent.

The problem was arithmetic. The studio had twenty-four tracks and the opera section needed far more voices than that, so the only route was to record a group of harmonies, mix them down onto a single track to free up space, and record over the top. Every bounce is a generation of tape loss, and the oxide physically degrades where it passes the heads repeatedly.

Freddie Mercury, Brian May, and Roger Taylor sang the operatic passage for something like ten to twelve hours a day across several days, three voices multiplied until they read as a choir. The band has said that holding the tape up to light showed it worn nearly clear.

The song's structure was equally unorthodox: a ballad, an operatic passage, a hard rock section, and a coda, with no chorus and no repeated verse. EMI wanted it shortened for radio and the band refused.

The sleeve noted that no synthesizers were used, which at the time was a point of pride — it was a way of insisting that everything audible had been played or sung by someone in the room, however many times it had been recorded over.
facts: The band sang 10-12 hours a day for the opera section
No synthesizers were used; the album sleeve said so proudly

11-08.title: The Beatles' last live show was on a roof
11-08.story:
With no venue and no plan, the band played atop their Savile Row office. London police shut it down after 42 minutes, which is why the film has an ending.

The rooftop was a decision reached by exhaustion. The Get Back project was meant to end with a live performance and the band had spent weeks rejecting proposals — an amphitheatre in Tunisia, an ocean liner, a Roman venue — until playing on the roof of their own building became the only option nobody objected to strongly enough.

They had not performed publicly since 1966, having given up touring when screaming crowds and inadequate PA systems made it pointless. The rooftop set was therefore the first time in nearly three years that all four played live together, and it was the last.

The sound carried across the West End and stopped traffic. Office workers watched from surrounding buildings. Complaints brought police to the door, and the band kept playing while officers made their way up, which gave the documentary a genuine ending rather than a staged one.

'Get Back' was performed several times across the set. Lennon's closing line — hoping they had passed the audition — is one of the last things the four of them said together in public, and it is funnier and sadder than it was probably meant to be.
facts: Office workers watched from surrounding rooftops
It was the final time all four performed publicly together

11-09.title: Prince changed his name to a symbol to escape a contract
11-09.story:
In a dispute with Warner Bros., Prince adopted an unpronounceable glyph and wrote 'slave' on his face at appearances.

The dispute was about ownership and pace. Prince recorded faster than Warner wanted to release — the label had a commercial interest in spacing albums out and protecting the value of each — and he did not own his master recordings, which meant the catalogue he had made belonged to someone else.

The symbol was a legal manoeuvre as much as a gesture. His contract obligated Prince to deliver albums; an artist with no pronounceable name and a different legal identity complicated the label's ability to market him and made the situation actively expensive.

Warner mailed floppy disks to the press containing a custom font so publications could reproduce the glyph. Most gave up and wrote 'the artist formerly known as Prince'.

Writing 'slave' on his cheek at public appearances was widely mocked at the time, including by people who thought a multi-millionaire had chosen an obscene comparison. The substantive point underneath — that standard recording contracts transferred ownership of an artist's life's work in perpetuity — was one the industry has since had to concede repeatedly.

He regained his masters in 2014. Artists renegotiating master ownership now are working ground he cleared at considerable reputational cost.
facts: Media resorted to calling him 'the artist formerly known as'
Floppy disks with the symbol font were mailed to press

11-10.title: Ditmas Park's block parties keep the sound-system tradition
11-10.story:
Summer street closures along Cortelyou and Rugby Road turned into speaker-stack parties, echoing Caribbean sound-system culture nearby.

The mechanics are bureaucratic and the results are not. A block association applies to the city for a street activity permit, the street closes for a day, and what fills it is determined entirely by who lives there. In this part of Brooklyn that has meant, reliably, speaker stacks and a generator.

The lineage is direct. Central Brooklyn holds one of the largest Caribbean populations outside the islands, and Jamaican sound system practice — the mobile rig, the operator, the bass pushed far past what indoor listening requires — arrived with the migration and never left. A Cortelyou block party is running the same format as a Kingston yard dance, adapted to a street permit.

The housing stock helps. Detached houses with front lawns and porches mean a block can absorb amplified music in a way a wall-to-wall tenement street cannot.

DJs still run generators for outdoor sets because there is no other reliable power, which is its own continuity with the tradition.

It is also, quietly, one of the few remaining occasions when an entire block is outside at the same time and has to negotiate volume, space, and each other in person.
facts: Permits are typically pulled by block associations
DJs still run generators for outdoor sets

11-11.title: Bessie Smith outsold nearly every artist of her era
11-11.story:
Smith's records sold in the hundreds of thousands to Black audiences largely ignored by the mainstream industry.

The commercial scale is the part that gets understated. Her records sold in the hundreds of thousands at a time when the industry had assumed no significant Black record-buying market existed, and her success — following Mamie Smith's 'Crazy Blues' in 1920 — is what created the race records category and the entire structure of Black popular recording that followed.

She toured in her own railroad car, which was both a display of success and a practical necessity: segregated travel across the South made ordinary touring dangerous and frequently impossible, and owning the car meant the company could sleep and move without depending on facilities that would not accept them.

The voice itself required no microphone. She recorded acoustically for much of her career and could fill a tent without amplification, with a power and precision of pitch that is audible even through the limitations of 1920s recording.

Her material was frank about sex, drinking, violence, and independence in ways that later decades became squeamish about.

She died in 1937 after a car accident in Mississippi. The long-repeated story that she was refused treatment at a whites-only hospital appears not to be accurate, though the circumstances of her death were shaped by segregation regardless.
facts: She toured in her own railroad car
Her success proved a market executives had denied existed

11-12.title: Chopin and the piano that never left the room
11-12.story:
Chopin wrote almost exclusively for solo piano, rarely performing in large halls because his playing was too quiet. He preferred salons of a few dozen listeners.

The scale was a genuine limitation rather than an affectation. Contemporaries who heard him in a small room described the playing as extraordinary; those who heard him in a concert hall complained they could barely make it out. He gave roughly thirty public concerts in his entire life, which for a musician of his stature in the nineteenth century is almost nothing, and made most of his income teaching wealthy students.

That setting shaped the music. Writing for a room of forty people rather than a hall of two thousand permits an enormous dynamic range at the quiet end, and Chopin's scores are full of markings that only make sense if the listener is close enough to hear a whisper.

His rubato — the elastic stretching of tempo within a phrase — was described by his pupils with a specific image: the left hand keeps strict time while the right hand moves freely around it, like a tree standing still while its leaves sway. Most modern performances loosen both hands, which is a different effect entirely.

He was born in Poland, left at twenty, and never returned. Almost everything he wrote was composed in exile.
facts: He gave roughly 30 public concerts in his entire life
His pupils described his rubato as 'the tree keeps time, the leaves sway'

11-13.title: Ella Fitzgerald invented her scat by copying horns
11-13.story:
Fitzgerald built solos by imitating trumpet and saxophone lines rather than singing words, turning her voice into a brass instrument.

Scat existed before her, but she systematised it. Rather than treating wordless singing as decoration between verses, she approached a solo the way a horn player would — building lines from the same bebop vocabulary, using the same rhythmic displacement, and phrasing across the bar rather than within it.

She could reproduce recorded solos note for note, which is a skill closer to transcription than to improvisation and which gave her an enormous stock of material to draw on. Her live version of 'How High the Moon' quotes a long string of other melodies inside a single solo, at speed, as an audible joke for anyone tracking it.

The technical prerequisite is intonation. Singing chromatic bebop lines without an instrument to check against requires pitch accuracy that very few singers have, and it is why so few have attempted the approach seriously since.

The Songbook series she recorded for Verve across the late fifties and early sixties — Gershwin, Porter, Ellington, Berlin, and more — did a different kind of work. It gathered the American popular repertoire into a canonical form at exactly the point when rock and roll was displacing it, and largely determined which songs survived as standards.
facts: She could reproduce bebop solos note for note
Her 'Songbook' series helped canonize American standards

11-14.title: Nas recorded 'Illmatic' with four different producers
11-14.story:
Rather than one house sound, Nas invited DJ Premier, Pete Rock, Q-Tip and Large Professor. The album runs under 40 minutes with no filler.

The convention at the time was a single producer or a single crew supplying a coherent sound across an album. Assembling four of the best working producers on one record risked incoherence, and the fact that it does not sound fragmented is largely down to the material — the writing is specific enough to hold the record together regardless of who made the beat.

He was twenty when it came out, writing about the Queensbridge Houses with a level of detail and compression that has kept the album on critics' lists for thirty years. The imagery is dense and the perspective is fixed: it is reportage from one place rather than a career narrative.

The brevity was deliberate. Ten tracks, under forty minutes, with material cut for repeating an idea already covered — at a point when the CD had pushed rap albums toward seventy minutes because the format allowed it. Almost every long album of the era has filler, and this one has none because it refused the space.

It sold modestly at first. Its reputation was built by other rappers, which is generally the more durable route.
facts: He was 20 when it was released
Its brevity was deliberate; he cut anything that repeated an idea

11-15.title: Aretha Franklin was born, and learned in her father's church
11-15.story:
Franklin grew up singing gospel in Detroit under her preacher father, absorbing a call-and-response phrasing she never abandoned in secular music.

C. L. Franklin was a nationally known preacher whose recorded sermons sold well, and the household was a stop for touring gospel musicians. Mahalia Jackson, Clara Ward, and Sam Cooke were present in her childhood, which is an education no conservatory can supply.

What gospel gave her structurally was call and response — a lead line answered by a group, with the answer shaping what the lead does next. That architecture is present in almost all her secular work, and it is why her records feel like an event happening in a room rather than a performance delivered at one.

Her first label got it wrong. Columbia signed her and spent years trying to make her a supper-club pop singer, recording standards with orchestral arrangements that gave her nothing to push against. The records are competent and inert.

The move to Atlantic and to Muscle Shoals in 1967 fixed it in a single session, largely by putting her behind a piano with a rhythm section and letting her lead.

She played piano on a great deal of her own work, which is frequently left out of descriptions of her, and it is a substantial part of why the arrangements sit where they do.
facts: She played piano on many of her own recordings
Her Atlantic breakthrough came after Columbia tried to make her a pop crooner

11-16.title: Which 'Blinded by the Light' wins: Springsteen or Manfred Mann?
11-16.story:
Springsteen's original is a wordy folk-rock rush. Manfred Mann's Earth Band slowed it, changed a lyric and scored the only Springsteen-written US number one.

The original, from Greetings from Asbury Park, is early Springsteen at his most verbally dense — a torrent of internal rhyme delivered at speed, closer to Dylan than to anything he would do later. It sold almost nothing.

Manfred Mann's Earth Band rebuilt it three years later as a prog-inflected arrangement with a long instrumental introduction, a slower tempo, and considerably more space around the words. It went to number one in America.

The famous misheard lyric belongs to that version. Springsteen wrote 'cut loose like a deuce'; Mann sang 'revved up like a deuce', and the combination of the phrasing and the arrangement has produced decades of listeners hearing something anatomical instead.

Springsteen has joked about the situation more than once: the only American number one he has written as a songwriter is a record by somebody else, and it contains a lyric he did not write.

The pairing is a decent argument that tempo is a compositional decision. The words are largely the same and the second version is legible in a way the first is not, simply because the listener is given room to follow it.
facts: Springsteen has joked he never had a chart-topper with his own version
The famous misheard lyric comes from Mann's rewrite

11-17.title: Bo Hansson and the rise of the bedroom studio
11-17.story:
Long before home recording was normal, musicians began assembling private studios, shifting power away from label-owned rooms.

The economics had been fixed for decades. Recording required a studio, a studio cost money by the hour, and the label paid — which meant the label controlled access, scheduling, and ultimately what got made. An artist without a deal had essentially no route to a finished record.

Multitrack tape machines becoming affordable in the seventies broke that. Once a musician could own four or eight tracks, they could work at their own pace, experiment without a meter running, and arrive at a label with something finished rather than a request.

The Swedish keyboardist Bo Hansson is an early and fairly obscure example — his Lord of the Rings album was assembled largely in a private setup — and the pattern repeats through Brian Eno, through eighties four-track cassette recording, through the sampler and the sequencer, and into the laptop.

What changed each time was not sound quality but who was permitted to make a record.

The current end point is that professional-standard production is available on hardware most people already own. The consequence is an enormous increase in supply and a corresponding collapse in the value of distribution, which is the industry's actual problem now.
facts: Multitrack tape became affordable in the seventies
This lineage runs directly to laptop production today

11-18.title: Delia Derbyshire realized the Doctor Who theme with tape
11-18.story:
Working without synthesizers, Derbyshire built the theme by recording single tones, cutting the tape and splicing pitches by hand.

The BBC Radiophonic Workshop had no synthesizers because none existed commercially. What it had was oscillators, tape machines, filters, and an enormous amount of patience, and every sound had to be constructed physically.

Derbyshire's method for the theme was close to insane by modern standards. Individual notes were generated as single tones, recorded to tape, cut to length with a razor, and spliced together in sequence — with the length of each piece of tape determining the duration of the note and the tape speed determining its pitch. Lengths were measured with a ruler.

The bassline, the swooping effects, and the melody were all assembled this way and then synchronised across multiple machines running simultaneously, because there was no multitrack.

Ron Grainer wrote the melody and, on hearing what she had made of it, reportedly asked whether he had written it. He wanted to give her a co-credit and BBC policy prevented it — Workshop staff were not credited as composers. She received no on-screen credit for years.

It is one of the first pieces of electronic music heard weekly by a mass audience, and it was made by cutting up tape with a blade.
facts: Each note was measured with a ruler
She received no on-screen composer credit for years

11-19.title: Which 'Killing Me Softly' wins: Flack or the Fugees?
11-19.story:
Roberta Flack's version is intimate and slow. The Fugees rebuilt it in 1996 over a hip-hop break with Lauryn Hill's lead.

Flack's is the definitive reading for a generation: slow, close, with an arrangement that recedes almost entirely behind the voice.
